===== PDF idx 177 (printed 166) =====
SUPERTRAINING
been established that weightlifters who time their rest intervals carefully make 20% fewer failures than those who 
do not (Klimonov, 1965).
TIME AFTER PRECEDING WORK (mlns)
Figure 3.29 Change in height o f a vertical jump executed after different types of tonic work ( I ■ barbell squat; 2 * take-off after a 
depth jump). (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999).
The deiayed-effect of strength work depends on the volume and intensity of the preceding loads. For example, a 
moderate volume of barbell exercises produces a positive tonic influence on the motor apparatus of athletes on the 
next day or the day after (Diachkov, 1961). The use of depth (plyometric) jumps as a means of stimulation 
delayed this effect for 5-6 days (Verkhoshansky, 1963; Khodykin, 1976).
The use of the after-effect phenomenon offers some interesting opportunities for increasing the effectiveness 
of strength preparation via a more limited volume of training work. Athletes and coaches have great potential for 
creativity, which can significantly enrich the theory and practice of sports training.
3.4.3 Additional Movement
Some experienced coaches judge the mastery of a sprinter by the action of his jaws. If the teeth are clenched and 
the face has a strained expression during a race, then the level of proficiency is regarded as low. If the jaw is 
relaxed and the face is calm, then their movements are fluid and unconstrained and the athlete displays the skill for 
running fast. Although subjective, it is a reasonably accurate evaluation of mastery in cyclic movements when the 
muscles work in a rapid sequence of tension and relaxation. Clinically, this observation would appear to relate, at 
least in part, to the TMJ (tempcro-mandibular joint) syndrome sometimes treated by physical therapists to 
relieve muscular stress in various parts of the body which are distant from the jaw.
However, in acyclic movements requiring the display of powerful force, it is not possible to evaluate 
proficiency in this way. In this case, muscular force is concentrated in a single instantaneous contraction and even 
the anatomical antagonists may function as synergists. Under these conditions, the so-called additional movement 
contributes to raising the working effect. In physiotherapeutic PNF (see 7.2), this phenomenon is regarded as a 
consequence of what is termed overflow or irradiation from stronger to weaker or more fatigued muscles (Knott & 
Voss, 1968).
Muscular activity (an indicator of electrical excitation) is dependent not only on the processes taking place 
within the prime movers, but also on the state of the other muscle groups. Both unloaded and loaded movements 
with large resistance elicit electrical activity in the unexercised musculature of the body (Farfel, 1961; Levin, 1964; 
Sills & Olson, 1958). Furthermore, the strength and endurance of the arm musclcs executing dynamic work 
increase significantly by including other skeletal muscles in the work (Gorbunova & Khabarova, 1955; 
Mukhamedova, 1958). Exercising the muscles on one side of the body causes an increase in strength on the 
unexercised side, i.e., the well-known 'cross training' phenomenon (Wissler & Richardson, 1900; Davis, 1942; 
Hellebrant et al, 1947; Laun, 1954; Enoka, 1988).
Thus, an additional movement which does not serve to increase the economy of the motor action, has a 
specific physiological value and its systematic involvement can be very useful.
The combination of two or several muscle groups involved simultaneously or sequentially offers several 
advantages. Thus, the amount o f force developed by the right arm is significantly influenced by the muscles 
taking part in the additional movement: a momentary contraction of the extensors of the left elbow increases the 
strength and speed of the flexors of the right elbow to a larger degree than a contraction of the left elbow flexors 
(Mukhammedova, 1958). If, during rhythmic flexing of the right arm, the extensors of the left are momentarily
166

===== PDF idx 178 (printed 167) =====
SUPERTRAINING
tensed, then the work capacity of the right arm will increase by 39-42%; if the flexors of the left arm are tensed, it 
will decrease by 8-22%. Tensing the extensors of the left arm after first fatiguing the flexors of the right, increases 
the capacity of the latter to do significantly more work. Tensing the flexors o f the left arm has no effect in this 
case (Popov, 1938).
Thus, the change in the work capacity of one muscle group by recruiting others into the work depends on 
many factors and varies under different circumstances. The athlete's fitness, the type of muscular activity during 
the additional dynamic or static work, as well as a decrease or increase in the load and work rhythm all influence 
the working effect (Vinogradov, 1966). Thus, in the above-mentioned experiments by Mukhammedova, a large 
stimulatory effect is obtained when the additional effort of the left arm reaches 25-33% of that of the right arm.
Finally, results are determined by the functional state of the motor system. Research indicates that, to obtain 
a definite stimulatory effect, the appropriate motor centre in the brain should be in a state of stable excitation and 
reactiveness. The excitation of one neurocentre stimulates this process in the other motor centres, if the latter 
centres become significantly dominant.
Thus, tension in the additional muscle groups increases the excitability of the dominant centre because of the 
afferent impulses coming from them and enhances the effector process in the fundamental muscle groups. The 
basis for this dominance phenomenon is obvious: in the initial stages of work when dominance is still only 
forming, involvement of the other muscle groups will be counter-productive. The effect appears only after some 
time has passed, when dominance has already been established (Shatenstein & Yordanskaya, 1955).
In athletics there are examples where the motor effect is produced (while using additional movement) by the 
dominant centre and by clearly mechanical factors. This is observed in exercises involving a take-off from a 
support using rotary movement (e.g. pole-vaulting). In this case the concentration of muscular excitation, which 
is crucial for rotational acceleration of the body's links, enhances excitation of the dominant centre, thereby 
involving the key element of the take-off, namely the action of the extensor muscles. At the same time, reactive 
force resulting from muscle stretching during the amortisation phase increases the power of the muscles executing 
the take-off (for example, by an average of 25% in the vertical jump). Thus, additional movement is an example 
of the body's adaptive capability, playing a useful role when it becomes necessary to produce maximal tension. 
Clearly, it has a place in strength training.
3.4.4 Preparatory M ovem ent
If one attempts to execute a vertical jump from a half-squat position, it will become immediately obvious that this 
is very difficult without a preliminary movement. Considerable muscle tension will be needed to restrain the 
natural preparatory movement which man consciously or unconsciously resorts to each time he is preparing to 
execute an action requiring the production of significant force.
The preparatory movement is different in each specific case, depending upon the situation and the given 
motor task. However, the objective is still the same, i.e. to increase the working range and prepare the muscles for 
a more powerful effort. The latter is accomplished by stretching the muscles, which produces a strong motor 
impulse via the myotatic reflex and creates additional elastic tension.
The fact that preliminary muscular tension precedes an effort requiring the intense production of strength has 
been noted in several investigations using EMG analysis (Salchenko, 1960; Kotelnikov, 1966; Popov, 1968; 
Asmussen & Bonde-Peterson, 1974). Obviously one should not conclude that preliminary muscle tension is 
always necessary for the execution of exercises. Preliminary tension can be appropriate if it is well timed and 
immediately precedes the working-effort, or if it is accomplished during the preparatory movement and its 
magnitude is optimal. Thus, it may be appropriate to use preparatory movements when it is necessary to produce 
great strength and speed, as well as to enhance the economy of a motor action.
3.4.5 Coordination in Muscular Work

# Tensing Additional, Non-Prime-Mover Muscle Groups Can Raise or Lower Working-Limb Force

**What it is** — In acyclic movements that require a single instantaneous maximal
contraction (so proficiency cannot be judged by the fluid tension-relaxation sequencing
used in cyclic movements, unlike the jaw-tension example the authors give for judging a
sprinter's mastery), deliberately involving additional muscle groups not directly needed
for the task, an "additional movement," can change the working effect. The authors
attribute this to "overflow" or "irradiation" from stronger to weaker or more fatigued
muscles, a concept from PNF (Knott & Voss, 1968), plus excitation of the dominant motor
centre by afferent impulses from the additional muscle groups, which raises effector-process
excitability in the prime-mover muscle groups. Concrete numbers (Mukhammedova, 1958): during
rhythmic flexing of the right arm, momentarily tensing the left elbow's extensors raised
right-arm flexor work capacity by 39-42%, while tensing the left elbow's flexors after first
fatiguing the right flexors increased the right's capacity to do more work; tensing the left
flexors alone (without prior right-arm fatigue) decreased right-arm work capacity by 8-22%.
A large stimulatory effect appeared when the left arm's additional effort reached 25-33% of
the right arm's effort. Separately, the authors cite the unexercised-limb "cross-training"
phenomenon (training one side of the body increases strength on the unexercised side):
Wissler & Richardson, 1900; Davis, 1942; Hellebrant et al, 1947; Laun, 1954; Enoka, 1988.
(PDF p. 177, printed p. 166, "3.4.3 Additional Movement.")

**Why it works** — The authors give the mechanism directly: afferent impulses from the
additional muscle groups raise excitability of the dominant motor centre, which is
counter-productive early in an effort (before dominance has formed) but becomes
stimulatory once dominance is established (Shatenstein & Yordanskaya, 1955). They also
note the size and direction of the effect depends on the athlete's fitness, the type of
additional activity (dynamic vs static), and changes in load or work rhythm (Vinogradov,
1966), so this is not a fixed-magnitude effect.

**When NOT to apply** — The quantified numbers come from one small, dated lab study of
contralateral elbow flexion/extension (Mukhammedova, 1958), not from a validated training
method; the direction of the effect (raise vs lower) depends on which muscle group is
tensed and when, so "add tension elsewhere" is not a safe blanket cue. The authors' own
timing caveat matters: involving other muscle groups before the prime-mover motor centre
has established dominance in that effort "will be counter-productive." The book gives no
applied strength-training protocol built on this effect, only the underlying phenomenon
and its role in athletics (they mention pole-vault takeoff as an example of mechanically,
not just neurally, mediated additional movement).

**Example** — Inference: a coach cueing a lifter to actively grip and brace with the
non-working hand or forearm during a heavy unilateral press or pull, once the lifter is
already committed to the effort, is consistent with the irradiation effect raising
prime-mover output; the book gives no such applied strength-training example itself.

**Related** — [[claim--bilateral-deficit-and-limb-training-specificity]] (Ch1, a different
cross-limb neural phenomenon: bilateral force deficit vs this irradiation/cross-education
effect; both concern neural interaction between limbs but are not the same mechanism).

14	# Skilled Lifters Spend Less Energy per Lift, and Discrete Singles Cost More Than a Continuous Set
15	
16	**What it is** — Based on Vorobyev's (1978) weightlifting data (Tables 3.10-3.12), energy
17	expenditure in resistance training varies with bodymass, exercise, and skill level. Rate of
18	energy expenditure (kJ/min, Table 3.10) rises with bodymass class (from 9.9 kJ/min for
19	Class I-II lifters in the 56 kg division to 23.0 kJ/min in the >90 kg division) and is
20	lower at the same bodymass division for Masters of Sport than for Class I-III lifters.
21	Absolute energy expenditure for a 1RM attempt (kcal, Table 3.12) is generally lower for
22	"elite" lifters than for lower-ranked ("ranked") lifters on the same exercise: e.g. clean
23	and jerk, 13.7 kcal (elite) vs 15.5 kcal (ranked); bench press, 8.4 vs 12.2 kcal. (One
24	exception visible in the table but not discussed by the authors: front squat runs slightly
25	higher for elite lifters than ranked, 12.7 vs 11.8 kcal.) Relative to bodymass (Table 3.11),
26	the clean and jerk is the most economical major lift and the press from the rack the most
27	expensive, because its prime movers are the comparatively small arm muscles rather than
28	the large muscle mass used in the clean and jerk. Separately, and independent of the skill
29	tables: the specific energy expenditure of a series of single repetitions performed with
30	rest between each (an "interval" style) is 35% greater than a continuous set of several
31	repetitions with the same load. (PDF pp. 179-180, printed pp. 168-169, "3.4.6 Efficiency of
32	Energy Expenditure," Tables 3.10-3.12, Fig 3.30.)
33	
34	**Why it works** — The authors give the mechanism for the interval-vs-continuous finding
35	directly: continuous-style exercise (as in traditional bodybuilding or circuit training)
36	relies more heavily on momentum and on elastic energy stored in the tendons between
37	repetitions, and minimizes the amount of eccentric, starting-strength, and isometric work,
38	all of which raise the metabolic cost of a discrete single repetition performed from a dead
39	stop. Improving movement efficiency (skill) is described as reducing energy cost for any
40	level of strength, speed-strength, strength-endurance, or other fitness component; the

# Skilled Lifters Spend Less Energy per Lift, and Discrete Singles Cost More Than a Continuous Set

**What it is** — Based on Vorobyev's (1978) weightlifting data (Tables 3.10-3.12), energy
expenditure in resistance training varies with bodymass, exercise, and skill level. Rate of
energy expenditure (kJ/min, Table 3.10) rises with bodymass class (from 9.9 kJ/min for
Class I-II lifters in the 56 kg division to 23.0 kJ/min in the >90 kg division) and is
lower at the same bodymass division for Masters of Sport than for Class I-III lifters.
Absolute energy expenditure for a 1RM attempt (kcal, Table 3.12) is generally lower for
"elite" lifters than for lower-ranked ("ranked") lifters on the same exercise: e.g. clean
and jerk, 13.7 kcal (elite) vs 15.5 kcal (ranked); bench press, 8.4 vs 12.2 kcal. (One
exception visible in the table but not discussed by the authors: front squat runs slightly
higher for elite lifters than ranked, 12.7 vs 11.8 kcal.) Relative to bodymass (Table 3.11),
the clean and jerk is the most economical major lift and the press from the rack the most
expensive, because its prime movers are the comparatively small arm muscles rather than
the large muscle mass used in the clean and jerk. Separately, and independent of the skill
tables: the specific energy expenditure of a series of single repetitions performed with
rest between each (an "interval" style) is 35% greater than a continuous set of several
repetitions with the same load. (PDF pp. 179-180, printed pp. 168-169, "3.4.6 Efficiency of
Energy Expenditure," Tables 3.10-3.12, Fig 3.30.)

**Why it works** — The authors give the mechanism for the interval-vs-continuous finding
directly: continuous-style exercise (as in traditional bodybuilding or circuit training)
relies more heavily on momentum and on elastic energy stored in the tendons between
repetitions, and minimizes the amount of eccentric, starting-strength, and isometric work,
all of which raise the metabolic cost of a discrete single repetition performed from a dead
stop. Improving movement efficiency (skill) is described as reducing energy cost for any
level of strength, speed-strength, strength-endurance, or other fitness component; the
authors give no mechanism for why skill specifically lowers per-lift energy cost beyond
this general efficiency claim.

**When to apply** — Use this to caution against summing kcal or kJ figures across exercise
types to compare training-session cost, and to expect that the same external load performed
as discrete singles with rest between reps (e.g., cluster sets) is more metabolically
demanding per repetition than the same reps done continuously.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors explicitly warn that "a simplistic calculation of
energy expenditure... can be very misleading" because it fails to account for rest
intervals between exercises or the interaction of successive training sessions; two
sessions should not be treated as equivalent training stress just because their summed
energy expenditure is similar. The skill/bodymass tables are single-lab, Soviet-era
weightlifting data (Vorobyev, 1978) specific to the snatch, clean and jerk, and their
component pulls and presses; they are not established as generalizable to other lifts or
populations.

**Example** — Inference: cluster sets (discrete reps with intra-set rest at a fixed load)
likely impose a higher energy cost per repetition than the same reps performed continuously,
consistent with the 35% figure above, though the book presents no cluster-set experiment
itself.

**Related** — None found in the staging library or vault on this specific angle
(skill-linked lifting economy); flagged for a reciprocal link if a future entry on cluster
sets or lifting economy is added.

14	# Emotional State, Hypnosis, and an Audience Can Each Change Measured Strength
15	
16	**What it is** — The authors report several psychological effects on strength expression,
17	each from a single old citation with no modern replication given. Strong positive emotions
18	can immediately increase the energy of muscular contraction by as much as four times
19	(Vinogradov, 1966). Under certain conditions, hypnosis has been shown to increase muscular
20	strength by 22.5% and to decrease it by 31.7% (Ikai & Steinhaus, 1961); the authors give no
21	detail on what conditions produced which direction. Group activities produce greater results
22	than individual activities (Gurnee, 1937; Abel, 1938; Weyner & Zeaman, 1956; Beasley, 1958;
23	Cratty, 1965). The presence of spectators also increases the effectiveness of motor activity
24	(Gates, 1924; Lazaruc et al, 1952; Cratty & Hutten, 1964), with novices showing a
25	significantly greater improvement from an audience than advanced athletes (Singer, 1965).
26	The authors' summary: "carefully directed training creates a specific emotional background
27	which makes strength work more productive." (PDF p. 182, printed p. 171, "3.4.7 Emotion and
28	Other Psychological Factors.")
29	
30	**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism connecting emotion, hypnosis, or social
31	presence to measured force output beyond naming the findings themselves. Inference: these
32	are most plausibly framed as changes in voluntary activation or willingness to approach the
33	true physiological ceiling (raising the "expressed" fraction of maximal strength) rather
34	than a change in the muscle's underlying contractile capacity, but the source does not state
35	this explanation.
36	
37	**When NOT to apply** — Every figure here rests on a single citation from 1924-1965, with
38	no magnitude-reproducing modern study named; do not treat the 22.5%/31.7% hypnosis figures
39	or the fourfold emotion figure as established, reproducible effect sizes. Hypnosis for
40	performance manipulation is not a documented Baylor Applied Performance or Athletic
41	Performance practice and raises consent and oversight questions this source does not
42	address; this entry documents the claim, it does not endorse using hypnosis as an
43	intervention. The social-facilitation effect is explicitly reported as larger in novices
44	than advanced athletes, so it should not be assumed to transfer to elite competitors
45	unchanged.
46	
47	**Example** — Inference: a coach who has observed that certain athletes perform noticeably
48	better in a full weight room with teammates present than alone is consistent with the
49	group/spectator findings above, though the book gives no team-sport or strength-training
50	example of its own.

# Emotional State, Hypnosis, and an Audience Can Each Change Measured Strength

**What it is** — The authors report several psychological effects on strength expression,
each from a single old citation with no modern replication given. Strong positive emotions
can immediately increase the energy of muscular contraction by as much as four times
(Vinogradov, 1966). Under certain conditions, hypnosis has been shown to increase muscular
strength by 22.5% and to decrease it by 31.7% (Ikai & Steinhaus, 1961); the authors give no
detail on what conditions produced which direction. Group activities produce greater results
than individual activities (Gurnee, 1937; Abel, 1938; Weyner & Zeaman, 1956; Beasley, 1958;
Cratty, 1965). The presence of spectators also increases the effectiveness of motor activity
(Gates, 1924; Lazaruc et al, 1952; Cratty & Hutten, 1964), with novices showing a
significantly greater improvement from an audience than advanced athletes (Singer, 1965).
The authors' summary: "carefully directed training creates a specific emotional background
which makes strength work more productive." (PDF p. 182, printed p. 171, "3.4.7 Emotion and
Other Psychological Factors.")

**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism connecting emotion, hypnosis, or social
presence to measured force output beyond naming the findings themselves. Inference: these
are most plausibly framed as changes in voluntary activation or willingness to approach the
true physiological ceiling (raising the "expressed" fraction of maximal strength) rather
than a change in the muscle's underlying contractile capacity, but the source does not state
this explanation.

**When NOT to apply** — Every figure here rests on a single citation from 1924-1965, with
no magnitude-reproducing modern study named; do not treat the 22.5%/31.7% hypnosis figures
or the fourfold emotion figure as established, reproducible effect sizes. Hypnosis for
performance manipulation is not a documented Baylor Applied Performance or Athletic
Performance practice and raises consent and oversight questions this source does not
address; this entry documents the claim, it does not endorse using hypnosis as an
intervention. The social-facilitation effect is explicitly reported as larger in novices
than advanced athletes, so it should not be assumed to transfer to elite competitors
unchanged.

**Example** — Inference: a coach who has observed that certain athletes perform noticeably
better in a full weight room with teammates present than alone is consistent with the
group/spectator findings above, though the book gives no team-sport or strength-training
example of its own.

**Related** — None found in the staging library or vault; this is a distinct angle from
[[heuristic--instruction-type-and-verbal-framing-shape-strength-output]] (same source
subsection, coaching-instruction effects rather than emotional/social state effects).

(Zimkin, 1962; Korobova, 1964). Well-prepared athletes use only those combinations which enable them to use 
their motor potential most efficiently.
Changes in the character of muscular activity during the execution of movement can occur in several forms 
(Averianov, 1963; Moikin, 1964):
• changc in the sequence of different muscle groups participating in the movement
• change in the number of muscle groups participating in the movement
• change in the relative degree of participation of different muscles in the movement.
In cyclic movements, the duration of the active and relative rest phases changes (Kuchin, I960; Ratishvili, 1966), 
and the maximal contribution shifts from one group of muscles to another (Lazareva, 1966; Absalyamov, 1968).
Movements associated with overcoming large resistance or executed with great speed characteristically switch 
the activity to the muscles o f the proximal links (Ivanitsky, 1956; Lebedev, 1962; Moikin, 1964), as well as 
produce a differentiation in the activity of different parts of the muscle (Averianov & Shibanov, 1964).
In complex multi-joint movements, the resulting force does not equal the sum of the individual maximum 
tensions of which each of the contributing muscle groups is capable. For example, the largest summatcd force 
which a rower develops is at the beginning of the movement, although at this instant the legs are working at an 
disadvantageous angle in the knee and hip joints (Table 3.9). However, the percentage utilisation of absolute 
strength (the sum of the maximum force that the muscles of the arms, torso and legs develop individually) is 
largest at this moment (Egorov, 1966). 
Thus, the disadvantageous conditions for the work of one muscle can be 
compensated for by the more advantageous conditions for another’s work through the effective coordination of 
contributory actions (in this instance, the back muscles).

The most important aspect of muscular coordination in spced-strength exercises is the increase in force at 
biomechanically crucial stages of the movement. In particular, one of the most typical characteristics of motor 
skills will be the increase in muscular force where the dynamic emphasis is necessary in a complex motor act to 
raise its total working effect.
3.4.6 Efficiency of Energy Expenditure
The efficiency with which an athlete executes a given movement has a profound effect on the functional use of 
strength, specd-strength, strength-endurance and all other components of fitness. Energy expenditure in any 
individual is affected not only by neuromuscular efficiency, but also by factors such as bodymass and type of 
exercise.
For instance, after the warm-up, the rate of energy expenditure of Class I-III weightlifters varies from under 8 
kjoulcs/min in the 56 kg division to over 23 kJ/min in the +110kg division, while the mean energy expenditure for 
Class I-III weightlifters across all bodymass divisions is 14.8 kJ/min (see Table 3.10). Energy expenditure tends 
to decrease with increasing level of sports proficiency, thereby emphasizing the importance of improving 
movement skills in physical training. Tables 3.10 and 3.11 show clearly that elite competitors generally use 
energy more economically than lower ranked athletes. The last column of Table 3.11 reveals that the relative 
energy expenditure (i.e. energy per unit bodymass) is greater for exercises requiring the use o f smaller muscle 
mass.

However, a simplistic calculation of energy expenditure as given in popular athletic training or body weight 
reduction books can be very misleading, because they usually fail to take into account the effect of rest intervals 
between exercises or the interaction of successive training sessions. For instance, we are not justified in equating 
ihe effects o f two different types o f training session just because they may have used virtually identical expenditures 
of energy. One of these sessions may have been for bodybuilding purposes using moderate weights for higher 
repetitions and with short rest periods, whereas the other may have been a pre-contest Olympic weightlifting 
session using near-maximal weights for few repetitions and with long rest periods between repetitions and sets.
Optimal training versus overtraining is not merely the consequence of calculating the appropriate amount of 
energy expended, since so many different bodily systems are involved in the production of work. 
Western 
research has paid scant attention to the differences in energy consumption among athletes of different levels of 
expertise and fatigue, yet charts o f calorific or energy usage in different sports are applied universally and
169

===== PDF idx 181 (printed 170) =====
SUPERTRAINING
unquestioningly. The problems are compounded further by the fact that no research has ever managed to quantilj 
the differences between neural, cardiac and muscular fatigue in any activity.
Overtraining is not a single syndrome and generally is regarded as comprising overload (excessive intensity« 
load) and overuse (excessive work output) types, so it cannot be assessed on the basis o f energy expenditun 
alone. A workout consisting of a few maximal attempts may be elicit an overload type of overtraining far mort 
readily than a much longer workout relying on many sets with moderate weights. Even then, overload maybe 
more a consequence o f inappropriate technique that imposes greater stress (force per unit area) on a bodily 
structure than training with maximal loads. This issue is discussed later in greater depth (Ch 8.7).
The increasing expenditure of energy for the different lifts may be seen more clearly if the information from 
Table 3.12 is expressed graphically (Fig 3.30).
170
The expenditure of energy in heavy resistance training sessions is characterised by short bursts of intense activity 
interspersed with longer rest periods. Unless the training is for muscle endurance, continuous loading over 
prolonged periods is inappropriate and interval training generally is necessary. This is borne out by the fact that, 
during a strength session lasting 1.5-2.5 hours, actual physical work occupies 5-12 minutes. It is also interesting 
to note that the specific energy expenditure for an exercise using a scries of single repetitions is 35% greater than a 
continuous set of several repetitions with the same load.
In other words, interval training with a series o f single concentrated efforts places greater demands on the 
body than continuous training, as done in traditional bodybuilding or circuit training. Very often, the continuous 
style of exercising allows one to rely more strongly on momentum and stored clastic energy in the tendons. It also 
tends to minimise the amount of eccentric, starting-strength and isometric training. This explains why it is far 
more difficult to execute a set of bench presses or squats if the load is replaced briefly on the racks between each 
repetition, instead of performing the same number of repetitions continuously.
3.4.7 Em otion and Other Psychological Factors
Muscular activity, including the display of strength, is not isolated from psychological processes but closely 
related to the individual's motivational level and objective. This objective is the basic reaction of the athlete to the 
situation in which he executes sporting tasks. Characteristically, it prepares one for undertaking a certain activity 
and constitutes a major factor in determining the outcome of all sports performance.
Physiological fitness for action is associated with the sensory receptors, which facilitate an adequate 
perception of stimuli, and via the activation of the motor units, determine muscle action. The motor objective in 
sport, which prepares the athlete's body for the forthcoming action, is influenced by the situation and the 
instructions of the coach, and clearly determines the motor task (Ozolin, 1949; Shoikhet, 1966; Eremin, 1968). 
The formation of such 'tuners' creates the prerequisite for successful performance.
Thus, a preliminary verbal command concerning the heaviness of the load can change the tonus of the 
working muscles. For example, the words 'heavy load' increase the tension in the working muscles of the arm, 
whereas the words 'light load' decrease the tonus of the same muscles (Farfel, 1961). Research has also shown 
that, under certain conditions, hypnosis can increase muscular strength. It can increase strength by 22.5% and 
lower it by 31.7% (Ikai & Steinhaus, 1961). The correct instructions can have a significant effect on strength if

===== PDF idx 182 (printed 171) =====
SUPERTRAINING
they orient the athlete to execute the movement by emphasizing certain characteristics or improve coordination. 
This can ensure the optimal combination of force, speed and amplitude of a speed-strength movement to produce 
the maximum effect for a given functional state.
However, active guidance of the action helps to produce the effective combination more rapidly. Athletes 
•vith little experience execute the take-off after a depth jump more slowly or more quickly than usual (Table 3.13), 
which leads to an increase or a decrease in the height attained, respectively (Verkhoshansky, 1963).
Qualified instruction can ensure the maximal utilisation of force by a more effective distribution of muscular 
effort. For instance, rowers were informed of the magnitude of the force developed by the sum of the action of all 
the muscles during the beginning, middle and end phases of the rowing stroke. Then they were told to repeat the 
effort in these positions by exploiting the force advantages of the relevant muscle groups. All o f the subjects 
increased their strength scores in the rowing phases (Table 3.14), thereby revealing the value of using feedback 
about this sort of information (Egorov, 1966).
These examples indicate the effectiveness of instructions if they are based on the correct dynamic structure of 
the movement. These examples also point to the necessity for taking into consideration the qualification of the 
athlete. Here, it must be noted that the effectiveness of instruction decreases with the increase in qualification, 
since a Master of Sport to a large degree learns to mobilise his potential to a greater extent.
Instructions should always be given with a precise motor aim in mind and be divided into two types: 
ku/im'c(what must be done) and concrete (how it must be done). In other words, heuristic instruction is the 
precise description of the movement’s structure. The athlete is given the task of individually developing his 
specific technique so as to execute it most effectively. Specific instructions concentrate on the appropriate 
method of executing the specific details of the action from the coach's point of view. The combined use of these 
types of instruction by the experienced coach invariably increases the effectiveness of the strength exercises.

The force produced is significantly influenced by emotional state. Strong positive emotions can immediately 
increase the energy of muscular contraction by as much as four times (Vinogradov, 1966). 
In athletics, 
observations have shown that group activities produce greater results than individual activities (Gurnee, 1937; 
Abel, 1938; Weyner & Zeaman, 1956; Beasley, 1958; Cratty, 1965). The presence of spectators also increases the 
effectiveness of the motor activity (Gates, 1924; Lazaruc et al, 1952; Cratty & Hutten, 1964), with novices 
demonstrating a significantly higher level of improvement than advanced athletes (Singer, 1965). Thus, carefully 
directed training creates a specific emotional background which makes strength work more productive.
3.4.8 The Effect of Cold Application
Work ability may be increased by a variety of sensory stimuli, with a significant acute effect being exerted by the 
application of cold to certain parts of the body. The beneficial effects of warming-up have been discussed earlier, 
but it is a little known fact that appropriate use of cold may also have a similar influence, although not as a form 
of pre-exercise preparation.
171

===== PDF idx 183 (printed 172) =====
SUPERTRAINING
For instance, in 1957 Michael concluded that cold showers increase work capacity, an effect which is greater 
among trained athletes than the general public (Vorobyev, 1978). In support of his own experiences with Russian 
weightlifters, Vorobyev quotes the findings of Happ (1947), Rosen (1952) and O'Rolev (1956) which reveal that 
cold compresses laid on the abdomen of athletes during intervals between exercises improved their performance. 
He found similar improvement in performance of weightliftcrs who were sponged down with cold water in the 
intervals between lifts in competition. He suggests that the muscle contraction induced by shivering, increased 
activity of the adrenal glands and a survival-directed central nervous reaction to peripheral excitation contribute to 
producing this effect.
With reference to the above research, it is apparent that the application of cold was brief in each case; 
prolonged exposure to cold which may lower muscle temperature or core temperature obviously is contraindicated 
as an ergogenic aid. The somewhat more prolonged application (5-15 minutes) of cold in the form of ice can be 
very effective in treating muscle and other soft tissue trauma.
3.4.9 Breathing and Strength Production
Normal breathing is an involuntary act to which little attention is paid by the average person. However, the 
pattern, duration and rate of breathing are all factors which can have a profound effect on the production of 
strength in a given situation. For instance, the Valsalva manoeuvre associated with breath-holding plays a vital 
role in increasing the intra-abdominal pressure to support and stabilise the lumbar spine during heavy lifting. The 
importance of strong abdominal and oblique muscles in acting as an anatomical corset then becomes obvious. It 
has been corroborated on many occasions that spinal stress is diminished during any movement against high 
resistance loading and that exhalation during lifting increases the risk of lumbar injury. Thus, it is unwise to 
follow the popular medical advice that one should exhale during effort. While this may be appropriate for patients 
with cardiac disease or hypertension, such action by an athlete during strenuous lifting, squatting or overhead 
pressing can seriously compromise spinal stability and safety. 
1
Moreover, common sporting actions such as jumping, throwing, pushing against an opponent, striking a ball, 
standing from a squat or kicking usually elicit involuntary breath-holding, since this serves to enhance 
performance and accuracy of control in short duration movements. In archery and pistol shooting, stability and 
accuracy are intimately connected with brief phases of breath-holding. Other research has shown that speed* 
strength actions are optimally enhanced if the volume of air in the lungs is maintained at about 75% of their 
maximum capacity (Vorobyev, 1978).
Against this background of information, a study was done to investigate more precisely the relationship 
between the different phases of weightlifting movements and breathing (Blokhin & Monastirskii, 1985). Using a 
group of 34 highly qualified weightlifters, bar movement during the clcan-and-jcrk was recorded biomechanically 
and breathing patterns were monitored with an electronic spirometer. Each athlete was required to perforin

• change in the number of muscle groups participating in the movement

produce a differentiation in the activity of different parts of the muscle (Averianov & Shibanov, 1964).

tensions of which each of the contributing muscle groups is capable. For example, the largest summatcd force 
which a rower develops is at the beginning of the movement, although at this instant the legs are working at an 
disadvantageous angle in the knee and hip joints (Table 3.9). However, the percentage utilisation of absolute 
strength (the sum of the maximum force that the muscles of the arms, torso and legs develop individually) is 
largest at this moment (Egorov, 1966).

compensated for by the more advantageous conditions for another’s work through the effective coordination of 
contributory actions (in this instance, the back muscles).

reduction books can be very misleading, because they usually fail to take into account the effect of rest intervals 
between exercises or the interaction of successive training sessions. For instance, we are not justified in equating 
ihe effects o f two different types o f training session just because they may have used virtually identical expenditures 
of energy. One of these sessions may have been for bodybuilding purposes using moderate weights for higher 
repetitions and with short rest periods, whereas the other may have been a pre-contest Olympic weightlifting 
session using near-maximal weights for few repetitions and with long rest periods between repetitions and sets.
Optimal training versus overtraining is not merely the consequence of calculating the appropriate amount of 
energy expended, since so many different bodily systems are involved in the production of work. 
Western 
research has paid scant attention to the differences in energy consumption among athletes of different levels of 
expertise and fatigue, yet charts o f calorific or energy usage in different sports are applied universally and

Overtraining is not a single syndrome and generally is regarded as comprising overload (excessive intensity« 
load) and overuse (excessive work output) types, so it cannot be assessed on the basis o f energy expenditun 
alone. A workout consisting of a few maximal attempts may be elicit an overload type of overtraining far mort 
readily than a much longer workout relying on many sets with moderate weights. Even then, overload maybe 
more a consequence o f inappropriate technique that imposes greater stress (force per unit area) on a bodily 
structure than training with maximal loads. This issue is discussed later in greater depth (Ch 8.7).

The expenditure of energy in heavy resistance training sessions is characterised by short bursts of intense activity 
interspersed with longer rest periods. Unless the training is for muscle endurance, continuous loading over 
prolonged periods is inappropriate and interval training generally is necessary. This is borne out by the fact that, 
during a strength session lasting 1.5-2.5 hours, actual physical work occupies 5-12 minutes. It is also interesting 
to note that the specific energy expenditure for an exercise using a scries of single repetitions is 35% greater than a 
continuous set of several repetitions with the same load.
In other words, interval training with a series o f single concentrated efforts places greater demands on the 
body than continuous training, as done in traditional bodybuilding or circuit training. Very often, the continuous 
style of exercising allows one to rely more strongly on momentum and stored clastic energy in the tendons. It also 
tends to minimise the amount of eccentric, starting-strength and isometric training. This explains why it is far 
more difficult to execute a set of bench presses or squats if the load is replaced briefly on the racks between each 
repetition, instead of performing the same number of repetitions continuously.
3.4.7 Em otion and Other Psychological Factors
Muscular activity, including the display of strength, is not isolated from psychological processes but closely 
related to the individual's motivational level and objective. This objective is the basic reaction of the athlete to the 
situation in which he executes sporting tasks. Characteristically, it prepares one for undertaking a certain activity 
and constitutes a major factor in determining the outcome of all sports performance.
Physiological fitness for action is associated with the sensory receptors, which facilitate an adequate 
perception of stimuli, and via the activation of the motor units, determine muscle action. The motor objective in 
sport, which prepares the athlete's body for the forthcoming action, is influenced by the situation and the 
instructions of the coach, and clearly determines the motor task (Ozolin, 1949; Shoikhet, 1966; Eremin, 1968). 
The formation of such 'tuners' creates the prerequisite for successful performance.
Thus, a preliminary verbal command concerning the heaviness of the load can change the tonus of the 
working muscles. For example, the words 'heavy load' increase the tension in the working muscles of the arm, 
whereas the words 'light load' decrease the tonus of the same muscles (Farfel, 1961). Research has also shown 
that, under certain conditions, hypnosis can increase muscular strength. It can increase strength by 22.5% and 
lower it by 31.7% (Ikai & Steinhaus, 1961). The correct instructions can have a significant effect on strength if

This can ensure the optimal combination of force, speed and amplitude of a speed-strength movement to produce 
the maximum effect for a given functional state.
However, active guidance of the action helps to produce the effective combination more rapidly. Athletes 
•vith little experience execute the take-off after a depth jump more slowly or more quickly than usual (Table 3.13), 
which leads to an increase or a decrease in the height attained, respectively (Verkhoshansky, 1963).
Qualified instruction can ensure the maximal utilisation of force by a more effective distribution of muscular 
effort. For instance, rowers were informed of the magnitude of the force developed by the sum of the action of all 
the muscles during the beginning, middle and end phases of the rowing stroke. Then they were told to repeat the 
effort in these positions by exploiting the force advantages of the relevant muscle groups. All o f the subjects 
increased their strength scores in the rowing phases (Table 3.14), thereby revealing the value of using feedback 
about this sort of information (Egorov, 1966).
These examples indicate the effectiveness of instructions if they are based on the correct dynamic structure of 
the movement. These examples also point to the necessity for taking into consideration the qualification of the 
athlete. Here, it must be noted that the effectiveness of instruction decreases with the increase in qualification, 
since a Master of Sport to a large degree learns to mobilise his potential to a greater extent.
Instructions should always be given with a precise motor aim in mind and be divided into two types: 
ku/im'c(what must be done) and concrete (how it must be done). In other words, heuristic instruction is the 
precise description of the movement’s structure. The athlete is given the task of individually developing his 
specific technique so as to execute it most effectively. Specific instructions concentrate on the appropriate 
method of executing the specific details of the action from the coach's point of view. The combined use of these 
types of instruction by the experienced coach invariably increases the effectiveness of the strength exercises.

expenditure in resistance training varies with bodymass, exercise, and skill level. Rate of

"elite" lifters than for lower-ranked ("ranked") lifters on the same exercise: e.g. clean

higher for elite lifters than ranked, 12.7 vs 11.8 kcal.) Relative to bodymass (Table 3.11),

expensive, because its prime movers are the comparatively small arm muscles rather than

tables: the specific energy expenditure of a series of single repetitions performed with
rest between each (an "interval" style) is 35% greater than a continuous set of several
repetitions with the same load. (PDF pp. 179-180, printed pp. 168-169, "3.4.6 Efficiency of
Energy Expenditure," Tables 3.10-3.12, Fig 3.30.)

# Skilled Lifters Spend Less Energy per Lift, and Discrete Singles Cost More Than a Continuous Set

**What it is** — Based on Vorobyev's (1978) weightlifting data (Tables 3.10-3.12), energy
expenditure in resistance training varies with bodymass, exercise, and skill level. Rate of
energy expenditure (kJ/min, Table 3.10) rises with bodymass class (from 9.9 kJ/min for
Class I-II lifters in the 56 kg division to 23.0 kJ/min in the >90 kg division) and is
lower at the same bodymass division for Masters of Sport than for Class I-III lifters.
Absolute energy expenditure for a 1RM attempt (kcal, Table 3.12) is generally lower for
"elite" lifters than for lower-ranked ("ranked") lifters on the same exercise: e.g. clean
and jerk, 13.7 kcal (elite) vs 15.5 kcal (ranked); bench press, 8.4 vs 12.2 kcal. (One
exception visible in the table but not discussed by the authors: front squat runs slightly
higher for elite lifters than ranked, 12.7 vs 11.8 kcal.) Relative to bodymass (Table 3.11),
the clean and jerk is the most economical major lift and the press from the rack the most
expensive, because its prime movers are the comparatively small arm muscles rather than
the large muscle mass used in the clean and jerk. Separately, and independent of the skill
tables: the specific energy expenditure of a series of single repetitions performed with
rest between each (an "interval" style) is 35% greater than a continuous set of several
repetitions with the same load. (PDF pp. 179-180, printed pp. 168-169, "3.4.6 Efficiency of
Energy Expenditure," Tables 3.10-3.12, Fig 3.30.)

**Why it works** — The authors give the mechanism for the interval-vs-continuous finding
directly: continuous-style exercise (as in traditional bodybuilding or circuit training)
relies more heavily on momentum and on elastic energy stored in the tendons between
repetitions, and minimizes the amount of eccentric, starting-strength, and isometric work,
all of which raise the metabolic cost of a discrete single repetition performed from a dead
stop. Improving movement efficiency (skill) is described as reducing energy cost for any
level of strength, speed-strength, strength-endurance, or other fitness component; the
authors give no mechanism for why skill specifically lowers per-lift energy cost beyond
this general efficiency claim.

**When to apply** — Use this to caution against summing kcal or kJ figures across exercise
types to compare training-session cost, and to expect that the same external load performed
as discrete singles with rest between reps (e.g., cluster sets) is more metabolically
demanding per repetition than the same reps done continuously.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors explicitly warn that "a simplistic calculation of
energy expenditure... can be very misleading" because it fails to account for rest
intervals between exercises or the interaction of successive training sessions; two
sessions should not be treated as equivalent training stress just because their summed
energy expenditure is similar. The skill/bodymass tables are single-lab, Soviet-era
weightlifting data (Vorobyev, 1978) specific to the snatch, clean and jerk, and their
component pulls and presses; they are not established as generalizable to other lifts or
populations.

**Example** — Inference: cluster sets (discrete reps with intra-set rest at a fixed load)
likely impose a higher energy cost per repetition than the same reps performed continuously,
consistent with the 35% figure above, though the book presents no cluster-set experiment
itself.

(skill-linked lifting economy); flagged for a reciprocal link if a future entry on cluster
sets or lifting economy is added.

14	# Brief Cold Exposure May Raise Work Capacity; Prolonged Cold Is Contraindicated as an Ergogenic Aid
15	
16	**What it is** — The authors report that brief application of cold to the body can
17	increase work capacity, citing Michael (1957, via Vorobyev, 1978): cold showers increase
18	work capacity, more so in trained athletes than in the general public. In support, the
19	authors cite older findings (Happ, 1947; Rosen, 1952; O'Rolev, 1956) that cold compresses
20	applied to the abdomen between exercise sets improved performance, and report a similar
21	improvement when Russian weightlifters were sponged with cold water between competition
22	lifts. The application described in every cited case was brief. Prolonged cold exposure
23	that lowers muscle or core temperature is explicitly described as contraindicated as an
24	ergogenic aid. A longer cold application (5-15 minutes, typically ice) is named as
25	effective for a different purpose: treating muscle and other soft-tissue trauma, not
26	boosting performance. (PDF pp. 182-183, printed pp. 171-172, "3.4.8 The Effect of Cold
27	Application.")
28	
29	**Why it works** — The source presents this as Vorobyev's own suggested explanation, not
30	an established mechanism: the muscle contraction induced by shivering, increased adrenal

# Brief Cold Exposure May Raise Work Capacity; Prolonged Cold Is Contraindicated as an Ergogenic Aid

**What it is** — The authors report that brief application of cold to the body can
increase work capacity, citing Michael (1957, via Vorobyev, 1978): cold showers increase
work capacity, more so in trained athletes than in the general public. In support, the
authors cite older findings (Happ, 1947; Rosen, 1952; O'Rolev, 1956) that cold compresses
applied to the abdomen between exercise sets improved performance, and report a similar
improvement when Russian weightlifters were sponged with cold water between competition
lifts. The application described in every cited case was brief. Prolonged cold exposure
that lowers muscle or core temperature is explicitly described as contraindicated as an
ergogenic aid. A longer cold application (5-15 minutes, typically ice) is named as
effective for a different purpose: treating muscle and other soft-tissue trauma, not
boosting performance. (PDF pp. 182-183, printed pp. 171-172, "3.4.8 The Effect of Cold
Application.")

**Why it works** — The source presents this as Vorobyev's own suggested explanation, not
an established mechanism: the muscle contraction induced by shivering, increased adrenal
gland activity, and a survival-directed central nervous system reaction to peripheral cold
stimulation. The authors do not independently verify this mechanism; it is reported as a
proposed explanation, not a demonstrated one.

**When to apply** — As a brief, targeted stimulus (cold shower, localized cold compress, or
cold sponging) between sets or attempts in a competition or training setting where a
trained athlete's work capacity needs a short-term lift, consistent with the cited findings.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use prolonged cold exposure, or any application that lowers
muscle or core temperature, as a pre-performance or between-set strategy; the source states
this directly as contraindicated. The supporting citations are old (1947-1965) and largely
single-source per claim, with no magnitude or dose-response data given (how brief is
"brief," how cold is "cold"). The proposed mechanism is the source's own conjecture, not
independently tested within this text. This entry is about acute work-capacity effects, not
about cold application for recovery or injury treatment, which the source treats as a
separate, longer-duration use.

**Example** — Inference: a brief cold-water face or forearm splash between attempts at a
competition, rather than an ice bath or prolonged cold-water immersion beforehand, is the
kind of application consistent with the cited findings; the book gives no specific modern
protocol.

**Related** — None found in the staging library or vault on acute cold exposure and work
capacity specifically (distinct from post-exercise cold-water immersion for recovery,
which this entry does not address).

# Split Instruction into "Heuristic" (What) and "Concrete" (How), and Expect Less Return from It as Athletes Advance

**What it is** — The authors give two applied findings about verbal coaching input and
strength expression. First, a preliminary verbal command about the perceived heaviness of
a load can change the tonus of the working muscles without changing the actual load: the
words "heavy load" increase tension in the working arm muscles and "light load" decrease it
(Farfel, 1961). Second, instruction should always target a precise motor aim and can be
divided into two types: **heuristic** instruction (what must be done, leaving the athlete
to individually develop the specific technique to accomplish the task) and **concrete**
instruction (how it must be done, the coach specifying the execution details). The combined
use of both types by an experienced coach increases the effectiveness of strength exercises.
Active, qualified guidance produces the optimal force-speed-amplitude combination for a
speed-strength movement faster than unguided practice; the authors cite a depth-jump takeoff
study (Table 3.13, Verkhoshansky, 1963) where less experienced athletes executing the
takeoff faster or slower than usual changed jump height, and a rowing-feedback study
(Table 3.14, Egorov, 1966) where telling rowers the actual force contribution of each
phase of the stroke raised their stroke force scores across all skill classes. The authors
state that instruction effectiveness decreases as athlete qualification rises, because a
Master of Sport learns, to a large degree, to mobilise their own potential. (PDF pp.
181-182, printed pp. 170-171, "3.4.7 Emotion and Other Psychological Factors.")

**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism for the verbal-framing effect beyond
citing the finding itself (Farfel, 1961). Inference: the load-framing result implies verbal
cues can shift motor-unit recruitment or intended effort independent of the true
mechanical demand, which is consistent with why coaches' language during a lift ("this one's
heavy") is not neutral.

**When to apply** — Pair heuristic instruction (state the outcome: "get the bar moving as
fast as possible off the chest") with concrete instruction (specify execution: "keep your
elbows under the bar") deliberately, rather than defaulting to only one type. Expect
outcome-based feedback about actual force or timing (as in the rowing example) to improve
execution even in already-trained athletes.

**When NOT to apply** — The qualification-effectiveness claim ("effectiveness of
instruction decreases with the increase in qualification") is stated without a quantified
threshold or citation of its own; treat it as the authors' generalization, not a measured
result. The supporting studies (Table 3.13, Table 3.14) are single-lab Soviet
weightlifting/rowing data collected in testing or lab settings, not shown as a
longitudinal training method. The verbal-framing finding (Farfel, 1961) is a single old
citation with no magnitude given, only direction.

**Example** — Inference: telling a lifter "this set is your top set, make it fast" versus
"this is a light warm-up" for the same actual %1RM could, per the Farfel finding, shift bar
speed or perceived effort independent of the load itself; the book gives no strength-training
example of this specific kind.

**Related** — [[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]] (Ch1,
also connects training-age to how much a variable, there programming complexity, here
coaching instruction, needs to be managed for less-trained athletes).

# Split Instruction into "Heuristic" (What) and "Concrete" (How), and Expect Less Return from It as Athletes Advance

**What it is** — The authors give two applied findings about verbal coaching input and
strength expression. First, a preliminary verbal command about the perceived heaviness of
a load can change the tonus of the working muscles without changing the actual load: the
words "heavy load" increase tension in the working arm muscles and "light load" decrease it
(Farfel, 1961). Second, instruction should always target a precise motor aim and can be
divided into two types: **heuristic** instruction (what must be done, leaving the athlete
to individually develop the specific technique to accomplish the task) and **concrete**
instruction (how it must be done, the coach specifying the execution details). The combined
use of both types by an experienced coach increases the effectiveness of strength exercises.
Active, qualified guidance produces the optimal force-speed-amplitude combination for a
speed-strength movement faster than unguided practice; the authors cite a depth-jump takeoff
study (Table 3.13, Verkhoshansky, 1963) where less experienced athletes executing the
takeoff faster or slower than usual changed jump height, and a rowing-feedback study
(Table 3.14, Egorov, 1966) where telling rowers the actual force contribution of each
phase of the stroke raised their stroke force scores across all skill classes. The authors
state that instruction effectiveness decreases as athlete qualification rises, because a
Master of Sport learns, to a large degree, to mobilise their own potential. (PDF pp.
181-182, printed pp. 170-171, "3.4.7 Emotion and Other Psychological Factors.")

**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism for the verbal-framing effect beyond
citing the finding itself (Farfel, 1961). Inference: the load-framing result implies verbal
cues can shift motor-unit recruitment or intended effort independent of the true
mechanical demand, which is consistent with why coaches' language during a lift ("this one's
heavy") is not neutral.

**When to apply** — Inference: pair heuristic instruction (state the outcome, e.g. "get the
bar moving as fast as possible off the chest") with concrete instruction (specify
execution, e.g. "keep your elbows under the bar") deliberately, rather than defaulting to
only one type; the book gives no cue examples of its own. Expect outcome-based feedback
about actual force or timing (as in the rowing example) to improve execution even in
already-trained athletes.

**When NOT to apply** — The qualification-effectiveness claim ("effectiveness of
instruction decreases with the increase in qualification") is stated without a quantified
threshold or citation of its own; treat it as the authors' generalization, not a measured
result. The supporting studies are single-lab Soviet depth-jump take-off (Table 3.13) and
rowing (Table 3.14) data collected in testing or lab settings, not shown as a longitudinal
training method. The verbal-framing finding (Farfel, 1961) is a single old citation with no
magnitude given, only direction.

**Example** — Inference: telling a lifter "this set is your top set, make it fast" versus
"this is a light warm-up" for the same actual %1RM could, per the Farfel finding, shift bar
speed or perceived effort independent of the load itself; the book gives no strength-training
example of this specific kind.

coaching instruction, needs to be managed for less-trained athletes). Tension: Myszka

intention-calibration` (vault, `skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/`) favour
manipulating the task and constraints over prescriptive "how" cues, which is this book's

# Brief Cold Exposure May Raise Work Capacity; Prolonged Cold Is Contraindicated as an Ergogenic Aid

**What it is** — The authors report that brief application of cold to the body can
increase work capacity, citing Michael (1957, via Vorobyev, 1978): cold showers increase
work capacity, more so in trained athletes than in the general public. In support, the
authors cite older findings (Happ, 1947; Rosen, 1952; O'Rolev, 1956) that cold compresses
applied to the abdomen between exercise sets improved performance, and report a similar
improvement when Russian weightlifters were sponged with cold water between competition
lifts. The application described in every cited case was brief. Prolonged cold exposure
that lowers muscle or core temperature is explicitly described as contraindicated as an
ergogenic aid. A longer cold application (5-15 minutes, typically ice) is named as
effective for a different purpose: treating muscle and other soft-tissue trauma, not
boosting performance. (PDF pp. 182-183, printed pp. 171-172, "3.4.8 The Effect of Cold
Application.")

**Why it works** — The source presents this as Vorobyev's own suggested explanation, not
an established mechanism: the muscle contraction induced by shivering, increased adrenal
gland activity, and a survival-directed central nervous system reaction to peripheral cold
stimulation. The authors do not independently verify this mechanism; it is reported as a
proposed explanation, not a demonstrated one.

**When to apply** — As a brief, targeted stimulus (cold shower, localized cold compress, or
cold sponging) between sets or attempts in a competition or training setting where a
trained athlete's work capacity needs a short-term lift, consistent with the cited findings.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use prolonged cold exposure, or any application that lowers
muscle or core temperature, as a pre-performance or between-set strategy; the source states
this directly as contraindicated. The supporting citations are old (1947-1965) and largely
single-source per claim, with no magnitude or dose-response data given (how brief is
"brief," how cold is "cold"). The proposed mechanism is the source's own conjecture, not
independently tested within this text. This entry is about acute work-capacity effects, not
about cold application for recovery or injury treatment, which the source treats as a
separate, longer-duration use.

**Example** — Inference: a brief cold-water face or forearm splash between attempts at a
competition, rather than an ice bath or prolonged cold-water immersion beforehand, is the
kind of application consistent with the cited findings; the book gives no specific modern
protocol.

**Related** — None found in the staging library or vault on acute cold exposure and work
capacity specifically (distinct from post-exercise cold-water immersion for recovery,
which this entry does not address).

14	# Breath-Holding (Valsalva) Stabilises the Spine Under Heavy Load; Exhaling Through Effort Is the Authors' Named Risk, Except for Cardiac or Hypertensive Athletes
15	
16	**What it is** — The authors state that breathing pattern, duration, and rate have a
17	profound effect on strength production. The Valsalva manoeuvre, breath-holding, plays a
18	vital role in raising intra-abdominal pressure to support and stabilise the lumbar spine
19	during heavy lifting, with the abdominal and oblique muscles acting as an anatomical
20	corset. Spinal stress is diminished during high-resistance-loaded movement against
21	resistance when breath is held, and exhalation during lifting increases the risk of lumbar
22	injury; the authors call it unwise to follow the popular medical advice to exhale during
23	effort during strenuous lifting, squatting, or overhead pressing, though they name that
24	advice as appropriate specifically for patients with cardiac disease or hypertension.
25	Common sporting actions, jumping, throwing, pushing against an opponent, striking a ball,
26	standing up from a squat, kicking, elicit involuntary breath-holding because it enhances
27	performance and control accuracy in short-duration movements; archery and pistol shooting
28	stability and accuracy are tied to brief breath-holding phases; other cited research found
29	speed-strength actions are optimally enhanced when lung air volume is held at about 75% of
30	maximum capacity (Vorobyev, 1978). A study of 34 qualified weightlifters (Blokhin &
31	Monastirskii, 1985) recorded bar movement and breathing (spirometry) during the clean and
32	jerk at 60-90% of 1RM and identified three breathing-phase variants (A, B, C) across the
33	pull, rack, and jerk. All lifters held their breath during the pull and during the jerk in
34	every variant; when breathing did occur at other phases, exhalation volume always exceeded
35	inhalation volume by at least 125 ml. Variant B was judged optimal for maximal effort;
36	variant A occurs when the athlete makes technical corrections mid-lift; variant C is
37	characteristic of submaximal lifts. Recommendation: breath-holding should precede and
38	accompany maximal efforts, followed by brief exhalation-inhalation unless a technical
39	correction is needed, in which case breath-holding should persist; submaximal loads can use
40	longer normal-breathing phases and shorter breath-holding phases; neither rapid short
41	hyperventilation nor a forced maximal inhalation is desirable during maximal-effort lifting.
42	(PDF pp. 183-184, printed pp. 172-173, "3.4.9 Breathing and Strength Production," Fig 3.31.)

# Breath-Holding (Valsalva) Stabilises the Spine Under Heavy Load; Exhaling Through Effort Is the Authors' Named Risk, Except for Cardiac or Hypertensive Athletes

**What it is** — The authors state that breathing pattern, duration, and rate have a
profound effect on strength production. The Valsalva manoeuvre, breath-holding, plays a
vital role in raising intra-abdominal pressure to support and stabilise the lumbar spine
during heavy lifting, with the abdominal and oblique muscles acting as an anatomical
corset. Spinal stress is diminished during high-resistance-loaded movement against
resistance when breath is held, and exhalation during lifting increases the risk of lumbar
injury; the authors call it unwise to follow the popular medical advice to exhale during
effort during strenuous lifting, squatting, or overhead pressing, though they name that
advice as appropriate specifically for patients with cardiac disease or hypertension.
Common sporting actions, jumping, throwing, pushing against an opponent, striking a ball,
standing up from a squat, kicking, elicit involuntary breath-holding because it enhances
performance and control accuracy in short-duration movements; archery and pistol shooting
stability and accuracy are tied to brief breath-holding phases; other cited research found
speed-strength actions are optimally enhanced when lung air volume is held at about 75% of
maximum capacity (Vorobyev, 1978). A study of 34 qualified weightlifters (Blokhin &
Monastirskii, 1985) recorded bar movement and breathing (spirometry) during the clean and
jerk at 60-90% of 1RM and identified three breathing-phase variants (A, B, C) across the
pull, rack, and jerk. All lifters held their breath during the pull and during the jerk in
every variant; when breathing did occur at other phases, exhalation volume always exceeded
inhalation volume by at least 125 ml. Variant B was judged optimal for maximal effort;
variant A occurs when the athlete makes technical corrections mid-lift; variant C is
characteristic of submaximal lifts. Recommendation: breath-holding should precede and
accompany maximal efforts, followed by brief exhalation-inhalation unless a technical
correction is needed, in which case breath-holding should persist; submaximal loads can use
longer normal-breathing phases and shorter breath-holding phases; neither rapid short
hyperventilation nor a forced maximal inhalation is desirable during maximal-effort lifting.
(PDF pp. 183-184, printed pp. 172-173, "3.4.9 Breathing and Strength Production," Fig 3.31.)

**Why it works** — The authors give the mechanism directly: breath-holding raises
intra-abdominal pressure, and the abdominal and oblique muscles use that pressure as an
anatomical corset to support and stabilise the lumbar spine, reducing spinal stress under
high-resistance loading. Inference: this is broadly consistent with the modern
strength-training convention of Valsalva or bracing during heavy compound lifts, though
this entry does not independently verify that separate literature.

**When to apply** — Cue breath-holding through the concentric drive of a heavy
compound lift (squat, deadlift, overhead press), with a brief exhale-inhale at or near
lockout rather than exhaling through the sticking point, for healthy athletes lifting near
maximal loads. For submaximal work, normal breathing between reps is acceptable, with
breath-holding reserved for the effort phase itself.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors themselves name the exception: athletes with cardiac
disease or hypertension should follow the standard medical advice to exhale during effort,
not hold their breath, because Valsalva raises intrathoracic and blood pressure. The source
does not discuss that blood-pressure risk itself, or give any guidance on how long a breath
hold is safe; it addresses spinal stability and performance, not cardiovascular risk
management. The 34-lifter breathing-phase study is specific to the snatch/clean-and-jerk
pull-rack-jerk sequence at 60-90% of 1RM; it is not validated for sustained isometric
holds, high-rep sets, or other lift patterns.

**Example** — Inference: cue a lifter to inhale to roughly the described optimal range,
hold through the pull off the floor and the drive through the sticking point of a heavy
deadlift or squat, then exhale briefly at lockout before the next rep, rather than exhaling
on the way up.

**Related** — None found in the staging library or vault on breathing pattern and lifting
technique specifically; flagged for a reciprocal link if a future entry addresses
intra-abdominal pressure or bracing directly.

16	**What it is** — The authors state that strength, efficiency, and safety of movement are
17	determined primarily by neuromuscular factors, in particular kinaesthesis and the
18	underlying proprioceptive mechanisms that inform the body about the position and motion of
19	its own components, integrated with input from the other senses (sight, sound, hearing,
20	touch). Proprioception receives little dedicated training attention despite its central
21	role in PNF (proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation) rehabilitation. One way to improve
22	proprioceptive efficiency is to diminish or block input from other sensory systems,
23	particularly vision: training with weights, or executing Olympic or powerlifting movements,
24	blindfolded can enhance technical skill and strength or power production. Research cited
25	(Roman, 1986) found blindfolding does not disrupt motor activity and that, on the contrary,
26	exercises are performed with greater precision and stability when the eyes are closed or in
27	darkness; athletes remember joint angles, degree of muscular tension, movement amplitude,
28	and movement patterns best with eyes closed, and that enhanced motor sensitivity is
29	preserved and improves technical skill once the movement is performed with eyes open again.
30	During normal training an athlete is largely unaware of errors and generally feels the
31	exercise is being done correctly; blindfolded practice increases proprioceptive sensitivity,
32	enabling more accurate internal self-correction. Practical protocol described: eyes are
33	lightly covered with soft, dark material (airline eye-covers are named as suitable); the
34	athlete repeats the starting position with the coach's tactile and verbal correction; the
35	athlete then performs the full movement with light weights, alternating eyes uncovered and
36	covered until it feels natural and stable, then progresses to heavier weights with the same
37	alternation until the movement is mastered blindfolded. The technique is usable for any
38	strength exercise where the body stays in contact with the bar or apparatus, and also for
39	select movements practiced blindfolded to improve proprioception (jumping, track-and-field
40	events, swimming, throwing), as well as in physiotherapy rehabilitation, applying PNF

48	movement to self-correct against.

51	safely (not a first exposure), where visual dependence (e.g., watching the bar path in a
52	mirror) may be masking coordination or positioning errors; in supervised rehabilitation
53	using PNF-style pattern drilling with reduced visual input.

56	light-to-heavy loading progression; this is not appropriate for a genuinely unfamiliar
57	movement, for high-injury-risk loads, or without a trusted coach spotting and cueing
58	throughout, none of which the source addresses directly. The single supporting citation
59	(Roman, 1986) is dated, and the source reports the rationale and a training procedure, not
60	a quantified measure of how much technical improvement resulted.

63	could perform light-load blindfolded reps with a coach's verbal and tactile cueing to build
64	internal proprioceptive awareness of depth and bar position, then remove the blindfold once
