===== PDF idx 184 (printed 173) =====
SUPERTRAfNING
Figure 3.31 Typical relationship between the phases of movement and breathing during the clean-and-jerk. A, B and C arc the different 
major variations of lifting. The vertical axis shows the volume of inspired air in the lungs.
3.4.10 Strength Developm ent and Proprioception
Strength, efficiency and safety of all movement is determined primarily by neuromuscular factors, in particular the 
sense of kinacsthesis and the underlying proprioceptive mechanisms which inform us about where all the 
components of our musculoskeletal system are and what they are doing relative to one another in space and time. 
The integration of information from all the other senses (sight, sound, hearing and touch, in particular), together 
with this proprioceptive information enables us to execute a given movement in the most appropriate way in 
terms of pattern, velocity, acceleration and timing. This involves coordination of eye-hand, eye-foot or body- 
apparatus, processes which receive a great deal o f attention in technical training. Inadequate time, however, is 
generally devoted to specific training of proprioception, even though its importance is central to the 
physiotherapy rehabilitation system known as PNF (proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation), which is 
discussed later in more depth (7.2).
One way of improving proprioceptive efficiency is to diminish or block input from other sensory systems 
such as the eyes. 
Thus, training with weights or even executing the Olympic or powerlifting movements 
blindfolded can be a valuable way of enhancing technical skills and producing strength or power more effectively. 
Research has shown that blindfolding does not disrupt motor activities; on the contrary, it has been found that 
exercises are performed with greater precision and stability when the eyes are closed or in darkness (Roman, 
1986). The athlete remembers joint angles, the degree of muscular tension, the amplitude of movement and 
movement patterns best with the eyes closed and reproduces them more easily. 
Subsequently, when the 
movements are done with the eyes open, the athlete's enhanced motor sensitivity is preserved and his technical 
skill improves.
During normal training, the athlete remains largely unaware of his errors and generally feels that the exercise is 
being done correctly. When the exercises are performed blindfolded, proprioceptive sensitivity is increased and 
this makes it possible for the athlete to make more accurate internal 'visualisations' of technique, thereby enabling 
him to correct errors more easily.
In practice, the eyes are covered lightly with a soft, dark material, the eye-covers supplied by many airlines 
for overnight flights being particularly suitable. The athlete assumes the starting position several times to become 
familiar with location and balance, with the coach making any necessary tactile and verbal corrections. He then 
executes the full movement with light weights, with eyes uncovered, then covered, until the action begins to feel 
natural and stable. The coach offers constant guidance and correction, which diminishes as expertise grows. The 
athlete progresses to heavier weights, still alternating between movements with eyes uncovered and covered, until 
the action is mastered with the eyes closed. Finally, when his technique with blindfolding has been perfected, he 
moves on to heavy weights.
Since the body is in contact with the bar or apparatus throughout all movements in resistance training, it is 
possible to use this technique for all strength exercises with free weights or machines. With some ingenuity to 
ensure the safety and confidence of the athlete, many movements (e.g. jumping, track-and-field events, swimming
173

===== PDF idx 185 (printed 174) =====
SUPERTRAINING
and throwing) may be practised blindfolded to improve proprioception. 
This technique may also be used 1 
successfully for rehabilitation from injury; for instance, a physiotherapist may apply PNF techniques and I 
patterns of movement with the client blindfolded
3.5 Flexibility and Sporting Performance
The functional production of strength in any athletic activity relies on neuromuscular control and joint stability I 
over a specific range of movement. In other words, the strength and flexibility components o f overall fitness 
must interact in a way which is optimal for each movement and each sporting action. 
To understand the training 
of strength and other fitness qualities which involve range of movement, such as strength-flexibility, flexibility- I 
speed and flexibility-endurance, it is necessary to analyse the mechanisms which underlie flexibility and I 
stretching.
The concept of flexibility would appear to be clearly and intuitively understood by everyone involved with 
physical activity, yet, on deeper analysis, it emerges that this is far from being true. Toe-touching has long been 
regarded as a test of flexibility or suppleness and most physical tests of flexibility still rely on the seated stretch- 
and-reach-for-the-toes manoeuvre, even though it is well known that flexibility is joint specific. Similarly, the 
ability to perform the 'splits' has always been extolled as one of the supreme indicators of flexibility. 
Nevertheless, it is common for toe-touches and splitters to be quite unable to sit on their haunches in a low squat 
position with heels flat on the ground.
The message here is that the nature of flexibility generally is inadequately appreciated. Flexibility, whatever 
people mean by that term, differs from joint to joint, displays different properties under dynamic versus static 
conditions, and concerns not only muscles but all components o f the musculoskeletal system, as well as the 
various types of stretch reflex in the neuromuscular control circuits of the body.
3.5.1 A Definition of Flexibility
Flexibility actually refers to the range of movement (ROM) of a specific joint with respect to a particular degree 
of freedom. In this respect, each joint exhibits statically or dynamically some or many of the following degrees of 
freedom:
• flexion-extension 
• inversion-cversion
• rotation (internal and external) 
• varus-valgus
• adduction-abduction 
• pronation-supination
• traction-approximation 
• anterior-posterior gliding, rocking (tilting)
• protraction-retraction 
• medial-lateral gliding, rocking (tilting)
Some actions, such as flexion, extension, rotation and adduction-abduction are under the active control of the 
muscles, while movement involving the other degrees of freedom may occur passively as a consequence of forces 
or torques imposed by external loads or changes in motion associated with active muscular processes. For 
instance, a sudden stop during running can cause the femoral surface o f the knee joint to glide anteriorly relative to 
its tibia! surface. Likewise, impact on the outside of the knee or a rapid swerve may produce lateral-medial gliding 
and rocking of the same bones of the leg relative to one another.
Flexibility, or range-of-movement, is determined by:
• the structural or architectural limitations of the relevant joint
• the mechanical properties of the muscles and other soft tissues of the joint

===== PDF idx 183 (printed 172) =====

For instance, in 1957 Michael concluded that cold showers increase work capacity, an effect which is greater 
among trained athletes than the general public (Vorobyev, 1978). In support of his own experiences with Russian 
weightlifters, Vorobyev quotes the findings of Happ (1947), Rosen (1952) and O'Rolev (1956) which reveal that 
cold compresses laid on the abdomen of athletes during intervals between exercises improved their performance. 
He found similar improvement in performance of weightliftcrs who were sponged down with cold water in the 
intervals between lifts in competition. He suggests that the muscle contraction induced by shivering, increased 
activity of the adrenal glands and a survival-directed central nervous reaction to peripheral excitation contribute to 
producing this effect.
With reference to the above research, it is apparent that the application of cold was brief in each case; 
prolonged exposure to cold which may lower muscle temperature or core temperature obviously is contraindicated 
as an ergogenic aid. The somewhat more prolonged application (5-15 minutes) of cold in the form of ice can be 
very effective in treating muscle and other soft tissue trauma.

# Breath-Holding (Valsalva) Stabilises the Spine Under Heavy Load; Exhaling Through Effort Is the Authors' Named Risk, Except for Cardiac or Hypertensive Athletes

**What it is** — The authors state that breathing pattern, duration, and rate have a
profound effect on strength production. The Valsalva manoeuvre, breath-holding, plays a
vital role in raising intra-abdominal pressure to support and stabilise the lumbar spine
during heavy lifting, with the abdominal and oblique muscles acting as an anatomical
corset. Spinal stress is diminished during high-resistance-loaded movement against
resistance when breath is held, and exhalation during lifting increases the risk of lumbar
injury; the authors call it unwise to follow the popular medical advice to exhale during
effort during strenuous lifting, squatting, or overhead pressing, though they name that
advice as appropriate specifically for patients with cardiac disease or hypertension.
Common sporting actions, jumping, throwing, pushing against an opponent, striking a ball,
standing up from a squat, kicking, elicit involuntary breath-holding because it enhances
performance and control accuracy in short-duration movements; archery and pistol shooting
stability and accuracy are tied to brief breath-holding phases; other cited research found
speed-strength actions are optimally enhanced when lung air volume is held at about 75% of
maximum capacity (Vorobyev, 1978). A study of 34 qualified weightlifters (Blokhin &
Monastirskii, 1985) recorded bar movement and breathing (spirometry) during the clean and
jerk at 60-90% of 1RM and identified three breathing-phase variants (A, B, C) across the
pull, rack, and jerk. All lifters held their breath during the pull and during the jerk in
every variant; when breathing did occur at other phases, exhalation volume always exceeded
inhalation volume by at least 125 ml. Variant B was judged optimal for maximal effort;
variant A occurs when the athlete makes technical corrections mid-lift; variant C is
characteristic of submaximal lifts. Recommendation: breath-holding should precede and
accompany maximal efforts, followed by brief exhalation-inhalation unless a technical
correction is needed, in which case breath-holding should persist; submaximal loads can use
longer normal-breathing phases and shorter breath-holding phases; neither rapid short
hyperventilation nor a forced maximal inhalation is desirable during maximal-effort lifting.
(PDF pp. 183-184, printed pp. 172-173, "3.4.9 Breathing and Strength Production," Fig 3.31.)

**Why it works** — The authors give the mechanism directly: breath-holding raises
intra-abdominal pressure, and the abdominal and oblique muscles use that pressure as an
anatomical corset to support and stabilise the lumbar spine, reducing spinal stress under
high-resistance loading. Inference: this is broadly consistent with the modern
strength-training convention of Valsalva or bracing during heavy compound lifts, though
this entry does not independently verify that separate literature.

**When to apply** — Cue breath-holding through the concentric drive of a heavy
compound lift (squat, deadlift, overhead press), with a brief exhale-inhale at or near
lockout rather than exhaling through the sticking point, for healthy athletes lifting near
maximal loads. For submaximal work, normal breathing between reps is acceptable, with
breath-holding reserved for the effort phase itself.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors themselves name the exception: athletes with cardiac
disease or hypertension should follow the standard medical advice to exhale during effort,
not hold their breath, because Valsalva raises intrathoracic and blood pressure. The source
does not discuss that blood-pressure risk itself, or give any guidance on how long a breath
hold is safe; it addresses spinal stability and performance, not cardiovascular risk
management. The 34-lifter breathing-phase study is specific to the snatch/clean-and-jerk
pull-rack-jerk sequence at 60-90% of 1RM; it is not validated for sustained isometric
holds, high-rep sets, or other lift patterns.

**Example** — Inference: cue a lifter to inhale to roughly the described optimal range,
hold through the pull off the floor and the drive through the sticking point of a heavy
deadlift or squat, then exhale briefly at lockout before the next rep, rather than exhaling
on the way up.

**Related** — None found in the staging library or vault on breathing pattern and lifting
technique specifically; flagged for a reciprocal link if a future entry addresses
intra-abdominal pressure or bracing directly.

technique specifically; flagged for a reciprocal link if a future entry addresses

# Removing Vision During Practice Can Sharpen Proprioceptive Awareness and Technical Skill

**What it is** — The authors state that strength, efficiency, and safety of movement are
determined primarily by neuromuscular factors, in particular kinaesthesis and the
underlying proprioceptive mechanisms that inform the body about the position and motion of
its own components, integrated with input from the other senses (sight, sound, hearing,
touch). Proprioception receives little dedicated training attention despite its central
role in PNF (proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation) rehabilitation. One way to improve
proprioceptive efficiency is to diminish or block input from other sensory systems,
particularly vision: training with weights, or executing Olympic or powerlifting movements,
blindfolded can enhance technical skill and strength or power production. Research cited
(Roman, 1986) found blindfolding does not disrupt motor activity and that, on the contrary,
exercises are performed with greater precision and stability when the eyes are closed or in
darkness; athletes remember joint angles, degree of muscular tension, movement amplitude,
and movement patterns best with eyes closed, and that enhanced motor sensitivity is
preserved and improves technical skill once the movement is performed with eyes open again.
During normal training an athlete is largely unaware of errors and generally feels the
exercise is being done correctly; blindfolded practice increases proprioceptive sensitivity,
enabling more accurate internal self-correction. Practical protocol described: eyes are
lightly covered with soft, dark material (airline eye-covers are named as suitable); the
athlete repeats the starting position with the coach's tactile and verbal correction; the
athlete then performs the full movement with light weights, alternating eyes uncovered and
covered until it feels natural and stable, then progresses to heavier weights with the same
alternation until the movement is mastered blindfolded. The technique is usable for any
strength exercise where the body stays in contact with the bar or apparatus, and also for
select movements practiced blindfolded to improve proprioception (jumping, track-and-field
events, swimming, throwing), as well as in physiotherapy rehabilitation, applying PNF
techniques and movement patterns with the client blindfolded. (PDF pp. 184-185, printed pp.
173-174, "3.4.10 Strength Development and Proprioception.")

**Why it works** — The authors' own explanation: removing visual feedback forces reliance
on proprioceptive information, and the resulting heightened internal awareness of joint
angle, tension, amplitude, and pattern is retained and improves technique once vision is
restored, because the athlete can now form a more accurate internal "visualisation" of the
movement to self-correct against.

**When to apply** — For refining technique on a movement the athlete already performs
safely (not a first exposure), where visual dependence (e.g., watching the bar path in a
mirror) may be masking coordination or positioning errors; in supervised rehabilitation
using PNF-style pattern drilling with reduced visual input.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors give no safety protocol beyond soft eye-covers and a
light-to-heavy loading progression; this is not appropriate for a genuinely unfamiliar
movement, for high-injury-risk loads, or without a trusted coach spotting and cueing
throughout, none of which the source addresses directly. The single supporting citation
(Roman, 1986) is dated, and the source reports the rationale and a training procedure, not
a quantified measure of how much technical improvement resulted.

**Example** — Inference: a lifter who over-relies on watching the bar path during the squat
could perform light-load blindfolded reps with a coach's verbal and tactile cueing to build
internal proprioceptive awareness of depth and bar position, then remove the blindfold once
the pattern feels stable; the book does not give this specific example.

**Related** — [[framework--kinaesthetic-system-and-feedforward-visualization]] (Ch1, the
kinaesthetic system and mental-visualization content this entry's proprioceptive-training
method draws on).

14	# Flexibility Is Joint- and Direction-Specific Range of Movement, Not a Single Trait
15	
16	**What it is** — The authors define flexibility as the range of movement (ROM) of a
17	specific joint with respect to a particular degree of freedom, not a single global trait.
18	Each joint exhibits, statically or dynamically, some or many of: flexion-extension,
19	rotation, adduction-abduction, traction-approximation, protraction-retraction,
20	inversion-eversion, varus-valgus, pronation-supination, and various gliding/rocking
21	actions. Some degrees of freedom are under active muscular control; others occur only
22	passively from external force (the authors' example: a sudden stop during running can
23	glide the femur anteriorly on the tibia). ROM at any joint is determined by: the
24	structural/architectural limits of the joint itself, the mechanical properties of the
25	muscles and other soft tissues, neuromuscular processes controlling muscle tension and
26	length, the level of non-functional muscle tension present, and the individual's pain
27	threshold near end of range. Two types are distinguished: active flexibility (maximum ROM
28	producible under active muscular control) and passive flexibility (maximum ROM producible
29	passively by an external force without causing joint injury). The authors call
30	toe-touching and the "splits" commonly but wrongly treated as general indicators of
31	flexibility or suppleness, when flexibility is joint-specific: it is common for a toe-toucher
32	or a splitter to be unable to sit on their haunches with heels flat. (PDF p. 185, printed
33	p. 174.)
34	
35	A closing caution from the same section: joint tissues must balance mobility (the ability
36	to stretch) against stability (damping ratio, the ability to absorb tensile shocks). A
37	joint whose tissues have low stiffness (stretches easily) but a low damping ratio (absorbs
38	shock poorly) is described as especially susceptible to overload injury (Siff, 1986). (PDF
39	p. 187, printed p. 176.)
40	
41	**Why it works** — This is the authors' definitional framework for organizing the rest of
42	the chapter, not an empirical finding with its own mechanism to evaluate.
43	
44	**When to apply** — Use this to choose or interpret a flexibility test by joint and degree
45	of freedom relevant to the sport skill, rather than defaulting to one generic test (e.g.
46	sit-and-reach) as a stand-in for "flexibility." When a test or exercise is reported to
47	improve "flexibility," ask which joint, which degree of freedom, and active or passive.
48	
49	**When NOT to apply** — Do not treat one joint's ROM in one plane (a sit-and-reach score,
50	a static split) as representative of an athlete's flexibility generally; the text
51	explicitly calls this a common but mistaken assumption. Do not pursue maximal ROM as a
52	goal in isolation from the joint's stiffness/damping ratio: the text frames excess
53	mobility without adequate shock-absorption capacity as an injury-risk profile, not a
54	training win (Siff, 1986, printed 176).
55	
56	**Example** — Inference: a hurdler who scores well on a static hip-flexion split test may still lack
57	the *active* hip-flexion range needed at sprint cadence, because the static test measures
58	a different degree of freedom under different (passive, non-cyclic) conditions than the
59	sport skill requires.
60	
61	**Related** — [[framework--six-parameters-influencing-flexibility]],
62	[[framework--stretching-techniques-taxonomy-static-vs-dynamic]].

rotation, adduction-abduction, traction-approximation, protraction-retraction,
inversion-eversion, varus-valgus, pronation-supination, and various gliding/rocking

producible under active muscular control) and passive flexibility (maximum ROM producible
passively by an external force without causing joint injury). The authors call
toe-touching and the "splits" commonly but wrongly treated as general indicators of
flexibility or suppleness, when flexibility is joint-specific: it is common for a toe-toucher
or a splitter to be unable to sit on their haunches with heels flat. (PDF p. 185, printed
p. 174.)

A closing caution from the same section: joint tissues must balance mobility (the ability
to stretch) against stability (damping ratio, the ability to absorb tensile shocks). A
joint whose tissues have low stiffness (stretches easily) but a low damping ratio (absorbs
shock poorly) is described as especially susceptible to overload injury (Siff, 1986). (PDF
p. 187, printed p. 176.)

**Why it works** — This is the authors' definitional framework for organizing the rest of
the chapter, not an empirical finding with its own mechanism to evaluate.

**When to apply** — Use this to choose or interpret a flexibility test by joint and degree
of freedom relevant to the sport skill, rather than defaulting to one generic test (e.g.
sit-and-reach) as a stand-in for "flexibility." When a test or exercise is reported to
improve "flexibility," ask which joint, which degree of freedom, and active or passive.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not treat one joint's ROM in one plane (a sit-and-reach score,
a static split) as representative of an athlete's flexibility generally; the text
explicitly calls this a common but mistaken assumption. Do not pursue maximal ROM as a
goal in isolation from the joint's stiffness/damping ratio: the text frames excess
mobility without adequate shock-absorption capacity as an injury-risk profile, not a
training win (Siff, 1986, printed 176).

**Example** — Inference: a hurdler who scores well on a static hip-flexion split test may still lack
the *active* hip-flexion range needed at sprint cadence, because the static test measures
a different degree of freedom under different (passive, non-cyclic) conditions than the
sport skill requires.

14	# Four Ways to Increase ROM, Ranked by Speed of Effect and Durability
15	
16	**What it is** — The authors give four practical means of enhancing joint ROM, in order
17	of effectiveness, and note the first limitation on the list (skeletal structure) cannot be
18	overcome by any form of exercise:
19	1. Modifying the neuromuscular processes that control tension and length in the muscle
20	complex. This increases ROM most rapidly and most effectively, but the change tends to be
21	confined to short-term improvements unless the neuromuscular means are used as an ongoing
22	part of all training.
23	2. Increasing the length and strength of the soft tissues comprising the muscle complex,
24	especially collagenous tissues such as fascia. These changes are slower to produce but
25	long-term.
26	3. Lengthening and strengthening other soft tissues, especially those of the joint capsule
27	and ligaments. Also long-lasting, but if promoted to the point of joint laxity, joint
28	stability can be severely compromised.
29	4. Restructuring the articulating surfaces of the joints, a process mediated by many years
30	of regular heavy loading in specific patterns; not a practical training target, more a
31	by-product of loaded full-range sporting movement, and inappropriate/excessive loading can
32	instead produce degenerative changes that reduce ROM.
33	The authors add that stretching and flexibility training are not synonymous: some
34	flexibility exercises increase ROM without being stretching exercises at all, because they
35	work entirely by modifying neuromuscular processes (the stretch and tendon reflexes);
36	conversely, many stretching exercises pay no deliberate attention to neuromuscular
37	processes and instead aim at structural change in soft tissue, so static stretches may
38	change muscle length without adequately affecting the dynamic ROM a given sport requires.
39	(PDF pp. 185-186, printed pp. 174-175.)
40	
41	**Why it works** — The authors give no single unifying mechanism; the ordering reflects
42	which physiological layer (nervous system, muscle/fascia, joint capsule/ligament, bone) is
43	being changed and how quickly each layer adapts, from fastest-and-least-durable
44	(neuromuscular) to slowest-and-most-durable (bone).
45	
46	**When to apply** — Use this ordering to set expectations for a flexibility intervention:
47	a single session aimed at neuromuscular relaxation (e.g. PNF) can produce a same-day ROM
48	gain that will not persist without repetition, while a multi-week soft-tissue-lengthening
49	block is the one that produces a durable change. Match the method to the timeframe: a
50	pre-competition warm-up should rely on method 1 (rapid, neuromuscular, session-specific);
51	an off-season block targeting chronic ROM limits should emphasize methods 2-3.
52	
53	**When NOT to apply** — Do not expect a brief pre-event stretching routine to produce
54	long-term flexibility change; the text is explicit that this is a category error common in
55	"the average stretching programme." Do not pursue method 3 (ligament/capsule lengthening)
56	without limit: the text names joint laxity and compromised stability as the direct cost of
57	overdoing it. Method 4 should never be treated as a deliberate training target.
58	
59	**Example** — Inference: a pre-game mobility routine that relies on PNF contract-relax drills is
60	working through method 1 and will not, by itself, change an athlete's baseline hip ROM
61	measured a week later; that requires a sustained block emphasizing methods 2 and 3.
62	
63	**Related** — [[framework--flexibility-definition-and-rom-determinants]],
64	[[framework--joint-stabilization-sequence-across-range-of-motion]].

===== PDF idx 186 (printed 175) =====
SUPERTRAINING
It should also be remembered that range of movement for any given action (e.g. extension) may be influenced 
by the presence of any simultaneous movement in another direction (e.g. external rotation). 
We cannot 
automatically assume that movement in any given direction is entirely independent of preceding or concurrent 
movement in other directions, so that laboratory measurements of range of movement may not be as unequivocal 
is is intimated by research. The muscular system is characterised by the integrated action and interaction of many 
muscles associated with each joint, so that limited flexibility in a certain direction may not simply be due to the 
musculature directly opposing movement in that direction alone, but also to limitations imposed by other 
synergistic muscles and other stabilising soft tissues.
The preceding list enables us to consider several methods for increasing range of joint movement, some of 
which are impractical or impossible. Only the first-named limitation cannot be overcome by training. If restricted 
movement is due to the skeletal structure of the joint, then it is impossible to remove them by an form of exercise. 
This leaves three other types of limitation that can be reduced or overcome by appropriate choice of strategy. 
The success enjoyed by physiotherapeutic PNF (proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation) 'stretching' 
manoeuvres emphasizes that the greatest and most rapid gains in ROM may be made by modifying the degree of 
nervous control of muscle tension and length.
Research and experience reveal the existence of the following practical means of enhancing ROM, given in 
order of effectiveness:
1. Modifying the neuromuscular processes that control tension and length of tissues in the muscle complex. 
This increases the ROM most rapidly and most effectively, but the changes tends to be confined to short­
term improvements unless the neuromuscular means are used as an ongoing part of all training.
2. Increasing the length and strength of the different soft tissues comprising the muscle complex, especially the

Sometimes, the spasm will be relieved by utilisation of reciprocal inhibition via voluntary contraction of the 
agonistic muscle on the opposite side of the limb while the joint is held fixed.

The different soft tissues associated with any joint each contribute to joint flexibility or stiffness to a differing 
extent. If stretch reflex mechanisms are minimally involved and the muscles are relaxed (which rarely is the case 
during dynamic functional movement), the relative contributions of the soft tissues to joint stiffness are as follows

• muscles and their fascial sheaths 
41%
• structures of the joint capsule, including ligaments 
35%
•skin 
11%
• tendons and their sheaths 
10%
Since nothing can be done to alter joint structure in order to increase flexibility, it is obvious that appropriate 
stretching manoeuvres have to be imposed on the soft tissues to achieve this aim. In doing so, it is important to 
recognize that stretching may result in short-term (elastic), long-term (plastic) or combined short/long term 
changes in tissue characteristics.
If the average stretching programme is examined it becomes apparent that this distinction is insufficiently 
emphasized. If one analyses the usual type of pre-event or pre-training warm-up session, it is obvious that it is 
intended primarily to enhance short-term flexibility for the physical activity which is just about to commence. 
These brief preparatory sessions arc often inadequate to alter long-term flexibility, which requires a specific type 
of regular conditioning to be built into the overall training programme. The design of such a programme 
necessitates a fairly thorough understanding of the physiology and biomechanics of the soft tissues involved.

outline those factors which influence flexibility in general:
1. Exercise and Training History
Regular exercise which involves the full range of joint motion generally enhances flexibility. It should be noted, 
however, that athletes tend to develop patterns o f flexibility which are characteristic of their particular sport.

# Four Ways to Increase ROM, Ranked by Speed of Effect and Durability

**What it is** — The authors give four practical means of enhancing joint ROM, in order
of effectiveness, and note the first limitation on the list (skeletal structure) cannot be
overcome by any form of exercise:
1. Modifying the neuromuscular processes that control tension and length in the muscle
complex. This increases ROM most rapidly and most effectively, but the change tends to be
confined to short-term improvements unless the neuromuscular means are used as an ongoing
part of all training.
2. Increasing the length and strength of the soft tissues comprising the muscle complex,
especially collagenous tissues such as fascia. These changes are slower to produce but
long-term.
3. Lengthening and strengthening other soft tissues, especially those of the joint capsule
and ligaments. Also long-lasting, but if promoted to the point of joint laxity, joint
stability can be severely compromised.
4. Restructuring the articulating surfaces of the joints, a process mediated by many years
of regular heavy loading in specific patterns; not a practical training target, more a
by-product of loaded full-range sporting movement, and inappropriate/excessive loading can
instead produce degenerative changes that reduce ROM.
The authors add that stretching and flexibility training are not synonymous: some
flexibility exercises increase ROM without being stretching exercises at all, because they
work entirely by modifying neuromuscular processes (the stretch and tendon reflexes);
conversely, many stretching exercises pay no deliberate attention to neuromuscular
processes and instead aim at structural change in soft tissue, so static stretches may
change muscle length without adequately affecting the dynamic ROM a given sport requires.
(PDF pp. 185-186, printed pp. 174-175.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no single unifying mechanism; the ordering reflects
which physiological layer (nervous system, muscle/fascia, joint capsule/ligament, bone) is
being changed and how quickly each layer adapts, from fastest-and-least-durable
(neuromuscular) to slowest-and-most-durable (bone).

**When to apply** — Use this ordering to set expectations for a flexibility intervention:
a single session aimed at neuromuscular relaxation (e.g. PNF) can produce a same-day ROM
gain that will not persist without repetition, while a multi-week soft-tissue-lengthening
block is the one that produces a durable change. Match the method to the timeframe: a
pre-competition warm-up should rely on method 1 (rapid, neuromuscular, session-specific);
an off-season block targeting chronic ROM limits should emphasize methods 2-3.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not expect a brief pre-event stretching routine to produce
long-term flexibility change; the text is explicit that this is a category error common in
"the average stretching programme." Do not pursue method 3 (ligament/capsule lengthening)
without limit: the text names joint laxity and compromised stability as the direct cost of
overdoing it. Method 4 should never be treated as a deliberate training target.

**Example** — Inference: a pre-game mobility routine that relies on PNF contract-relax drills is
working through method 1 and will not, by itself, change an athlete's baseline hip ROM
measured a week later; that requires a sustained block emphasizing methods 2 and 3.

[[framework--joint-stabilization-sequence-across-range-of-motion]].

14	# Active Flexibility, Not Passive, Is the One That Tracks Sporting Proficiency
15	
16	**What it is** — Citing a single Russian study of over 200 adult competitors (Iashvili,
17	1982), the authors report that sporting achievement (rated by competition standards)
18	correlates more strongly with active flexibility than with passive flexibility: R = 0.81
19	versus R = 0.69. The same study found traditional static and passive stretching develop
20	mainly passive flexibility, while combined strength-and-stretching exercises are
21	considerably more effective at developing active flexibility, particularly when the
22	strength conditioning is applied in the zone of active muscular inadequacy (i.e. the end
23	of the joint's active range). (PDF p. 186, printed p. 175.)
24	
25	A later section (3.5.8) returns to the same Iashvili (1982) study across "several Olympic
26	sports" with further detail: joint mobility level tracks sporting proficiency generally;
27	static/passive stretching enhances passive flexibility but only moderately improves active
28	mobility (described as "by far the most important flexibility quality needed in sport");
29	the pattern and range of joint mobility is sport-specific (e.g. backstroke/butterfly
30	swimmers show the greatest shoulder and ankle mobility, breast-strokers the least in those
31	joints but the greatest hip/knee mobility; javelinists show the greatest shoulder
32	mobility among throwers, hurdlers the greatest hip flexibility among track athletes); and
33	the active-passive correlation itself depends on training method, running 0.61-0.73 with
34	primarily static/passive stretching but rising to 0.91 when stretching is combined with
35	strengthening. (PDF pp. 196-197, printed pp. 185-186.)
36	
37	A related measurement framework from the same section (Tumanyan & Dzhanyan, 1980) defines
38	three flexibility indices from a pulley-loaded limb: maximum passive flexibility (PFmax,
39	at the pain threshold), active flexibility (AF, reached by non-ballistic muscular action),
40	and loaded passive flexibility (PF, with a progressively increased sub-pain-threshold
41	load), yielding a maximum active flexibility deficit (FDmax = PFmax - AF), a loaded active
42	flexibility deficit (FD = PF - AF), and an interval of flexibility pain threshold (FPT =
43	PFmax - PF). Using these indices, the same source reports: static/passive stretching
44	increases passive flexibility while leaving the active-passive gap unchanged; full-range
45	strength exercise increases passive flexibility and narrows that gap; and combined
46	strength-plus-flexibility exercise increases both and narrows the gap most. A large
47	active-passive gap ("flexibility deficit") is reported to correlate strongly with the
48	incidence of soft-tissue injury. (PDF p. 197, printed p. 186.)
49	
50	**Why it works** — The book gives no physiological mechanism for why active flexibility
51	specifically tracks proficiency; it reports only the correlational and intervention
52	results above.
53	
54	**When to apply** — Prefer testing and training active ROM (through the athlete's own
55	muscular control) over passive ROM (examiner- or gravity-assisted) when the goal is a
56	proxy for sporting flexibility demands, and prefer combined strength-and-stretch
57	programming over stretching alone when the goal is to close a large active-passive gap.
58	
59	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence capped at `supported`.** These are single-source,
60	Soviet-era correlational and intervention findings (Iashvili 1982; Tumanyan & Dzhanyan
61	1980) not independently replicated in this corpus; the correlation coefficients describe
62	association within that sample, not a causal mechanism, and "sporting proficiency" is the
63	study's own competition-standard rating, not defined here. Do not treat the specific
64	numbers (0.81, 0.69, 0.91, the sport-by-sport mobility patterns) as generalizable norms for
65	a Baylor football roster without independent verification.
66	
67	**Example** — Inference: two athletes with identical passive hip-flexion ROM on a table test may
68	differ substantially in active hip flexion under their own muscular control during a
69	sprint stride; per this claim, the active measure (and a program that narrows any gap
70	between the two) is the one that tracks performance, not the passive number alone.

14	# The Book's Stretching-Benefits List Includes Items Modern Evidence Disputes
15	
16	**What it is** — Citing a literature and empirical-evidence review (Keith, 1977; Weiss,
17	1976; Holland, 1968; de Vries, 1966, 1966), the authors list these benefits of stretching:
18	increase in range of useful movement; reduction in the incidence of injury; decrease in
19	the severity of injury; delay in the onset of muscular fatigue; prevention and alleviation
20	of muscle soreness after exercise; increase in the level of skill and muscular efficiency;
21	prolongation of sporting life. In the same section they also caution that inappropriate
22	stretching can be detrimental: tendons and ligaments can be permanently deformed or
23	damaged by over-zealous or prolonged stretching, impairing joint stability; unskilled
24	ballistic stretching can cause muscle soreness and stiffness; and overstretching of the
25	cervical or lumbar spine can damage nerves, discs and blood vessels, particularly in
26	forceful yoga postures or amateur spinal manipulation. (PDF p. 187, printed p. 176.)
27	
28	**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for any item on the benefits list; it is
29	presented as a summary of a 1960s-70s literature review, not derived from a stated
30	physiological pathway in this text.
31	
32	**When to apply** — Treat "increase in range of useful movement" as the best-supported
33	item on this list, consistent with the book's own later, more specific claim that ROM
34	gains from routine stretching mainly reflect increased stretch tolerance (see
35	[[claim--static-cyclic-stretching-increases-rom-via-stretch-tolerance-not-tissue-change]]).
36	
37	**When NOT to apply** — **`contested`, named reason:** the muscle-soreness-prevention claim
38	on this list is disputed by a later systematic review of randomized trials: Herbert RD, de
39	Noronha M, Kamper SJ, "Stretching to prevent or reduce muscle soreness after exercise,"
40	Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2011, concluded that stretching (before, after, or
41	both) produces little to no reduction in delayed-onset muscle soreness, whether performed
42	pre- or post-exercise. The injury-incidence and injury-severity items are also not

# The Book's Stretching-Benefits List Includes Items Modern Evidence Disputes

**What it is** — Citing a literature and empirical-evidence review (Keith, 1977; Weiss,
1976; Holland, 1968; de Vries, 1966, 1966), the authors list these benefits of stretching:
increase in range of useful movement; reduction in the incidence of injury; decrease in
the severity of injury; delay in the onset of muscular fatigue; prevention and alleviation
of muscle soreness after exercise; increase in the level of skill and muscular efficiency;
prolongation of sporting life. In the same section they also caution that inappropriate
stretching can be detrimental: tendons and ligaments can be permanently deformed or
damaged by over-zealous or prolonged stretching, impairing joint stability; unskilled
ballistic stretching can cause muscle soreness and stiffness; and overstretching of the
cervical or lumbar spine can damage nerves, discs and blood vessels, particularly in
forceful yoga postures or amateur spinal manipulation. (PDF p. 187, printed p. 176.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for any item on the benefits list; it is
presented as a summary of a 1960s-70s literature review, not derived from a stated
physiological pathway in this text.

**When to apply** — Treat "increase in range of useful movement" as the best-supported
item on this list, consistent with the book's own later, more specific claim that ROM
gains from routine stretching mainly reflect increased stretch tolerance (see
[[claim--static-cyclic-stretching-increases-rom-via-stretch-tolerance-not-tissue-change]]).

**When NOT to apply** — **`contested`, named reason:** the muscle-soreness-prevention claim
on this list is disputed by a later systematic review of randomized trials: Herbert RD, de
Noronha M, Kamper SJ, "Stretching to prevent or reduce muscle soreness after exercise,"
Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2011, concluded that stretching (before, after, or
both) produces little to no reduction in delayed-onset muscle soreness, whether performed
pre- or post-exercise. The injury-incidence and injury-severity items are also not
supported by a specific modern trial in this entry; do not cite this 1966-1977 review list
as current evidence for injury prevention or soreness reduction without independent
verification. Inference: several items (skill/efficiency increase, prolongation of
sporting life) are broad, difficult-to-falsify claims not tied to a specific outcome
measure in the cited sources, and should be treated as unverified assertions rather than
established findings.

**Example** — Inference: a staff member citing "stretching reduces soreness" to justify a mandatory
post-lift static stretching block would be relying on the disputed half of this list; the
Cochrane review found this benefit does not hold up under randomized-trial evidence.

**Related** — [[claim--static-cyclic-stretching-increases-rom-via-stretch-tolerance-not-tissue-change]].

===== PDF idx 196 (printed 185) =====
SUPERTRAINING
For the competitive athlete or rehabilitating patient, static stretching is insufficient to develop the full range of 
movement strength, power, mobility and stability required in sport. It must be combined with high intensity 
static and dynamic activities to condition the collagenous tissues, full-range resistance training to increase muscle 
length, and low-intensity cardiovascular and muscle endurance activity to enhance capitalisation and circulatory 
efficiency.
After all, it is active flexibility of the appropriate degrees of joint freedom which correlates most strongly 
with sporting proficiency and resistance to injury (Iashvili, 1982). This same study of several Olympic sports 
revealed some further interesting results:
• The level of joint mobility generally relates strongly to sporting proficiency. The higher the level of sporting 
proficiency, the greater is passive and active flexibility.
• Static and passive stretching enhance passive flexibility, but only moderately improve active joint mobility, 
which is by far the most important flexibility quality needed in sport.
• Active flexibility correlates more strongly (R = 0.81) with sporting proficiency than passive flexibility (R = 
0.69).
• The pattern and range of joint mobility is sport specific. For example in swimmers, the greatest shoulder and 
ankle mobility occurs in backstroke and butterfly specialists, whereas breast-stroke swimmers have the 
lowest flexibility in these joints. Breast-strokcrs, however, have the greatest range of hip and knee mobility. 
In track-and-field athletics, throwers, especially javelinists, display the greatest level of shoulder mobility, 
while the greatest hip flexibility is found among hurdlers.
• The relative relationship between active and passive flexibility depends on the training methods used. If 
primarily static and passive stretching methods are used, the coefficient of correlation between active and 
passive flexibility is 0.61-0.73, depending on the joint. The combined use of stretching and strengthening 
exercises increases this value to 0.91.
• A large difference between active and passive flexibility (a measure which we may call the flexibility deficit 
FD) correlates strongly with the incidence of soft tissue injury.
• The flexibility deficit decreases significantly by means of the concurrent use of stretching and resistance 
training, particularly if strength exercises are performed in the zone of active flexibility deficiency.
Since active flexibility is a function of soft tissue mechanical stiffness and length (see 1.6.4), as well as the 
strength of the muscles to move a joint to the limit of its range, any stretching routine should identify which of 
these factors demands most emphasis in improving active flexibility. Static stretching methods are used where the 
emphasis needs to be on tissue qualities, whereas dynamic methods are essential for rectifying deficits in full range 
strength performance. However, it is not only active flexibility, but active functional range of movement in the 
specific sporting action, that is of central importance to sporting proficiency.
Some scientists have criticised the traditional methods of flexibility measurement, since the examiner usually 
guides or forces subjects to reach their limits of passive or active movement. A more objective way is to attach a 
load via a pulley system to the relevant limb and allow the load to pull it in a relaxed state to the limit of range 
(Tumanyan & Dzhanyan, 1980). Several ranges of flexibility may then be defined:
• maximum passive flexibility (PFmax), measured when one reaches the pain threshold of movement
• active flexibility (AF). reached by the non-ballistic action of muscles on the limb
• loaded passive flexibility (PF), measured with a progressively increased load which does not take one to the 
pain threshold.
This now enables one to calculate three indices of flexibility:
• Maximum active flexibility deficit 
FDmax = PFmax - A F
• Loaded active flexibility deficit 
FD  
= PF - A F
• Interval of flexibility pain threshold FPT  
= P F m a x -P F
Using these measures, it was found that (Tumanyan & Dzhanyan, 1980):
185

===== PDF idx 197 (printed 186) =====
SUPERTRAINING
• Static and passive stretches increase passive flexibility. Increases in passive and active flexibility are the same 
and the difference between them remains unchanged.
• Full range strength exercises increase passive flexibility and decrease the difference between active and passive 
flexibility.
• Concurrent strength and flexibility exercises increase passive and active flexibility and decrease the difference 
between them.
Thus, dynamic stretching executed while one deliberately concentrates on progressively contracting and relaxing 
the muscle complex being stretched can prove invaluable in enhancing active flexibility. Although most fitness 
instructors believe stretching a relaxed muscle to be safer and more effective, the proven PNF techniques using 
phases o f contraction and relaxation can be both safe and very effective (see Ch 7). Application o f the PNF 
principles of spiral and diagonal patterns of movement can also produce superior three-dimensional functional 
ROM (range o f movement) to standard static stretches. In this respect, it is interesting to note that many 
conventional stretches are executed in only one plane at a time and very few rotational stretches about the 
longitudinal axes of the limbs are ever used. Thus, many of these stretches could be enhanced if they included 
elements of rotation and twisting, especially if they followed some of the patterns encountered in actual sport.
The use of quasi-isometric activity can be especially useful in developing active flexibility (see 1.9). This 
requires one to exercise a limb through a full range of movement against a resistance which is allowed to stretch a 
joint gently beyond its limit of static flexibility without producing any sudden movement which may recruit the 
myotatic reflex. Free weights, pulley and other functional training machines can be particularly versatile in 
allowing one to execute natural patterns of movement against resistance (see 4.2.7). In addition, longer periods of 
progressive isometric or quasi-isometric activity in full range movement produce greater gains in active flexibility.
Eccentric quasi-isometrics can be especially useful for enhancing functional range of movement, if one allows 
the load to force the joint to move slowly and eccentrically beyond its limit of static flexibility. Used as a method 
of improving flexibility, it does not have to be performed against very heavy loads; one should commcnce with 
small loads and use the progressive overload principle to gradually work up to near-maximal loads. In training 
with light or heavy loads, one should use multiple repetitions, gradually increasing the range of movement with 
each repetition. Both modes of quasi-isometrics may be used in conjunction with PNF techniques and patterns 
to improve fitness qualities such as static strength, static flexibility, dynamic flexibility, flcxibility-strength and 
flexibility-cndurance (see Ch 7).
Starting-strength is also extremely important to human muscular performance, so the use of injudicious 
stretching or part-range resistance training which can impair this quality should be discouraged. Conversely, 
resistance training of gradually increasing intensity in any zones of activc muscular inadequacy, particularly in the 
region of full extension, is to be encouraged. Unfortunately, most isokinetic machines display a small lag in their 
early phases and therefore are inadequate for developing starting-strength or functional flexibility in this critical 
joint zone. If the inertia of weights, machines or pulley systems renders them unsuitable for early rehabilitation, 
progressively sequenced isometric contractions at a variety of joint angles or work against elastic bands (with the 
fixed end moved to appropriate starting positions) can prove to be especially useful.
“Functional” stretching conditioning also has to cnhance the qualities of Jlexibility-speed. flexibility-strength 
(static and dynamic) and flexibility-endurance (static and dynamic) which are required for high level performance 
in sport. Flexibility-speed refers to the ability to produce efficient full ROM at speed; flexibility-strength to the 
ability to produce efficient, powerful static and dynamic movements over a full ROM; and flexibility-endurance to 
the ability to repetitively produce efficient full ROM under static and dynamic conditions. The importance of 
using a wide variety of carefully sequenced stretching methods of cyclically periodised intensity, duration and 
complexity then bccomes obvious.
The Use of Ballistic Stretching
All too often, it is stated that ballistic stretching generally is harmful and should be avoided at all costs. This well- 
meaning, but very misleading, statement makes no distinction between the rates at which ballistic stretching is 
imposed or the different techniques that may be used in applying it. In fact, most forms of ballistic stretching 
could quite safely be included within the scope of PNF. If gentle bouncing forms of ballistic stretching are used 
over a gradually increasing range of movement, they will be seen to be a special type of contract-rclax or hold-relax 
PNF activity and therefore may be applied safely and effectively. One may also alternate static stretches with 
periodic gentle ballistic stretches to enhance the effectiveness of any stretch and one may even carry out ballistic

# Active Flexibility, Not Passive, Is the One That Tracks Sporting Proficiency

**What it is** — Citing a single Russian study of over 200 adult competitors (Iashvili,
1982), the authors report that sporting achievement (rated by competition standards)
correlates more strongly with active flexibility than with passive flexibility: R = 0.81
versus R = 0.69. The same study found traditional static and passive stretching develop
mainly passive flexibility, while combined strength-and-stretching exercises are
considerably more effective at developing active flexibility, particularly when the
strength conditioning is applied in the zone of active muscular inadequacy (i.e. the end
of the joint's active range). (PDF p. 186, printed p. 175.)

A later section (3.5.8) returns to the same Iashvili (1982) study across "several Olympic
sports" with further detail: joint mobility level tracks sporting proficiency generally;
static/passive stretching enhances passive flexibility but only moderately improves active
mobility (described as "by far the most important flexibility quality needed in sport");
the pattern and range of joint mobility is sport-specific (e.g. backstroke/butterfly
swimmers show the greatest shoulder and ankle mobility, breast-strokers the least in those
joints but the greatest hip/knee mobility; javelinists show the greatest shoulder
mobility among throwers, hurdlers the greatest hip flexibility among track athletes); and
the active-passive correlation itself depends on training method, running 0.61-0.73 with
primarily static/passive stretching but rising to 0.91 when stretching is combined with
strengthening. (PDF pp. 196-197, printed pp. 185-186.)

A related measurement framework from the same section (Tumanyan & Dzhanyan, 1980) defines
three flexibility indices from a pulley-loaded limb: maximum passive flexibility (PFmax,
at the pain threshold), active flexibility (AF, reached by non-ballistic muscular action),
and loaded passive flexibility (PF, with a progressively increased sub-pain-threshold
load), yielding a maximum active flexibility deficit (FDmax = PFmax - AF), a loaded active
flexibility deficit (FD = PF - AF), and an interval of flexibility pain threshold (FPT =
PFmax - PF). Using these indices, the same source reports: static/passive stretching
increases passive flexibility while leaving the active-passive gap unchanged; full-range
strength exercise increases passive flexibility and narrows that gap; and combined
strength-plus-flexibility exercise increases both and narrows the gap most. A large
active-passive gap ("flexibility deficit") is reported to correlate strongly with the
incidence of soft-tissue injury. (PDF p. 197, printed p. 186.)

**Why it works** — The book gives no physiological mechanism for why active flexibility
specifically tracks proficiency; it reports only the correlational and intervention
results above.

# Active Flexibility, Not Passive, Is the One That Tracks Sporting Proficiency

**What it is** — Citing a single Russian study of over 200 adult competitors (Iashvili,
1982), the authors report that sporting achievement (rated by competition standards)
correlates more strongly with active flexibility than with passive flexibility: R = 0.81
versus R = 0.69. The same study found traditional static and passive stretching develop
mainly passive flexibility, while combined strength-and-stretching exercises are
considerably more effective at developing active flexibility, particularly when the
strength conditioning is applied in the zone of active muscular inadequacy (i.e. the end
of the joint's active range). (PDF p. 186, printed p. 175.)

A later section (3.5.8) returns to the same Iashvili (1982) study across "several Olympic
sports" with further detail, and states there that active flexibility "correlates most
strongly with sporting proficiency and resistance to injury" (Iashvili, 1982, printed 185):
joint mobility level tracks sporting proficiency generally; static and passive stretching
enhance passive flexibility but "only moderately improve active joint mobility," which is
called "by far the most important flexibility quality needed in sport" (printed 185); the
pattern and range of joint mobility is sport-specific (e.g. backstroke/butterfly swimmers
show the greatest shoulder and ankle mobility, breast-strokers the least in those joints but
the greatest hip/knee mobility; throwers, especially javelinists, have the greatest shoulder
mobility of track-and-field athletes, hurdlers the greatest hip flexibility among track
athletes); and the active-passive correlation itself depends on training method, running
0.61-0.73 with primarily static/passive stretching but rising to 0.91 when stretching is
combined with strengthening. (PDF pp. 196-197, printed pp. 185-186.)

G5, internal tension not resolved by the authors: Iashvili (1982, printed 185) says static
and passive stretching "only moderately improve active joint mobility." Tumanyan & Dzhanyan
(1980, printed 186), using a different measurement method (below), say static and passive
stretches "increase passive flexibility," and "increases in passive and active flexibility
are the same and the difference between them remains unchanged," which reads as static and
passive stretching moving active flexibility just as much as passive. Both as printed.

A related measurement framework from the same section (Tumanyan & Dzhanyan, 1980) defines
three flexibility indices from a pulley-loaded limb: maximum passive flexibility (PFmax,
at the pain threshold), active flexibility (AF, reached by non-ballistic muscular action),
and loaded passive flexibility (PF, with a progressively increased sub-pain-threshold
load), yielding a maximum active flexibility deficit (FDmax = PFmax - AF), a loaded active
flexibility deficit (FD = PF - AF), and an interval of flexibility pain threshold (FPT =
PFmax - PF). Using these indices, the same source reports: static/passive stretching
increases passive flexibility while leaving the active-passive gap unchanged; full-range
strength exercise increases passive flexibility and narrows that gap; and combined
strength-plus-flexibility exercise increases both and narrows the gap most. A large
active-passive gap ("flexibility deficit") is reported to correlate strongly with the
incidence of soft-tissue injury. (PDF p. 197, printed p. 186.)

specifically tracks proficiency; it reports only the correlational and intervention
results above.

considerably more effective at developing active flexibility, particularly when the

sports" with further detail, and states there that active flexibility "correlates most

22:> Dupuy, O., Douzi, W., Theurot, D., Bosquet, L., & Dugué, B. (2018). An evidence-based approach for choosing post-exercise recovery techniques to reduce markers of muscle damage, soreness, fatigue, and inflammation: A systematic review with meta-analysis. *Frontiers in Physiology, 9*, 403. https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2018.00403
26:This review informs selection of post-exercise recovery modalities when the immediate goals are reducing soreness, perceived fatigue, muscle-damage markers, or inflammation.
30:How do commonly used post-exercise recovery techniques compare for delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS), perceived fatigue, muscle-damage markers, and inflammatory markers?
34:- Participants: Healthy adults aged 18 to under 65 across 99 eligible studies; 1,188 participants contributed to the DOMS analysis and 266 to perceived fatigue.
44:- Measurements and outcomes: DOMS, perceived fatigue, creatine kinase, C-reactive protein, and interleukin-6.
49:- Across modalities, recovery interventions reduced DOMS (SMD -0.78, 95% CI -0.94 to -0.61; I² 56.62%) and perceived fatigue (SMD -1.40, 95% CI -1.92 to -0.89; I² 33%). [p. 4]
50:- Active recovery, massage, compression garments, immersion, contrast water therapy, and cryotherapy produced small-to-large reductions in DOMS (Hedges' g range -2.26 to -0.40), whereas the other reviewed methods did not. [p. 5]
52:- Stretching and electrostimulation did not significantly improve DOMS or fatigue in the pooled analyses. [p. 11]
56:- Publication and English/French language restriction bias may have inflated effects. [p. 11]
57:- Substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity remained, and the interaction between the preceding training load and modality effectiveness could not be resolved. [p. 11]
58:- Blinding was generally infeasible, so placebo and expectancy effects could not be eliminated. [p. 11]
59:- Performance recovery was not evaluated, repeated use and combined modalities were excluded, and changes in soreness or biomarkers should not be assumed to equal restored performance. [pp. 11-12]
64:Massage, compression garments, and water immersion are reasonable options when short-term soreness or perceived fatigue is the target, but the expected benefit is outcome-specific. Recovery decisions should be individualized and should not substitute subjective recovery changes or biomarker changes for direct readiness or performance assessment.
71:| Overall pooled DOMS and fatigue effects | p. 4 | result |
72:| Modality-specific DOMS effects | p. 5 | result |
74:| Bias, heterogeneity, blinding, and outcome limitations | pp. 11-12 | limitation |

**When NOT to apply** — **`contested`, named reason:** the muscle-soreness-prevention claim
on this list is disputed by a later systematic review of randomized trials: Herbert RD, de
Noronha M, Kamper SJ, "Stretching to prevent or reduce muscle soreness after exercise,"

meta-analysis, found stretching did not significantly improve DOMS or fatigue in pooled
analyses (p. 11). The injury-incidence and injury-severity items are not supported by a
specific modern trial in this entry; naming one would require independent verification this
ingest cannot provide, so it is left out rather than inserted unconfirmed. A separate,
later part of this same book undercuts the injury item on its own terms: "many athletes
dispense entirely with special stretching or even warm-up sessions... without suffering
injury" (printed 192, in the context of arguing dedicated stretching is not always
necessary). Do not cite this 1966-1977 review list as current evidence for injury
prevention or soreness reduction without independent verification. Inference: several items
(skill/efficiency increase, prolongation of sporting life) are broad, difficult-to-falsify
claims not tied to a specific outcome measure in the cited sources, and should be treated as
unverified assertions rather than established findings. Eric's baseline: injury risk can be
reduced, not eliminated, through sound programming and progression, an explicit refusal to
promise injury prevention (`docs/method-baseline.md`), consistent with treating this list's
injury claims cautiously.

# The Muscle Spindle, Golgi Tendon Organ, and the Stretch Reflex Family

**What it is** — Joint flexibility is shaped not only by tissue structure and mechanical
properties but by the degree of motor unit activity in the relevant muscles: muscle
contraction raises muscle tension, which counteracts stretching. Two receptor types govern
this: muscle spindles (Fig 3.32), which detect changes in muscle fibre length and rate of
length change, and Golgi tendon organs (GTOs), which monitor tension in the muscle tendon
during contraction or stretching. The spindle produces the "stretch reflex" (contraction in
response to lengthening); the GTO produces the "inverse stretch reflex" (relaxing a
contracting muscle if its tension becomes excessive). Spindles contain 3-10 intrafusal
fibres of two types (nuclear bag and nuclear chain), innervated by primary (large type Ia)
and secondary (smaller type II) sensory receptors; primary receptors innervate both fibre
types and are held responsible for the strong dynamic response, while nuclear chain fibres
(innervated by both receptor types) are held responsible for the static response. Gamma
efferent fibres split similarly into gamma-dynamic (exciting bag fibres, powerful dynamic
response) and gamma-static (exciting chain fibres, persistent static response) (Guyton,
1984). The full stretch reflex (myotatic reflex, Fig 3.33) comprises a dynamic (phasic)
reflex (strong but brief contraction on sudden length change), a static (tonic) reflex
(weaker but sustained for up to several hours while tension persists), and a negative
stretch reflex (inhibitory relaxation when a muscle is suddenly shortened, opposing
shortening the way the myotatic reflex opposes lengthening). GTO firing shows the same
dynamic/static split: an intense initial (dynamic) response to sudden tension change,
settling to a lower steady-state (static) response proportional to tension; it is now
understood to continuously monitor, not just protect against excess, muscle tension
(Matthews, 1973). Repeated reflex production, like voluntary effort, fatigues: reflex
tension diminishes with repeated stimulation, and "rebound" (a second reflex of the same
type becoming progressively harder to elicit for a time after the first) is named as a
likely contributor to cyclic activities such as locomotion, swimming and cycling (Guyton,
1984). (PDF pp. 187-189, printed pp. 176-178, Figs 3.32-3.33.)

**Why it works** — This is established, independent-of-text mammalian neurophysiology
(muscle spindle and GTO structure and reflex function, per Guyton and Matthews, cited in
the text); the book's own extensions (rebound's role in specific cyclic sports, the
practical stretching implications below) are less established and are flagged separately
in Related entries.

**When to apply** — Use the dynamic-vs-static split to explain why a fast, sudden stretch
provokes a strong protective contraction (via the dynamic stretch reflex) while a slow,
sustained stretch allows the muscle to relax further into the new length (the dynamic
component fades quickly, leaving only the weaker static response): this is the
physiological basis for preferring slow entry into a static stretch over a fast one.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry covers the basic reflex arcs only; it does not by
itself justify any specific stretching protocol, duration, or frequency. **Confidence is
`proven` for the core spindle/GTO/stretch-reflex mechanisms described (established,
independent physiology); it is not proven** for the book's applied claims about rebound's
role in specific sports or the fatigue-of-reflex claim's magnitude, which are stated
without a specific citation beyond Guyton (1984).

**Example** — The book's own example: many "plyometric drills" are performed too slowly to
elicit the powerful dynamic spindle response essential for speed-strength development,
because the dynamic response requires a rapid rate of length change, not just any
stretch-shorten action (printed 177).

**Related** — [[heuristic--reflex-based-techniques-for-flexibility-training]],
[[framework--joint-stabilization-sequence-across-range-of-motion]].

# The Muscle Spindle, Golgi Tendon Organ, and the Stretch Reflex Family

**What it is** — Joint flexibility is shaped not only by tissue structure and mechanical
properties but by the degree of motor unit activity in the relevant muscles: muscle
contraction raises muscle tension, which counteracts stretching. Two receptor types govern
this: muscle spindles (Fig 3.32), which detect changes in muscle fibre length and rate of
length change, and Golgi tendon organs (GTOs), which monitor tension in the muscle tendon
during contraction or stretching. The spindle produces the "stretch reflex" (contraction in
response to lengthening); the GTO produces the "inverse stretch reflex" (relaxing a
contracting muscle if its tension becomes excessive). Spindles contain 3-10 intrafusal
fibres of two types (nuclear bag and nuclear chain), innervated by primary (large type Ia)
and secondary (smaller type II) sensory receptors; primary receptors innervate both fibre
types and are held responsible for the strong dynamic response, while nuclear chain fibres
(innervated by both receptor types) are held responsible for the static response. Gamma
efferent fibres split similarly into gamma-dynamic (exciting bag fibres, powerful dynamic
response) and gamma-static (exciting chain fibres, persistent static response) (Guyton,
1984). The full stretch reflex (myotatic reflex, Fig 3.33) comprises a dynamic (phasic)
reflex (strong but brief contraction on sudden length change), a static (tonic) reflex
(weaker but sustained for up to several hours while tension persists), and a negative
stretch reflex (inhibitory relaxation when a muscle is suddenly shortened, opposing
shortening the way the myotatic reflex opposes lengthening). GTO firing shows the same
dynamic/static split: an intense initial (dynamic) response to sudden tension change,
settling to a lower steady-state (static) response proportional to tension; it is now
understood to continuously monitor, not just protect against excess, muscle tension
(Matthews, 1973). Repeated reflex production, like voluntary effort, fatigues: reflex
tension diminishes with repeated stimulation, and "rebound" (a second reflex of the same
type becoming progressively harder to elicit for a time after the first) is named as a
likely contributor to cyclic activities such as locomotion, swimming and cycling (Guyton,
1984). (PDF pp. 187-189, printed pp. 176-178, Figs 3.32-3.33.)

**Why it works** — This is established, independent-of-text mammalian neurophysiology
(muscle spindle and GTO structure and reflex function, per Guyton and Matthews, cited in
the text); the book's own extensions (rebound's role in specific cyclic sports, the
practical stretching implications below) are less established and are flagged separately
in Related entries.

**When to apply** — Use the dynamic-vs-static split to explain why a fast, sudden stretch
provokes a strong protective contraction (via the dynamic stretch reflex) while a slow,
sustained stretch allows the muscle to relax further into the new length (the dynamic
component fades quickly, leaving only the weaker static response): this is the
physiological basis for preferring slow entry into a static stretch over a fast one.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry covers the basic reflex arcs only; it does not by
itself justify any specific stretching protocol, duration, or frequency. **Confidence is
`proven` for the core spindle/GTO/stretch-reflex mechanisms described (established,
independent physiology); it is not proven** for the book's applied claims about rebound's
role in specific sports or the fatigue-of-reflex claim's magnitude, which are stated
without a specific citation beyond Guyton (1984).

**Example** — The book's own example: many "plyometric drills" are performed too slowly to
elicit the powerful dynamic spindle response essential for speed-strength development,
because the dynamic response requires a rapid rate of length change, not just any
stretch-shorten action (printed 177).

**Related** — [[heuristic--reflex-based-techniques-for-flexibility-training]],
[[framework--joint-stabilization-sequence-across-range-of-motion]].

# Two Reflex Phenomena With Direct Stretching Applications: The Positive Supportive Reaction and Voluntary Relaxation

**What it is** — Two specific, named reflex phenomena the authors connect directly to
stretching practice. First, the positive supportive reaction (Guyton, 1984): any form of
stretching that exerts pressure on the soles of the feet or palms of the hands produces
strong reflex extension of the limb concerned, stiffening and stabilizing it against
external pressure (including body/trunk weight). The authors state this makes toe-touching
stretches in standing versus seated positions neuromuscularly different procedures,
because the locus of pressure on the sole or palm determines which limb extends, a
mechanism physiotherapists use in PNF to guide a patient into a specific pattern. Second,
electromyographic (EMG) silence can persist in muscles being passively stretched,
regardless of stretch speed, meaning subjects can consciously relax a muscle below the
tension normal stretch reflexes would otherwise produce (Basmajian, 1978); the authors
infer from this that voluntary mental control or biofeedback techniques can play a useful
role in stretching and flexibility procedures. (PDF pp. 188-189, printed pp. 177-178.)

**Why it works** — The positive supportive reaction is presented as an established reflex
(Guyton, 1984) without further mechanism given here. The EMG-silence finding (Basmajian,
1978) demonstrates that voluntary control can override the expected reflex response, but
the book does not explain how; Inference: this implies stretch reflex tension is not a
fixed floor and can be reduced by conscious relaxation or biofeedback training, independent
of any change in the tissue's mechanical properties.

**When to apply** — Standing toe-touch and seated toe-touch are not neuromuscularly
interchangeable tests or stretches, per this entry, because standing loads the sole with
body weight (triggering the positive supportive reaction in the leg) while seated does
not. Consider cueing conscious relaxation or using biofeedback/visualization during static
stretching, on the premise that voluntary relaxation can reduce reflex-driven resistance
independent of tissue length change.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a Guyton-textbook physiology citation and a single
Basmajian (1978) EMG finding, not a study of stretching outcomes; the book does not report
that biofeedback-assisted stretching produces measurably greater ROM gains than
conventional stretching. Do not treat "voluntary relaxation matters" as license to ignore
tissue-level stretching methods (see
[[framework--four-methods-of-enhancing-rom-ranked-by-effectiveness]]).

**Example** — Inference: cueing an athlete to consciously "let the hamstring go" while
holding a static stretch, rather than relying only on time-under-tension, is an attempt to
use the voluntary-override pathway described here on top of the tissue-mechanical effect of
the stretch itself.

**Related** — [[framework--stretch-reflex-types-and-neuromuscular-control-of-flexibility]].

# Two Reflex Phenomena With Direct Stretching Applications: The Positive Supportive Reaction and Voluntary Relaxation

**What it is** — Two specific, named reflex phenomena the authors connect directly to
stretching practice. First, the positive supportive reaction (Guyton, 1984): any form of
stretching that exerts pressure on the soles of the feet or palms of the hands produces
strong reflex extension of the limb concerned, stiffening and stabilizing it against
external pressure (including body/trunk weight). The authors state this makes toe-touching
stretches in standing versus seated positions neuromuscularly different procedures,
because the locus of pressure on the sole or palm determines the position to which the
limb will extend, a mechanism physiotherapists use in PNF to guide a patient into a
specific pattern. Second, electromyographic (EMG) silence can persist in muscles being
passively stretched, regardless of stretch speed, meaning subjects can consciously relax a
muscle below the tension normal stretch reflexes would otherwise produce (Basmajian, 1978);
the authors infer from this that voluntary mental control or biofeedback techniques can
play a useful role in stretching and flexibility procedures. (PDF pp. 188-190, printed pp.
177-179.)

**Why it works** — The positive supportive reaction is presented as an established reflex
(Guyton, 1984) without further mechanism given here. The EMG-silence finding (Basmajian,
1978) demonstrates that voluntary control can override the expected reflex response, but
the book does not explain how; Inference: this implies stretch reflex tension is not a
fixed floor and can be reduced by conscious relaxation or biofeedback training, independent
of any change in the tissue's mechanical properties.

**When to apply** — Standing toe-touch and seated toe-touch are not neuromuscularly
interchangeable tests or stretches, per this entry, because standing loads the sole with
body weight (triggering the positive supportive reaction in the leg) while seated does
not. Consider cueing conscious relaxation or using biofeedback/visualization during static
stretching, on the premise that voluntary relaxation can reduce reflex-driven resistance
independent of tissue length change.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a Guyton-textbook physiology citation and a single
Basmajian (1978) EMG finding, not a study of stretching outcomes; the book does not report
that biofeedback-assisted stretching produces measurably greater ROM gains than
conventional stretching. Do not treat "voluntary relaxation matters" as license to ignore
tissue-level stretching methods (see
[[framework--four-methods-of-enhancing-rom-ranked-by-effectiveness]]).

**Example** — Inference: cueing an athlete to consciously "let the hamstring go" while
holding a static stretch, rather than relying only on time-under-tension, is an attempt to
use the voluntary-override pathway described here on top of the tissue-mechanical effect of
the stretch itself.

**Related** — [[framework--stretch-reflex-types-and-neuromuscular-control-of-flexibility]].
