14	# What Each Soft Tissue Contributes to Joint Stiffness, and Short- vs Long-Term Stretch Change
15	
16	**What it is** — With stretch reflex mechanisms minimally involved and muscles relaxed
17	(rarely the case during dynamic functional movement), the relative contribution of soft
18	tissues to joint stiffness is given as (Johns & Wright, 1962): muscles and their fascial
19	sheaths 41%, structures of the joint capsule including ligaments 35%, skin 11%, tendons and
20	their sheaths 10%. Since nothing can be done to alter joint structure itself, appropriate
21	stretching must target these soft tissues to increase flexibility, and stretching can
22	produce short-term (elastic), long-term (plastic), or combined short/long-term changes in
23	tissue characteristics. The authors state the average pre-event or pre-training warm-up
24	stretching session mainly targets short-term flexibility, and that this distinction is
25	often insufficiently emphasized: changing long-term flexibility requires a specific,
26	regularly repeated conditioning component built into the overall training programme, not
27	just brief preparatory sessions. (PDF p. 189, printed p. 178.)
28	
29	**Why it works** — The percentage breakdown is the authors' cited figure (Johns & Wright,
30	1962) with no further mechanism given; the elastic-vs-plastic distinction follows directly
31	from standard viscoelastic tissue behavior (elastic deformation recovers, plastic
32	deformation persists), which the book treats as background rather than derives here.
33	
34	**When to apply** — Use the percentage breakdown to set expectations: muscle/fascia is the
35	largest single lever (41%) for stretching-driven ROM change, but joint-capsule/ligament
36	tissue is a close second (35%) and carries the injury-risk caveat that lengthening it too
37	far compromises joint stability (see
38	[[framework--four-methods-of-enhancing-rom-ranked-by-effectiveness]]). Distinguish, when
39	programming, whether a stretching block is meant to produce same-session (short-term,
40	elastic) readiness or multi-week (long-term, plastic) ROM change, since a warm-up-style
41	session will not reliably produce the latter.
42	
43	**When NOT to apply** — The 1962 percentages describe relaxed-muscle, minimal-reflex
44	conditions; the authors state this rarely reflects dynamic functional movement, where
45	muscle tension (not passive tissue mechanics alone) dominates joint stiffness. Do not treat
46	a single pre-training stretch session as sufficient to produce durable ROM change; the text
47	is explicit that this is a common but mistaken programming assumption.
48	
49	**Example** — The book's own contrast: a brief pre-event stretch is "obvious[ly]...intended
50	primarily to enhance short-term flexibility for the physical activity which is just about
51	to commence," while durable change "requires a specific type of regular conditioning to be
52	built into the overall training programme" (printed 178).
53	
54	**Related** — [[framework--flexibility-definition-and-rom-determinants]],
55	[[claim--ligament-tendon-adaptation-and-detraining-response]].

14	# Six Factors That Shift an Individual's Flexibility
15	
16	**What it is** — The authors list six factors that influence flexibility in general:
17	1. **Exercise and training history.** Regular full-range exercise generally enhances
18	flexibility. Athletes develop patterns of flexibility characteristic of their sport;
19	long-term flexibility can be reduced by a sedentary lifestyle, by training that rarely
20	uses full-range joint motion, by excessive hypertrophy focus, or by soft-tissue injury.
21	Short-term flexibility can be decreased by overtraining-induced soreness, stiffness, or
22	injury; tissue mechanical stiffness stays fairly constant during exercise, but damping
23	ratio invariably increases (Siff, 1986). As a specific instance of this factor, the authors
24	report that Russian and Eastern European scientists discourage cycling for athletes who
25	need large trunk and hip ROM, because cycling is held to decrease functional ROM in those
26	joints; they instead favor intensive sprinting and interval training, and similarly
27	discourage conventional push-ups and sit-ups (which limit shoulder and trunk ROM
28	respectively) in favor of push-ups on dip bars/parallel bars and backward sit-ups over a
29	pommel horse or "Roman chair."
30	2. **Age.** Flexibility generally decreases with age, raising soft-tissue injury
31	susceptibility during intensive exercise; regular exercise combined with flexibility
32	training can minimize this. Maximum flexibility is not at its peak in the youngest infants
33	but is reached between ages 10 and 12, depending on gender (Beaulieu, 1986).
34	3. **Gender.** Females tend to be more flexible than males at equivalent joints; the
35	damping ratio of females' joint soft tissues is greater than males', implying females are
36	intrinsically better equipped to absorb elastic stretch, and the pain threshold for joint
37	torsion is generally significantly lower in females (Siff, 1986).
38	4. **Temperature.** Increased muscle temperature (active warm-up, passive massage,
39	ultrasound) increases flexibility, including improved plastic deformation of collagenous
40	tissue during stretching; a gentle rhythmic warm-up is recommended before flexibility
41	training. Prolonged heat or cold can produce analgesia or otherwise modify the
42	neuromuscular processes behind the stretch and tendon reflexes, enhancing relaxation and
43	stretching; cooling tissue with ice for the final minutes of stretching is reported to
44	stabilize connective tissue at its new length (Sapega et al., 1981).
45	5. **Type of joint.** Flexibility is specific to each joint; an overall flexibility index
46	can be built by averaging a representative sample of joints, but what matters
47	practically is establishing static and dynamic ROM for the specific joints most important
48	to a given sport.
49	6. **Type of movement.** The relative degree of flexibility differs for each degree of
50	joint freedom; increasing flexibility in a direction that would compromise a joint's
51	stability during a specific movement should be avoided. Optimum, not maximum, static and
52	dynamic flexibility is required for each degree of freedom; subjects hypermobile in
53	certain joints should avoid increasing flexibility further at the expense of stability.
54	(PDF pp. 189-191, printed pp. 178-180.)
55	
56	**Why it works** — No single mechanism unifies these six; each is the authors' summary of
57	a separate cited source (Siff 1986; Beaulieu 1986; Sapega et al. 1981) or an unsourced
58	general observation.
59	
60	**When to apply** — Use factor 6 as a direct programming caution: do not chase additional
61	ROM in a hypermobile athlete's already-loose joint, since the goal is optimum, not maximum,
62	flexibility per degree of freedom. Use factor 4 to sequence a session: warm before
63	stretching, and consider a brief cooling period at the end of a stretch to help "lock in"
64	a new tissue length (Sapega et al., 1981).
65	
66	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence capped at `supported`.** The cycling/push-up/sit-up
67	recommendation under factor 1 is attributed only to unnamed "Russian and Eastern European
68	scientists," with no specific citation or study design given; treat it as a single
69	tradition's programming preference, not an established finding, and do not extend it to
70	justify removing cycling or sit-ups from a Baylor program without independent evidence.
71	The gender pain-threshold and damping-ratio claims (Siff, 1986) are also single-source and
72	not cross-checked against a modern sex-differences study in this entry.
73	
74	**Example** — The book's own example: breast-stroke swimmers versus backstroke/butterfly
75	swimmers show opposite shoulder/ankle-versus-hip/knee mobility patterns, illustrating that
76	"type of joint" and training history jointly produce sport-specific flexibility profiles
77	rather than one general flexibility trait (see also
78	[[claim--active-flexibility-correlates-more-with-sporting-proficiency-than-passive]]).
79	
80	**Related** — [[framework--flexibility-definition-and-rom-determinants]],
81	[[claim--active-flexibility-correlates-more-with-sporting-proficiency-than-passive]].

# What Each Soft Tissue Contributes to Joint Stiffness, and Short- vs Long-Term Stretch Change

**What it is** — With stretch reflex mechanisms minimally involved and muscles relaxed
(rarely the case during dynamic functional movement), the relative contribution of soft
tissues to joint stiffness is given as (Johns & Wright, 1962): muscles and their fascial
sheaths 41%, structures of the joint capsule including ligaments 35%, skin 11%, tendons and
their sheaths 10%. Since nothing can be done to alter joint structure itself, appropriate
stretching must target these soft tissues to increase flexibility, and stretching can
produce short-term (elastic), long-term (plastic), or combined short/long-term changes in
tissue characteristics. The authors state the average pre-event or pre-training warm-up
stretching session mainly targets short-term flexibility, and that this distinction is
often insufficiently emphasized: changing long-term flexibility requires a specific,
regularly repeated conditioning component built into the overall training programme, not
just brief preparatory sessions. (PDF p. 189, printed p. 178.)

**Why it works** — The percentage breakdown is the authors' cited figure (Johns & Wright,
1962) with no further mechanism given; the elastic-vs-plastic distinction follows directly
from standard viscoelastic tissue behavior (elastic deformation recovers, plastic
deformation persists), which the book treats as background rather than derives here.

**When to apply** — Use the percentage breakdown to set expectations: muscle/fascia is the
largest single lever (41%) for stretching-driven ROM change, but joint-capsule/ligament
tissue is a close second (35%) and carries the injury-risk caveat that lengthening it too
far compromises joint stability (see
[[framework--four-methods-of-enhancing-rom-ranked-by-effectiveness]]). Distinguish, when
programming, whether a stretching block is meant to produce same-session (short-term,
elastic) readiness or multi-week (long-term, plastic) ROM change, since a warm-up-style
session will not reliably produce the latter.

**When NOT to apply** — The 1962 percentages describe relaxed-muscle, minimal-reflex
conditions; the authors state this rarely reflects dynamic functional movement, where
muscle tension (not passive tissue mechanics alone) dominates joint stiffness. Do not treat
a single pre-training stretch session as sufficient to produce durable ROM change; the text
is explicit that this is a common but mistaken programming assumption.

**Example** — The book's own contrast: a brief pre-event stretch is "obvious[ly]...intended
primarily to enhance short-term flexibility for the physical activity which is just about
to commence," while durable change "requires a specific type of regular conditioning to be
built into the overall training programme" (printed 178).

**Related** — [[framework--flexibility-definition-and-rom-determinants]],
[[claim--ligament-tendon-adaptation-and-detraining-response]].

SUPERTRAINING
soreness, stiffness or injury. In addition, tissue mechanical stiffness remains fairly constant during exercise, 
although damping ratio invariably increases (Siff, 1986).
2. Age
Flexibility generally tends to decrease with age and hence susceptibility to soft tissue injury increases during 
intensive exercise. Regular exercise combined with flexibility training, however, can minimise the effect of these 
physiological changes. At the other age extreme, maximum flexibility is not at a peak in the youngest infants, but 
seems to be reached between the ages of 10 and 12 years, depending on gender (Beaulieu, 1986).
3. Gender
Females tend to be more flexible than males of the same age with respect to equivalent joints. Moreover, the 
damping ratio for the soft tissues of the joints in females is greater than that in males, implying that they arc 
intrinsically better equipped to absorb elastic stretch (Siff 1986). Another contributory safety factor lies in the 
fact that the threshold of pain in response to joint torsion is generally significantly lower in females (Siff, 1986).
4. T em perature
An increase in muscle temperature produced, for instance, by active warming up, passive massage or ultrasound 
increases flexibility, including improved plastic deformation of collagenous tissues during stretching. An 
appropriate rhythmic, gentle warm-up is therefore recommended prior to any flexibility training. It should also be 
noted that the prolonged application of both heat and cold may produce analgesia or modification of the 
neuromuscular processes associated with the stretch and tendon reflexes, thereby enhancing muscle relaxation and 
stretching. In addition, cooling of the tissues with ice for the final few minutes of stretching seems to stabilise 
connective tissues at their new length (Sapega et al, 1981).
5. Type of Jo in t
Flexibility is specific to each joint, with every person displaying a different relative degree of flexibility from joint 
to joint. An index of overall flexibility may be determined by averaging the flexibility of a representative number 
of joints in the body, but what is more relevant is establishing the static and dynamic ranges o f movement for the 
most important joints used by a participant in a particular sport.
6. Type of M ovem ent
The relative degree of flexibility is different for each of the degrees of joint freedom discussed near the beginning of 
this article, such as flexion, extension, rotation and distraction. It is important to avoid increasing flexibility in any 
way or direction which may adversely affect the stability o f a joint during execution o f any specific physical 
manoeuvre. In this respect it is most important to remember that optimum, and not maximum, static and dynamic 
flexibility is required for each degree of freedom of every joint. In fact, subjects who arc hypermobile in certain 
joints should avoid increasing flexibility at the expense of stability.
3.5.6 Soft Tissue Biom echanics and Flexibility
Earlier the relative contributions to joint stiffness by the different soft tissues was discussed. To understand and 
apply the principles of judicious stretching to these various tissues, it is necessary to examine their biomechanical 
characteristics.
In doing so, it is useful to recall the model of the muscic complcx discussed in Chapter 1. It divided the soft 
tissues into a contractile system, comprising the actin-myosin muscic fibre complex, and a viscoelastic non* 
contractile system, comprising mainly the connective tissue of tendons, ligaments and capsules. The viscoelastic 
component of muscle was further analysed in terms of a series elastic component (SEC) and a parallel elastic 
component (PEC).
An in-depth biomechanical analysis of the different types and methods of strctching is beyond the scope of 
this text, but is covered elsewhere (Siff, 1987). Most relevant to this text arc the following points:
• Different methods are necessary for conditioning muscles, tendons, and other soft tissues
• Slow twitch muscle groups contain a greater proportion of conncctive tissue than fast twitch muscle groups
180

===== PDF idx 192 (printed 181) =====
SUPERTRAINING
• The high stiffness and low strain of slow muscle is most appropriate for muscle function intended for 
continuous support of posture
• Different brain and spinal cord mechanisms control high speed, low speed, and topological patterns of muscle 
activity
• All fitness conditioning, including flexibility enhancement, relies predominantly on neuromuscular stimulation
• All conditioning is primarily functional, since functional stimulation precedes structural change (Wolff’s Law)
- thus, it is erroneous to refer to any exercises as purely 'structural'
• Rapid ballistic stretching of contracted muscle (plyometric loading) should not be avoided by serious athletes, 
since the ability to use elastic energy is vital to all high level performance
• Static stretching of a relaxed muscle has a more pronounced effect on the PEC than ballistic stretching of a 
contracted muscle, which has a greater effect on the SEC (essential for any fast activities)
• Static and cyclic stretching, as commonly performed by athletes (up to 90 seconds duration each), increases 
joint range of motion by increasing stretch tolerance while the viscoelastic characteristics of the muscle remain 
unaltered (Magnussen et al, 1998)
• Different rates of loading and stretching have different effects on bone, tendon and muscle
• Prolonged slow stretching can cause permanent viscous deformation of connective tissue and high levels of 
strain in muscle
• Physiotherapeutic PNF shows that rapid or powerful recruitment o f the different stretch reflexes can be 
safely applied to rehabilitate and strengthen - contrary to common belief
• There is generally no such thing as an unsafe stretch or exercise: only an unsafe way of executing any 
movement for a specific individual at a specific time
• Elastic fibres occur in small concentrations in the intercellular matrix of tendons and most ligaments, and may 
help restore the crimped collagen fibre configuration after stretching or muscle contraction
• Multi-directional stretching is important, since the structural orientation o f the fibres is different for the 
different collagenous tissues and is specifically suited to the functions of each tissue
• The stress concentration at the insertion o f the ligament and tendon into the more rigid bone structure is 
decreased by the existence of three progressively stiffer transitional composite materials - a system which can 
be disrupted by ingestion of anabolic steroids
• At slow loading rates, the bony insertion of a ligament or tendon is the weakest component of the bone-soft 
tissue complex, whereas the soft tissues are the weakest components at very fast loading rates
• Tendons, unlike ligaments, are not simply passive stabilisers of joints - instead, together with strongly 
contracted muscle fibres (particularly during phases of eccentric contraction), they play a vital role in storing 
elastic energy during running and other impulsive motor acts, thereby saving energy and increasing the 
efficiency of muscular activity (Goldspink, 1978).
• No stretching manoeuvres must compromise the strength or ability of the tendons to store elastic energy 
throughout their range of movement - thus, tendon stretching exercises should be accompanied by strength 
conditioning against adequate resistance.
• Since tendons and ligaments arc viscoelastic, they exhibit sensitivity to loading rate, and undergo stress 
relaxation, creep and hysteresis.
• Russian and Eastern European scientists discourage the use of cycling by athletes who require large ranges of 
trunk and hip flexibility, since they have discovered that cycling tends to decrease the functional ROM for 
these types of athlete. Instead, they encourage intensive sprinting and interval training which tend to use and 
strengthen the hip and knee joints over a much fuller range of movement. The massive preoccupation of 
Western gym users with fixed bicycles or treadmill jogging to promote cardiovascular conditioning may then 
be seen to be potentially detrimental to serious athletes whose joints need to operate over a far more 
expansive range. These same scientists also discourage conventional pushups and situps because they tend to 
limit the functional ROM of the shoulder and trunk regions, respectively. 
Push-ups on floor dipping bars or 
on parallel bars arc preferred, as are backward lying situps over pommel horses or 'Roman chairs'.

• Physiotherapeutic PNF shows that rapid or powerful recruitment o f the different stretch reflexes can be 
safely applied to rehabilitate and strengthen - contrary to common belief
• There is generally no such thing as an unsafe stretch or exercise: only an unsafe way of executing any 
movement for a specific individual at a specific time

help restore the crimped collagen fibre configuration after stretching or muscle contraction

different collagenous tissues and is specifically suited to the functions of each tissue

decreased by the existence of three progressively stiffer transitional composite materials - a system which can 
be disrupted by ingestion of anabolic steroids

efficiency of muscular activity (Goldspink, 1978).

throughout their range of movement - thus, tendon stretching exercises should be accompanied by strength 
conditioning against adequate resistance.

relaxation, creep and hysteresis.

trunk and hip flexibility, since they have discovered that cycling tends to decrease the functional ROM for 
these types of athlete. Instead, they encourage intensive sprinting and interval training which tend to use and 
strengthen the hip and knee joints over a much fuller range of movement. The massive preoccupation of 
Western gym users with fixed bicycles or treadmill jogging to promote cardiovascular conditioning may then 
be seen to be potentially detrimental to serious athletes whose joints need to operate over a far more 
expansive range. These same scientists also discourage conventional pushups and situps because they tend to 
limit the functional ROM of the shoulder and trunk regions, respectively. 
Push-ups on floor dipping bars or 
on parallel bars arc preferred, as are backward lying situps over pommel horses or 'Roman chairs'.

# Six Factors That Shift an Individual's Flexibility

**What it is** — The authors list six factors that influence flexibility in general:
1. **Exercise and training history.** Regular full-range exercise generally enhances
flexibility. Athletes develop patterns of flexibility characteristic of their sport;
long-term flexibility can be reduced by a sedentary lifestyle, by training that rarely
uses full-range joint motion, by excessive hypertrophy focus, or by soft-tissue injury.
Short-term flexibility can be decreased by overtraining-induced soreness, stiffness, or
injury; tissue mechanical stiffness stays fairly constant during exercise, but damping
ratio invariably increases (Siff, 1986). As a specific instance of this factor, the authors
report that Russian and Eastern European scientists discourage cycling for athletes who
need large trunk and hip ROM, because cycling is held to decrease functional ROM in those
joints; they instead favor intensive sprinting and interval training, and similarly
discourage conventional push-ups and sit-ups (which limit shoulder and trunk ROM
respectively) in favor of push-ups on dip bars/parallel bars and backward sit-ups over a
pommel horse or "Roman chair."
2. **Age.** Flexibility generally decreases with age, raising soft-tissue injury
susceptibility during intensive exercise; regular exercise combined with flexibility
training can minimize this. Maximum flexibility is not at its peak in the youngest infants
but is reached between ages 10 and 12, depending on gender (Beaulieu, 1986).
3. **Gender.** Females tend to be more flexible than males at equivalent joints; the
damping ratio of females' joint soft tissues is greater than males', implying females are
intrinsically better equipped to absorb elastic stretch, and the pain threshold for joint
torsion is generally significantly lower in females (Siff, 1986).
4. **Temperature.** Increased muscle temperature (active warm-up, passive massage,
ultrasound) increases flexibility, including improved plastic deformation of collagenous
tissue during stretching; a gentle rhythmic warm-up is recommended before flexibility
training. Prolonged heat or cold can produce analgesia or otherwise modify the
neuromuscular processes behind the stretch and tendon reflexes, enhancing relaxation and
stretching; cooling tissue with ice for the final minutes of stretching is reported to
stabilize connective tissue at its new length (Sapega et al., 1981).
5. **Type of joint.** Flexibility is specific to each joint; an overall flexibility index
can be built by averaging a representative sample of joints, but what matters
practically is establishing static and dynamic ROM for the specific joints most important
to a given sport.
6. **Type of movement.** The relative degree of flexibility differs for each degree of
joint freedom; increasing flexibility in a direction that would compromise a joint's
stability during a specific movement should be avoided. Optimum, not maximum, static and
dynamic flexibility is required for each degree of freedom; subjects hypermobile in
certain joints should avoid increasing flexibility further at the expense of stability.
(PDF pp. 189-191, printed pp. 178-180.)

**Why it works** — No single mechanism unifies these six; each is the authors' summary of
a separate cited source (Siff 1986; Beaulieu 1986; Sapega et al. 1981) or an unsourced
general observation.

**When to apply** — Use factor 6 as a direct programming caution: do not chase additional
ROM in a hypermobile athlete's already-loose joint, since the goal is optimum, not maximum,
flexibility per degree of freedom. Use factor 4 to sequence a session: warm before
stretching, and consider a brief cooling period at the end of a stretch to help "lock in"
a new tissue length (Sapega et al., 1981).

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence capped at `supported`.** The cycling/push-up/sit-up
recommendation under factor 1 is attributed only to unnamed "Russian and Eastern European
scientists," with no specific citation or study design given; treat it as a single
tradition's programming preference, not an established finding, and do not extend it to
justify removing cycling or sit-ups from a Baylor program without independent evidence.
The gender pain-threshold and damping-ratio claims (Siff, 1986) are also single-source and
not cross-checked against a modern sex-differences study in this entry.

**Example** — The book's own example: breast-stroke swimmers versus backstroke/butterfly
swimmers show opposite shoulder/ankle-versus-hip/knee mobility patterns, illustrating that
"type of joint" and training history jointly produce sport-specific flexibility profiles
rather than one general flexibility trait (see also
[[claim--active-flexibility-correlates-more-with-sporting-proficiency-than-passive]]).

**Related** — [[framework--flexibility-definition-and-rom-determinants]],
[[claim--active-flexibility-correlates-more-with-sporting-proficiency-than-passive]].

# Six Factors That Shift an Individual's Flexibility

**What it is** — The authors list six factors that influence flexibility in general:
1. **Exercise and training history.** Regular full-range exercise generally enhances
flexibility. Athletes develop patterns of flexibility characteristic of their sport;
long-term flexibility can be reduced by a sedentary lifestyle, by training that rarely
uses full-range joint motion, by excessive hypertrophy focus, or by soft-tissue injury.
Short-term flexibility can be decreased by overtraining-induced soreness, stiffness, or
injury; tissue mechanical stiffness stays fairly constant during exercise, but damping
ratio invariably increases (Siff, 1986).
2. **Age.** Flexibility generally decreases with age, raising soft-tissue injury
susceptibility during intensive exercise; regular exercise combined with flexibility
training can minimize this. Maximum flexibility is not at its peak in the youngest infants
but is reached between ages 10 and 12, depending on gender (Beaulieu, 1986).
3. **Gender.** Females tend to be more flexible than males at equivalent joints; the
damping ratio of females' joint soft tissues is greater than males', implying females are
intrinsically better equipped to absorb elastic stretch, and the pain threshold for joint
torsion is generally significantly lower in females (Siff, 1986; this is Siff, one of the
book's own authors, citing his own separate work, not an independent source).
4. **Temperature.** Increased muscle temperature (active warm-up, passive massage,
ultrasound) increases flexibility, including improved plastic deformation of collagenous
tissue during stretching; a gentle rhythmic warm-up is recommended before flexibility
training. Prolonged heat or cold can produce analgesia or otherwise modify the
neuromuscular processes behind the stretch and tendon reflexes, enhancing relaxation and
stretching; cooling tissue with ice for the final minutes of stretching is reported to
stabilize connective tissue at its new length (Sapega et al., 1981).
5. **Type of joint.** Flexibility is specific to each joint; an overall flexibility index
can be built by averaging a representative sample of joints, but what matters
practically is establishing static and dynamic ROM for the specific joints most important
to a given sport.
6. **Type of movement.** The relative degree of flexibility differs for each degree of
joint freedom; increasing flexibility in a direction that would compromise a joint's
stability during a specific movement should be avoided. Optimum, not maximum, static and
dynamic flexibility is required for each degree of freedom; subjects hypermobile in
certain joints should avoid increasing flexibility further at the expense of stability.
(PDF pp. 190-192, printed pp. 179-181.)

Separately, in the following section's list of soft-tissue biomechanics points (3.5.6,
printed 181, not part of this six-factor list), the authors report without citation that
Russian and Eastern European scientists discourage cycling for athletes who need large
trunk and hip ROM, "since they have discovered that cycling tends to decrease the
functional ROM for these types of athlete"; they instead favor intensive sprinting and
interval training, and similarly discourage conventional push-ups and sit-ups (said to
limit shoulder and trunk ROM respectively) in favor of push-ups on dip bars/parallel bars
and backward sit-ups over a pommel horse or "Roman chair." Uncited aphorism; `untested`.
Elsewhere the book lists cycling as an indirect warm-up means that "can often enhance
performance" (Franks list, printed 164), which this passage does not address.

**Why it works** — No single mechanism unifies these six; each is the authors' summary of
a separate cited source (Siff 1986; Beaulieu 1986; Sapega et al. 1981) or an unsourced
general observation.

**When to apply** — Use factor 6 as a direct programming caution: do not chase additional
ROM in a hypermobile athlete's already-loose joint, since the goal is optimum, not maximum,
flexibility per degree of freedom. Use factor 4 to sequence a session: warm before
stretching, and consider a brief cooling period at the end of a stretch to help "lock in"
a new tissue length (Sapega et al., 1981).

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence capped at `supported`.** The cycling/push-up/sit-up
recommendation under factor 1 is attributed only to unnamed "Russian and Eastern European
scientists," with no specific citation or study design given; treat it as a single
tradition's programming preference, not an established finding, and do not extend it to
justify removing cycling or sit-ups from a Baylor program without independent evidence.
The gender pain-threshold and damping-ratio claims (Siff, 1986) are also single-source and
not cross-checked against a modern sex-differences study in this entry.

**Example** — The book's own example: breast-stroke swimmers versus backstroke/butterfly
swimmers show opposite shoulder/ankle-versus-hip/knee mobility patterns, illustrating that
"type of joint" and training history jointly produce sport-specific flexibility profiles
rather than one general flexibility trait (see also
[[claim--active-flexibility-correlates-more-with-sporting-proficiency-than-passive]]).

**Related** — [[framework--flexibility-definition-and-rom-determinants]],
[[claim--active-flexibility-correlates-more-with-sporting-proficiency-than-passive]].

14	# Ordinary Stretching Increases ROM by Raising Stretch Tolerance, Not by Changing Muscle Viscoelastic Properties
15	
16	**What it is** — The authors state: "Static and cyclic stretching, as commonly performed
17	by athletes (up to 90 seconds duration each), increases joint range of motion by
18	increasing stretch tolerance while the viscoelastic characteristics of the muscle remain
19	unaltered" (Magnussen et al., 1998). (PDF p. 191, printed p. 181.)
20	
21	**Why it works** — The authors give no further mechanism for why stretch tolerance itself
22	increases; the citation (Magnussen et al., 1998) is offered as the source of the finding,
23	not explained here. Inference: "stretch tolerance" implies the limiting factor in a typical
24	short-duration static/cyclic stretch is the point at which the nervous system perceives the
25	stretch as uncomfortable or reaches a reflex-protective threshold, not the muscle-tendon
26	unit's actual length-tension (stiffness) properties, which this citation reports as
27	unchanged.
28	
29	**When to apply** — Use this to set an accurate expectation for a single stretching
30	session or short block: an acute or short-term ROM gain from static/cyclic stretching in
31	this duration range should be read as increased tolerance to the sensation of stretch, not
32	as evidence the muscle-tendon unit itself has become mechanically more compliant. This is
33	consistent with, and gives a mechanism for, the book's separate claim that brief
34	pre-training stretching mainly produces short-term (not tissue-level, long-term) flexibility
35	change (see
36	[[framework--four-methods-of-enhancing-rom-ranked-by-effectiveness]]).
37	
38	**When NOT to apply** — Do not extend this specific claim (static/cyclic stretching, up to
39	90 seconds per stretch) to other stretching modes (ballistic, PNF, long-duration static
40	holds well beyond 90 seconds) without separate evidence; the book does not state this
41	mechanism applies to those. Do not use "stretch tolerance increased, tissue unchanged" to
42	argue stretching has no tissue-level benefit at all: this entry describes the mechanism of
43	short-duration ROM gain specifically, not the long-term soft-tissue adaptations covered
44	elsewhere (see [[claim--ligament-tendon-adaptation-and-detraining-response]]).
45	
46	**Example** — Inference: an athlete who gains 5 degrees of hip flexion after a single
47	90-second hamstring stretch has very likely become more tolerant of that stretch sensation
48	in that session, not changed the mechanical stiffness of the hamstring muscle-tendon unit;
49	retesting the next day without further stretching would be expected to show the gain has
50	mostly reverted.
51

53	[[claim--stretching-benefits-list-from-older-literature-review]].

# The Bone-Tendon Junction Has a Graded Stiffness Transition That Anabolic Steroids Can Disrupt

**What it is** — The authors state the stress concentration at the insertion of a ligament
or tendon into more rigid bone is decreased by the existence of three progressively
stiffer transitional composite materials, a system which "can be disrupted by ingestion of

p. 181.)

disruption claim); it is presented as an assertion, not a derived or referenced finding
here.

connective tissue injury risk with Athletic Medicine: this passage gives a specific,
though uncited, mechanism (disruption of the graded stiffness transition at the

**What it is** — The authors state: "Static and cyclic stretching, as commonly performed
by athletes (up to 90 seconds duration each), increases joint range of motion by
increasing stretch tolerance while the viscoelastic characteristics of the muscle remain
unaltered" (printed as "Magnussen et al, 1998"; likely Magnusson SP, 1998, a review in
Scand J Med Sci Sports 8:65-77, verify). (PDF p. 192, printed p. 181.)

G5, internal tension not recorded elsewhere, spanning four pages the authors do not
reconcile: printed 179 (PDF 190) frames pre-event stretching as producing "short-term
(elastic)" tissue change; printed 180 (PDF 191) says warmth improves "plastic deformation"
of collagenous tissue and that cooling with ice "seems to stabilise connective tissues at
their new length" (Sapega et al., 1981); printed 181 (this section) says static stretching
"has a more pronounced effect on the PEC" than ballistic, and that "prolonged slow
stretching can cause permanent viscous deformation of connective tissue"; printed 176 says
tendons and ligaments "can be permanently deformed or damaged by over-zealous or prolonged
stretching." All four describe some form of tissue-level change from stretching, which sits
against this section's own claim that viscoelastic properties "remain unaltered." Ch1
[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]] (printed 41-42) says static
stretching mainly loads the PEC, consistent with this section's PEC/SEC distinction but not
with "unaltered."

increases; the citation (Magnusson et al., 1998) is offered as the source of the finding,
not explained here. Inference: "stretch tolerance" implies the limiting factor in a typical
short-duration static/cyclic stretch is the point at which the nervous system perceives the
stretch as uncomfortable, a perceptual/sensory account, not the muscle-tendon unit's actual
length-tension (stiffness) properties, which this citation reports as unchanged. A separate,
weaker inference sometimes offered in the literature is a reflex-protective threshold
account (verify, e.g. Weppler & Magnusson 2010, Phys Ther 90:438); the book does not raise
this, and it is a distinct claim from sensory tolerance, not interchangeable with it.

**When to apply** — Inference: use this to set an accurate expectation for a single
stretching session or short block: an acute or short-term ROM gain from static/cyclic
stretching in this duration range should be read as increased tolerance to the sensation of
stretch, not as evidence the muscle-tendon unit itself has become mechanically more
compliant. The book's own separate claim that brief pre-training stretching mainly produces
short-term flexibility change (see
[[framework--four-methods-of-enhancing-rom-ranked-by-effectiveness]]) describes that
short-term change as elastic tissue change, not as a sensory-tolerance effect; the two
accounts are not the same mechanism, and the book does not connect them.

# Ordinary Stretching Increases ROM by Raising Stretch Tolerance, Not by Changing Muscle Viscoelastic Properties

**What it is** — The authors state: "Static and cyclic stretching, as commonly performed
by athletes (up to 90 seconds duration each), increases joint range of motion by
increasing stretch tolerance while the viscoelastic characteristics of the muscle remain
unaltered" (Magnussen et al., 1998). (PDF p. 191, printed p. 181.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no further mechanism for why stretch tolerance itself
increases; the citation (Magnussen et al., 1998) is offered as the source of the finding,
not explained here. Inference: "stretch tolerance" implies the limiting factor in a typical
short-duration static/cyclic stretch is the point at which the nervous system perceives the
stretch as uncomfortable or reaches a reflex-protective threshold, not the muscle-tendon
unit's actual length-tension (stiffness) properties, which this citation reports as
unchanged.

**When to apply** — Use this to set an accurate expectation for a single stretching
session or short block: an acute or short-term ROM gain from static/cyclic stretching in
this duration range should be read as increased tolerance to the sensation of stretch, not
as evidence the muscle-tendon unit itself has become mechanically more compliant. This is
consistent with, and gives a mechanism for, the book's separate claim that brief
pre-training stretching mainly produces short-term (not tissue-level, long-term) flexibility
change (see
[[framework--four-methods-of-enhancing-rom-ranked-by-effectiveness]]).

**When NOT to apply** — Do not extend this specific claim (static/cyclic stretching, up to
90 seconds per stretch) to other stretching modes (ballistic, PNF, long-duration static
holds well beyond 90 seconds) without separate evidence; the book does not state this
mechanism applies to those. Do not use "stretch tolerance increased, tissue unchanged" to
argue stretching has no tissue-level benefit at all: this entry describes the mechanism of
short-duration ROM gain specifically, not the long-term soft-tissue adaptations covered
elsewhere (see [[claim--ligament-tendon-adaptation-and-detraining-response]]).

**Example** — Inference: an athlete who gains 5 degrees of hip flexion after a single
90-second hamstring stretch has very likely become more tolerant of that stretch sensation
in that session, not changed the mechanical stiffness of the hamstring muscle-tendon unit;
retesting the next day without further stretching would be expected to show the gain has
mostly reverted.

**Related** — [[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]],
[[claim--stretching-benefits-list-from-older-literature-review]].

SUPERTRAINING
• Flexibility and motor skill are also affected by emotion and discomfort or perception of pain, because there are 
emotion-related and pain-interpreting centres in the cerebrum and the cerebellum that are closely related to the 
execution of patterned movement. The role of relaxation procedures and breathing regimes that promote 
relaxation, as taught in yoga, Tai Chi and childbirth, can be valuable in enhancing flexibility training. 
I!
Flexibility, Stability and Muscle A ctivity
Despite the widespread opinion that the muscles act as efficient synergistic stabilisers, it should be remembered 
that the musculature cannot respond quickly enough to protect a joint against injury if large impacts are applied 
rapidly, particularly if they arc torsional (Pope et al, 1978). It is probably more accurate to state that joint 
stabilisation takes place in the following manner:
1. The contractile element of muscle activated by the stretch reflex complex, together with the SEC of that 
musclc, act as primary stabilisers of the joint if the loading rate permits the muscles to respond rapidly 
enough.
2. If the joint reaches the physical limits of muscle length, strength or endurance, it has to rely on protection by 
ligaments and the SEC of its muscles. If, at the same time, the inverse stretch reflex signals the muscles to 
relax at their maximum length, then the PEC of the muscle will also contribute to joint stabilisation. 
However, it should be noted that receptors resembling Golgi tendon organs have been located on the surface 
of cruciate ligaments (Schultz ct al, 1984) and that muscles will show reflex contraction if ligaments are 
stretched until pain results (Basmajian, 1978).
3. If the joint is extended to its limits without sufficient muscle contraction becoming possible, primary 
stabilisation is afforded by the ligaments and the PEC of the muscles. As soon as the initial latency period 
for musclc excitation is over, the contracting musclcs and their SEC will contribute as secondary stabilisers.
4. In certain joints skeletal structure can act as the final stabiliser during movements to the limits of the joint.
Since joint stability involves three-dimensional actions over the many degrees of freedom outlined near the 
beginning of this section, the necessity for appropriately conditioning all the interacting soft tissues again becomes 
obvious. These facts are directly relevant to appreciating the difference between static, active, passive and ballistic 
modes of stretching, with slow and rapid loading rates having different effects on the each of the soft tissues.
3.5.7 The Influence of Exercise on C onnective Tissue
Most texts focus more on the effect of different training programmes on muscle than on the collagenous tissues, 
despite the fact that many animal studies have shown that physical training also strengthens the attachments of 
tendons and ligaments to bone. Trained ligaments are thicker and heavier, though the increase in mass is not 
necessarily associated with greater concentration of collagen, a process which is still poorly understood (Booth & 
Gould, 1975). In this regard, controlled strain on the soft tissues may increase the formulation of fibres in them, 
thereby contributing to enhanced elasticity and strength (Holland, 1968).
Regular resistance training produce not only musclc hypertrophy, but also an increase in the collagen content 
of the ligaments and the connective tissues that surround the muscle fibres (Tipton et al, 1975). At the same time, 
the activity of an enzyme involved with collagen synthesis is increased by training, an effect which may be 
stimulated by lactic acid production during exercise (Booth & Gould, 1975). It should be noted, however, that 
moderate intensity treadmill training of rats produces neither muscle hypertrophy nor increased growth of intra­
muscular connective tissue. Prolonged, low intensity training evidently suffices to condition the cardiovascular 
system significantly, but not the musculoskeletal system. Apparently it is anaerobic, muscle endurance training 
which has the most pronounced effect on enhancing the concentration and strength of collagenous tissue and its 
junction zones. Progressive stretching regimes in conjunction with this type of training would then be seen to be 
especially valuable as a component of all sports preparation.
In contrast to chronic training, single exercise sessions, occasional stretching or sprint training do not produce 
significant increase in junction strength, although sprinting produces marked increases in ligament mass and 
concentration (Tipton ct al, 1974). Then, just as ligaments become stronger and stiffer when subjected to 
increased stress, so they becomc weaker and less stiff with decreased stress, immobilisation and inactivity 
(Tipton et al, 1970). The similar changes noted with ageing may be due not only to the degenerative process but 
also to inactivity.
182

===== PDF idx 194 (printed 183) =====
SUPERTRAININC
In the light of the above analysis the choice of stretching regime must also take into account the subject's 
stale of training, age and health. Furthermore, alteration in hormonal balance during pregnancy, menstruation and 
administration of exogenous hormones (such as anabolic steroids and cortisone) can affect the mechanical 
characteristics of collagenous tissue, so that stretching techniques should be adjusted accordingly (Viidik, 1973).
3.5.8 Stretching Techniques
Practical experience has led to recognition for four fairly traditional categories of stretching, namely: static, 
ballistic, passive and contract-relax (or PNF - proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation) stretching. To this list 
may be added normal, full range of movement exercise, since it also tends to increase both active and passive 
flexibility. In addition, Olympic Weightlifters are amongst the most supple of all athletes, despite beliefs to the 
contrary (Siff, 1987). Furthermore, a combination of stretching and weight-training exercises as a supplement to a 
sprint-training programme produces significantly greater increases in speed over an unsupplemented sprint 
programme (Siff, 1987). Then, in several of the preceding sections, the role of resistance and muscle endurance 
training in enhancing tissue strength and flexibility was noted. In other words, suitable full-range resistance 
training also can improve joint flexibility.
With reference to PNF, it is misleading to regard it or even its contract-relax technique as a specialised system 
used primarily to enhance flexibility. There arc at least four distinct types of PNF stretching, anyway. 
In 
professional practice, PNF offers a comprehensive form of therapy which conditions neuromuscular processes, 
isometric and dynamic strength, muscular endurance and functional flexibility more completely than many 
machine routines (see Ch 7).
In achieving these ends, its various three-dimensional spiral and diagonal patterns and techniques of 
movement rely on numerous static, active, ballistic and passive manoeuvres. Thus, several o f the supposedly 
distinct types of stretching may be seen to form a subset of the entire discipline of PNF (see Ch 7).
Static stretching normally refers to flexibility exercises which use the weight of the body or its limbs to load 
the soft tissues. Rarely is this term applied to stretches which are forcibly produced by voluntary muscular 
contractions, yet this 'cat-strctch' technique is employed successfully in the cat kingdom, by most humans on 
waking in the morning and by bodybuilders in their posing routines. Obviously the concept of static stretching 
needs to be expanded.
These facts imply that a more comprehensive categorisation of stretching techniques is necessary. 
The 
following integrated model identifies two broad types of stretching, each containing a series of distinct, but 
related, categories of stretching (Fig 3.34):
1. Static S tretching
• Free Static Stretching, which imposes no external loading to increase ROM under conditions of (a) muscle 
relaxation or (b) isometric muscle contraction (sometimes called Active Static Stretching)
• Passive Static Stretching, which imposes external loading on (a) relaxed or (b) isometrically contracted 
muscles
2. Dynamic S tretching
• Ballistic Stretching, which imposes passive momentum to exceed static ROM on (a) the relaxed or (b) 
the contracted muscic complcx. The ballistic action may be done slowly or rapidly, as described later in 
this section.
• Active Stretching, which involves continuous muscle activity to exceed the static ROM, as encountered 
during normal full-range sporting activities
• PNF Stretching methods, which involve intermittent or continuous phases of static or dynamic muscic 
action, as well as relaxation or passive movement in specific patterns of activation and relaxation
• Plyometric (Impulsive) Stretching, which involves rapid termination of eccentric loading followed by a
brief isometric phase and an explosive rebound relying on stored elastic energy and powerful reflex 
muscle contraction. This 'stretch-shortening' action is not intended to increase ROM, but to use specific 
stretching phenomena to increase speed-strength of movement for a specific sporting purpose (see 
5.2.4). It may also be viewed as a form of ballistic stretching done impulsively or explosively.
183

# The Bone-Tendon Junction Has a Graded Stiffness Transition That Anabolic Steroids Can Disrupt

14	# What Actually Stabilizes a Joint Changes as It Approaches End-Range
15	
16	**What it is** — Against the "widespread opinion that muscles act as efficient synergistic
17	stabilisers," the authors argue muscle cannot always respond quickly enough to protect a
18	joint against a large, rapid (particularly torsional) impact (Pope et al., 1978), and
19	propose joint stabilization instead works in a sequence:
20	1. The contractile element (activated by the stretch reflex complex) together with the
21	muscle's series elastic component (SEC) act as primary stabilizers, if the loading rate
22	allows the muscle to respond in time.
23	2. If the joint reaches the physical limits of muscle length, strength, or endurance,
24	protection shifts to the ligaments and the SEC; if the inverse stretch reflex (GTO) signals
25	the muscle to relax at its maximum length, the muscle's parallel elastic component (PEC)
26	also contributes to stabilization. Receptors resembling Golgi tendon organs have been found
27	on the surface of cruciate ligaments (Schultz et al., 1984), and muscles show reflex
28	contraction if ligaments are stretched to the point of pain (Basmajian, 1978).
29	3. If the joint is extended to its limit without sufficient muscle contraction, primary
30	stabilization is provided by ligaments and the PEC; once the initial latency period for
31	muscle excitation passes, the contracting muscle and its SEC contribute as secondary
32	stabilizers.
33	4. In certain joints, skeletal structure itself can act as the final stabilizer at the
34	limits of joint movement.
35	(PDF p. 193, printed p. 182.)
36

38	the SEC, PEC, and stretch/inverse-stretch reflexes elsewhere in the text (see
39	[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]] and
40	[[framework--stretch-reflex-types-and-neuromuscular-control-of-flexibility]]), combined
41	with the cited finding that ligaments themselves carry GTO-like tension receptors (Schultz
42	et al., 1984) and can trigger protective muscle contraction (Basmajian, 1978).
43	
44	**When to apply** — Use this sequence to explain why a joint can be injured even with
45	strong, well-conditioned muscles around it: at high loading rates (stage 1's premise
46	fails), stabilization falls to ligament and PEC tissue that may not be conditioned to the
47	same standard as the muscle. This reframes injury-prevention conditioning as needing to
48	address ligament/capsule tissue specifically, not only muscular strength.
49	
50	**When NOT to apply** — This is the authors' synthesized model, not a single cited
51	experimental finding; treat the four numbered stages as an organizing framework for
52	reasoning about joint stabilization, not as a validated, measured sequence with defined
53	timing thresholds. Confidence is capped at `supported` because the sequence itself

# What Actually Stabilizes a Joint Changes as It Approaches End-Range

**What it is** — Against the "widespread opinion that muscles act as efficient synergistic
stabilisers," the authors argue muscle cannot always respond quickly enough to protect a
joint against a large, rapid (particularly torsional) impact (Pope et al., 1978), and
propose joint stabilization instead works in a sequence:
1. The contractile element (activated by the stretch reflex complex) together with the
muscle's series elastic component (SEC) act as primary stabilizers, if the loading rate
allows the muscle to respond in time.
2. If the joint reaches the physical limits of muscle length, strength, or endurance,
protection shifts to the ligaments and the SEC; if the inverse stretch reflex (GTO) signals
the muscle to relax at its maximum length, the muscle's parallel elastic component (PEC)
also contributes to stabilization. Receptors resembling Golgi tendon organs have been found
on the surface of cruciate ligaments (Schultz et al., 1984), and muscles show reflex
contraction if ligaments are stretched to the point of pain (Basmajian, 1978).
3. If the joint is extended to its limit without sufficient muscle contraction, primary
stabilization is provided by ligaments and the PEC; once the initial latency period for
muscle excitation passes, the contracting muscle and its SEC contribute as secondary
stabilizers.
4. In certain joints, skeletal structure itself can act as the final stabilizer at the
limits of joint movement.
(PDF p. 193, printed p. 182.)

**Why it works** — The sequence follows from the mechanical roles already established for
the SEC, PEC, and stretch/inverse-stretch reflexes elsewhere in the text (see
[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]] and
[[framework--stretch-reflex-types-and-neuromuscular-control-of-flexibility]]), combined
with the cited finding that ligaments themselves carry GTO-like tension receptors (Schultz
et al., 1984) and can trigger protective muscle contraction (Basmajian, 1978).

**When to apply** — Use this sequence to explain why a joint can be injured even with
strong, well-conditioned muscles around it: at high loading rates (stage 1's premise
fails), stabilization falls to ligament and PEC tissue that may not be conditioned to the
same standard as the muscle. This reframes injury-prevention conditioning as needing to
address ligament/capsule tissue specifically, not only muscular strength.

**When NOT to apply** — This is the authors' synthesized model, not a single cited
experimental finding; treat the four numbered stages as an organizing framework for
reasoning about joint stabilization, not as a validated, measured sequence with defined
timing thresholds. Confidence is capped at `supported` because the sequence itself
(as opposed to the individual cited facts feeding it) is not independently attributed to a
specific study.

**Example** — Inference: a sudden, high-velocity valgus torque to the knee arrives faster
than stage 1's muscular response can engage, meaning stages 2-3 (ligament and PEC) bear
more of the load than they would under a slower, anticipated movement, which is consistent
with why acute ligament injuries often occur on unanticipated contact.

[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].

14	# "There Is No Unsafe Stretch, Only an Unsafe Way of Executing It"
15	
16	**What it is** — In a bulleted list of biomechanical points on stretching, the authors
17	state: "There is generally no such thing as an unsafe stretch or exercise: only an unsafe
18	way of executing any movement for a specific individual at a specific time." (PDF p. 192,
19	printed p. 181.) This appears alongside a related claim in the same list that
20	physiotherapeutic PNF shows rapid or powerful recruitment of the different stretch
21	reflexes can be safely applied to rehabilitate and strengthen tissue, "contrary to common
22	belief."
23	
24	**Why it works** — The authors give no supporting mechanism, study, or citation for this
25	specific aphorism; it reads as a stated position, not a derived or evidenced conclusion in
26	this passage.
27	
28	**When to apply** — Useful as a reframing prompt when an exercise or stretch is being
29	categorically banned ("we never do ballistic stretching," "no PNF for this population"):
30	ask whether the concern is really about the movement class itself, or about a specific
31	athlete's readiness, technique, loading rate, or tissue state for that movement at that
32	time.
33	
34	**When NOT to apply** — **`untested`, unlabeled aphorism with no supporting citation in
35	this passage.** Do not use this claim to override a specific, evidence-based
36	contraindication (e.g. a known ligament laxity, an acute strain, a post-surgical range
37	restriction) on the reasoning that "there's no unsafe stretch, only unsafe execution": the
38	book gives no criteria here for what counts as safe execution, and the claim is broad
39	enough to be difficult to falsify. Treat it as a coaching-philosophy prompt, not a safety
40	rule.
41	
42	**Example** — The book's own paired example: it treats the popular blanket rule "ballistic

# "There Is No Unsafe Stretch, Only an Unsafe Way of Executing It"

**What it is** — In a bulleted list of biomechanical points on stretching, the authors
state: "There is generally no such thing as an unsafe stretch or exercise: only an unsafe
way of executing any movement for a specific individual at a specific time." (PDF p. 192,
printed p. 181.) This appears alongside a related claim in the same list that
physiotherapeutic PNF shows rapid or powerful recruitment of the different stretch
reflexes can be safely applied to rehabilitate and strengthen tissue, "contrary to common
belief."

**Why it works** — The authors give no supporting mechanism, study, or citation for this
specific aphorism; it reads as a stated position, not a derived or evidenced conclusion in
this passage.

**When to apply** — Useful as a reframing prompt when an exercise or stretch is being
categorically banned ("we never do ballistic stretching," "no PNF for this population"):
ask whether the concern is really about the movement class itself, or about a specific
athlete's readiness, technique, loading rate, or tissue state for that movement at that
time.

**When NOT to apply** — **`untested`, unlabeled aphorism with no supporting citation in
this passage.** Do not use this claim to override a specific, evidence-based
contraindication (e.g. a known ligament laxity, an acute strain, a post-surgical range
restriction) on the reasoning that "there's no unsafe stretch, only unsafe execution": the
book gives no criteria here for what counts as safe execution, and the claim is broad
enough to be difficult to falsify. Treat it as a coaching-philosophy prompt, not a safety
rule.

**Example** — The book's own paired example: it treats the popular blanket rule "ballistic
stretching should be avoided at all costs" as the kind of overgeneralization this heuristic
is meant to counter, arguing instead that rate and technique determine ballistic
stretching's safety (see
[[heuristic--ballistic-stretching-safe-with-gradual-progressive-protocol]]).

**Related** — [[heuristic--ballistic-stretching-safe-with-gradual-progressive-protocol]].

# What Actually Stabilizes a Joint Changes as It Approaches End-Range

**What it is** — Against the "widespread opinion that muscles act as efficient synergistic
stabilisers," the authors argue muscle cannot always respond quickly enough to protect a
joint against a large, rapid (particularly torsional) impact (Pope et al., 1978), and
propose joint stabilization instead works in a sequence:
1. The contractile element (activated by the stretch reflex complex) together with the
muscle's series elastic component (SEC) act as primary stabilizers, if the loading rate
allows the muscle to respond in time.
2. If the joint reaches the physical limits of muscle length, strength, or endurance,
protection shifts to the ligaments and the SEC; if the inverse stretch reflex (GTO) signals
the muscle to relax at its maximum length, the muscle's parallel elastic component (PEC)
also contributes to stabilization. Receptors resembling Golgi tendon organs have been found
on the surface of cruciate ligaments (Schultz et al., 1984), and muscles show reflex
contraction if ligaments are stretched to the point of pain (Basmajian, 1978).
3. If the joint is extended to its limit without sufficient muscle contraction, primary
stabilization is provided by ligaments and the PEC; once the initial latency period for
muscle excitation passes, the contracting muscle and its SEC contribute as secondary
stabilizers.
4. In certain joints, skeletal structure itself can act as the final stabilizer at the
limits of joint movement.
(PDF p. 193, printed p. 182.)

**Why it works** — The sequence follows from the mechanical roles already established for
the SEC, PEC, and stretch/inverse-stretch reflexes elsewhere in the text (see
[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]] and
[[framework--stretch-reflex-types-and-neuromuscular-control-of-flexibility]]), combined
with the cited finding that ligaments themselves carry GTO-like tension receptors (Schultz
et al., 1984) and can trigger protective muscle contraction (Basmajian, 1978).

**When to apply** — Use this sequence to explain why a joint can be injured even with
strong, well-conditioned muscles around it: at high loading rates (stage 1's premise
fails), stabilization falls to ligament and PEC tissue that may not be conditioned to the
same standard as the muscle. This reframes injury-prevention conditioning as needing to
address ligament/capsule tissue specifically, not only muscular strength.

**When NOT to apply** — This is the authors' synthesized model, not a single cited
experimental finding; treat the four numbered stages as an organizing framework for
reasoning about joint stabilization, not as a validated, measured sequence with defined
timing thresholds. Confidence is capped at `supported` because the sequence itself
(as opposed to the individual cited facts feeding it) is not independently attributed to a
specific study.

**Example** — Inference: a sudden, high-velocity valgus torque to the knee arrives faster
than stage 1's muscular response can engage, meaning stages 2-3 (ligament and PEC) bear
more of the load than they would under a slower, anticipated movement, which is consistent
with why acute ligament injuries often occur on unanticipated contact.

**Related** — [[framework--stretch-reflex-types-and-neuromuscular-control-of-flexibility]],
[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].

# "There Is No Unsafe Stretch, Only an Unsafe Way of Executing It"

**What it is** — In a bulleted list of biomechanical points on stretching, the authors
state: "There is generally no such thing as an unsafe stretch or exercise: only an unsafe
way of executing any movement for a specific individual at a specific time." (PDF p. 192,
printed p. 181.) This appears alongside a related claim in the same list that
physiotherapeutic PNF shows rapid or powerful recruitment of the different stretch
reflexes can be safely applied to rehabilitate and strengthen tissue, "contrary to common
belief."

**Why it works** — The authors give no supporting mechanism, study, or citation for this
specific aphorism; it reads as a stated position, not a derived or evidenced conclusion in
this passage.

**When to apply** — Useful as a reframing prompt when an exercise or stretch is being
categorically banned ("we never do ballistic stretching," "no PNF for this population"):
ask whether the concern is really about the movement class itself, or about a specific
athlete's readiness, technique, loading rate, or tissue state for that movement at that
time.

**When NOT to apply** — **`untested`, unlabeled aphorism with no supporting citation in
this passage.** Do not use this claim to override a specific, evidence-based
contraindication (e.g. a known ligament laxity, an acute strain, a post-surgical range
restriction) on the reasoning that "there's no unsafe stretch, only unsafe execution": the
book gives no criteria here for what counts as safe execution, and the claim is broad
enough to be difficult to falsify. Treat it as a coaching-philosophy prompt, not a safety
rule.

**Example** — The book's own paired example: it treats the popular blanket rule "ballistic
stretching should be avoided at all costs" as the kind of overgeneralization this heuristic
is meant to counter, arguing instead that rate and technique determine ballistic
stretching's safety (see
[[heuristic--ballistic-stretching-safe-with-gradual-progressive-protocol]]).

**Related** — [[heuristic--ballistic-stretching-safe-with-gradual-progressive-protocol]].

20	soft tissue may increase fibre formation, contributing to enhanced elasticity and strength

26	neither muscle hypertrophy nor increased intramuscular connective tissue growth; prolonged
27	low-intensity training conditions the cardiovascular system but not the musculoskeletal
28	system. The authors state it is anaerobic, muscle-endurance training specifically that most
29	strengthens collagenous tissue and its junction zones, making progressive stretching
30	alongside this type of training especially valuable. In contrast to chronic training,
31	single exercise sessions, occasional stretching, or sprint training alone do not produce
32	significant increases in junction strength, although sprinting does markedly increase
33	ligament mass and concentration (Tipton et al., 1974). Just as ligaments strengthen and
34	stiffen under increased stress, they become weaker and less stiff with decreased stress,
35	immobilization, and inactivity (Tipton et al., 1970); the authors note the similar changes

**What it is** — In arguing that stretching should not always be a discrete component of
training, the authors make two specific claims, both attributed to Siff (1987): (1)

contrary"; and (2) "a combination of stretching and weight-training exercises as a
supplement to a sprint-training programme produces significantly greater increases in
speed over an unsupplemented sprint programme." (PDF p. 194, printed p. 183.)

well-executed weightlifting and joint mobility are compatible, and that combining
stretching with resistance training may add to a sprint program's effect on speed beyond

1987 report) before being used to justify a specific program design.

# Ligaments and Tendons Thicken and Strengthen With Training, Weaken With Inactivity

**What it is** — The authors report that physical training strengthens the attachments of
tendons and ligaments to bone: trained ligaments are thicker and heavier, though the
increase in mass is not necessarily associated with a greater concentration of collagen,
a process described as still poorly understood (Booth & Gould, 1975); controlled strain on
soft tissue may increase fibre formation, contributing to enhanced elasticity and strength
(Holland, 1968). Regular resistance training increases not only muscle hypertrophy but also
the collagen content of ligaments and the connective tissue surrounding muscle fibres
(Tipton et al., 1975); training also increases the activity of an enzyme involved in
collagen synthesis, an effect possibly stimulated by lactic acid production during exercise
(Booth & Gould, 1975). By contrast, moderate-intensity treadmill training in rats produces
neither muscle hypertrophy nor increased intramuscular connective tissue growth; prolonged
low-intensity training conditions the cardiovascular system but not the musculoskeletal
system. "Apparently" it is anaerobic, muscle-endurance training specifically that most
strengthens collagenous tissue and its junction zones (the authors' own hedge, printed
182), making progressive stretching alongside this type of training especially valuable. In
contrast to chronic training, single exercise sessions, occasional stretching, or sprint
training alone do not produce significant increases in junction strength, although
sprinting does markedly increase ligament mass and concentration (Tipton et al., 1974). Just
as ligaments strengthen and stiffen under increased stress, they become weaker and less
stiff with decreased stress, immobilization, and inactivity (Tipton et al., 1970); the
authors note the similar changes seen with ageing may partly reflect inactivity rather than
degeneration alone. Separately, alteration in hormonal balance during pregnancy,
menstruation, and administration of exogenous hormones (anabolic steroids, cortisone) can
affect collagenous tissue's mechanical characteristics, so stretching technique "should be
adjusted accordingly" (Viidik, 1973, printed 183). (PDF p. 193, printed pp. 182-183.)

**Why it works** — This is presented as a summary of cited animal and human exercise
physiology findings (Tipton et al. 1970, 1974, 1975; Booth & Gould, 1975; Holland, 1968);
the authors do not add a mechanism beyond what each citation states.

**When to apply** — Use this to set expectations for how long connective tissue
conditioning takes: this entry supports chronic, repeated anaerobic/muscle-endurance
training as the driver of ligament and tendon strengthening, not occasional or single-bout
stretching or training. It also supports resuming ligament/tendon-specific loading
gradually after a period of inactivity or immobilization (e.g. post-injury), since the same
literature reports detraining weakens and destiffens these tissues.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence capped at `supported`.** Much of the underlying
evidence is animal-model research (rat treadmill studies; Tipton's ligament work), not
human athlete data, and the collagen-concentration-vs-mass distinction is itself described
in the source as poorly understood. Do not assume a single stretching or sprint session
meaningfully strengthens ligament-bone junctions; the text is explicit this requires
chronic training.

**Example** — The book's own example: sprint training increases ligament mass and
concentration even from acute exposure, but this is distinguished in the text from junction
*strength*, which the authors say requires chronic training rather than occasional
exposure (printed 182).

**Related** — [[framework--soft-tissue-contribution-to-joint-stiffness-and-stretch-duration-type]],
[[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]].

# Two Stretching "Myth-Busting" Claims From a Single Citation: Lifter Flexibility and Stretch-Plus-Strength for Speed

**What it is** — In arguing that stretching should not always be a discrete component of
training, the authors make two specific claims, both attributed to Siff (1987): (1)
"Olympic Weightlifters are amongst the most supple of all athletes, despite beliefs to the
contrary"; and (2) "a combination of stretching and weight-training exercises as a
supplement to a sprint-training programme produces significantly greater increases in
speed over an unsupplemented sprint programme." (PDF p. 194, printed p. 183.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for either claim in this passage; both are
presented as empirical findings attributed to the same 1987 source without further
methodological detail (sample, measurement, statistical result).

**When to apply** — Useful as a counter when an athlete or coach assumes heavy lifting and
flexibility are inherently opposed ("lifting makes you tight"); the book's position is that
well-executed weightlifting and joint mobility are compatible, and that combining
stretching with resistance training may add to a sprint program's effect on speed beyond
sprinting alone.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence `untested`: single citation (Siff, 1987), no sample
size, protocol, or effect size given in this passage, and not independently replicated
elsewhere in this text.** Do not treat "Olympic lifters are among the most supple athletes"
as a general population claim about all weightlifters, or the speed-improvement claim as an
established dose-response finding; both would need a primary-source check (the original
1987 report) before being used to justify a specific program design.

**Example** — Inference: citing this claim to justify adding static or PNF stretching
blocks to an in-season sprint-training program for speed gains would be extending a
single, unreplicated citation well beyond what it establishes.

**Related** — [[framework--stretching-techniques-taxonomy-static-vs-dynamic]].

14	# Stretch-Then-Shorten Is Not the Same as Shorten-Then-Stretch: Force History Depends on Order
15	
16	**What it is** — The authors state that stretch-shortening is not synonymous or
17	commutative with shortening-stretch: stretch-shortening and shortening-stretch cycles are
18	not commutative with respect to the isometric forces following the length changes, i.e.
19	stretch activation before muscle shortening does not produce the same result as muscle
20	shortening before stretch activation. Prior stretching of a muscle is well known to
21	decrease the isometric and maximal force the muscle can subsequently produce (force
22	depression following muscle shortening); this force depression is virtually unaffected by
23	previous stretching of the muscle, but force enhancement following stretch-shortening
24	depends, in a dose-dependent manner, on the amount of muscle shortening that precedes the
25	stretch (Herzog & Leonard, 2000). The history-dependence of isometric force following
26	stretch-shortening cycles is reported as independent of the stretch preceding the
27	shortening, except when stretching occurs at very high velocity (roughly 6-10 times fibre
28	length per second, as in ballistic movement). (PDF p. 195, printed p. 184.)
29	
30	**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism beyond citing Herzog & Leonard (2000) for
31	the specific dose-dependence and velocity-threshold findings; the general fact that prior
32	stretch reduces subsequent isometric/maximal force output is treated as established without
33	further explanation in this passage.
34	
35	**When to apply** — Use this to interpret force-plate or barbell-velocity data collected
36	immediately after a stretch-shortening action versus a shortening-stretch action; the order
37	of length change, not just the total length excursion, affects the force the muscle can
38	then produce. Relevant when sequencing a warm-up or a complex/contrast-training pairing
39	that alternates stretch and shortening actions.
40	
41	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence `supported`: single citation (Herzog & Leonard,
42	2000), no independent replication given in this text.** Do not generalize the specific
43	numeric velocity threshold (6-10 fibre lengths/second) beyond the ballistic-movement context
44	it is given in, and do not assume this history-dependence effect has the same magnitude
45	across all muscle groups or contraction intensities; the text does not state that.
46	
47	**Example** — Inference: a depth jump (stretch immediately preceding shortening, at high
48	velocity) and a paused, held-stretch-then-jump sequence are not mechanically interchangeable
49	by this claim, even if the total ROM and final shortening are similar, because the order
50	and velocity of the length change independently affect the resulting force.
51

**What it is** — The authors state that stretch-shortening is not synonymous or

movement, but to enhance the speed and intensity of muscle contraction. This action is usually imposed on a 
muscle by using a rapid eccentric contraction to recruit the stretch reflex in a specific muscle group so as to

after an active stretch, isometric force is enhanced, and the enhancement shrinks with the
amount of shortening that preceded the stretch; the exception is tentative ("perhaps"), not
established, for very fast stretch. This is cat soleus, in situ, steady-state isometric
force data. (PDF p. 195, printed p. 184.)

maximal force," conflicts with the cited paper's actual finding of force *enhancement*
