# A Two-Branch, Load/State-Based Taxonomy of Stretching Techniques

**What it is** — The authors argue the traditional four categories of stretching (static,
ballistic, passive, PNF/contract-relax) are an incomplete and sometimes overlapping way to
describe technique, and propose instead a model (Fig 3.34) built from two variables: the
rate of stretching, and the type of load and state of the muscle. This yields two broad
types, each with sub-categories:
1. **Static Stretching**: Free Static Stretching (no external load, under (a) muscle
relaxation or (b) isometric contraction, sometimes called Active Static Stretching), and
Passive Static Stretching (external load applied to (a) relaxed or (b) isometrically
contracted muscle).
2. **Dynamic Stretching**: Ballistic Stretching (passive momentum exceeds static ROM, on
(a) relaxed or (b) contracted muscle, done slowly or rapidly); Active Stretching
(continuous muscle activity exceeds static ROM, as in normal full-range sporting
movement); PNF Stretching (intermittent or continuous phases of static or dynamic muscle
action plus relaxation or passive movement, in specific activation/relaxation patterns);
and Plyometric (Impulsive) Stretching (rapid termination of eccentric loading, a brief
isometric phase, then an explosive rebound using stored elastic energy and powerful reflex
contraction; not intended to increase ROM but to increase speed-strength of movement,
viewable as a form of ballistic stretching done impulsively). The authors state PNF is
misleadingly regarded as a specialized flexibility-only system: in professional practice it
conditions neuromuscular processes, isometric and dynamic strength, muscular endurance, and
functional flexibility more completely than many machine-based routines, using
three-dimensional spiral and diagonal movement patterns, so several "distinct" stretching
types may be seen as a subset of PNF's full discipline. (PDF pp. 194-195, printed pp.
183-184.)

**Why it works** — The authors' rationale for the taxonomy is that specificity of exercise
means each category can be used effectively and safely for specific subjects at a specific
training stage to achieve optimal stability and mobility; they state active and PNF
stretching involving progressive contraction against external load, through and beyond the
static ROM, appear to offer the most effective means of improving full-range functional
sporting performance, though no comparative data are given in this passage.

**When to apply** — Use this two-variable scheme (rate x load/muscle-state) to classify
any named stretching modality encountered elsewhere, and to select a category matched to
training goal and stage: static stretching for the average person mainly targeting static
flexibility; active/PNF stretching against external load when the target is full-range
functional performance.

**When NOT to apply** — This is the authors' own reorganization of stretching
terminology, not an experimentally validated hierarchy of effectiveness; the claim that
active/PNF stretching is "the most effective" is stated without a comparative citation in
this passage. Confidence is capped at `supported` because the taxonomy is a classification
tool, not itself an empirical finding.

**Example** — The book's own example: gently bouncing ballistic stretching performed over
a gradually increasing ROM is, per this taxonomy, a special case of contract-relax/hold-relax
PNF activity, not a separate, inherently more dangerous category (printed 186; see
[[heuristic--ballistic-stretching-safe-with-gradual-progressive-protocol]]).

**Related** — [[heuristic--ballistic-stretching-safe-with-gradual-progressive-protocol]],
[[framework--flexibility-speed-strength-endurance-qualities]].

# Three "Functional" Flexibility Qualities: Flexibility-Speed, Flexibility-Strength, Flexibility-Endurance

**What it is** — Beyond raw ROM, the authors define three additional, sport-relevant
flexibility qualities that "functional" stretching conditioning must also address:
**flexibility-speed**, the ability to produce efficient full ROM at speed; **flexibility-
strength** (static and dynamic forms), the ability to produce efficient, powerful static
and dynamic movements over a full ROM; and **flexibility-endurance** (static and dynamic
forms), the ability to repetitively produce efficient full ROM under static and dynamic
conditions. The book gives flexibility-strength and flexibility-endurance each explicit
"(static and dynamic)" forms; flexibility-speed is not given that same static/dynamic split
in the text. This duplicates terminology already in Ch1
[[framework--s-factors-pyramidal-fitness-model]] (flexibility-strength, flexibility-
endurance, flexibility-speed); this entry's new angle is the definitions themselves. The
authors
state the importance of these qualities is why a wide variety of carefully sequenced
stretching methods, cyclically periodized in intensity, duration and complexity, is needed,
rather than a single stretching method or a fixed routine. (PDF p. 197, printed p. 186.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no separate mechanism for why these three qualities
are distinct from raw ROM; the definitions function as a vocabulary for specifying *how* a
given ROM must be produced (fast, forceful, or repeated) in a sport skill, extending the
active-vs-passive flexibility distinction already covered (see
[[claim--active-flexibility-correlates-more-with-sporting-proficiency-than-passive]]).

**When to apply** — Use this vocabulary when specifying a flexibility training goal beyond
"improve hip mobility": ask whether the sport skill needs that ROM produced quickly
(flexibility-speed), forcefully (flexibility-strength), or repeatedly across a competition
(flexibility-endurance), since these imply different training methods (e.g. active/PNF
stretching against resistance for flexibility-strength, versus repeated-exposure work for
flexibility-endurance).

**When NOT to apply** — This is a definitional vocabulary, not an empirically validated
set of independently measurable qualities; the book gives no test or normative data for
flexibility-speed, flexibility-strength, or flexibility-endurance separately from general
active/passive ROM measures. Do not treat these as three distinct, separately trainable
capacities without further evidence that they dissociate from one another.

**Example** — Inference: a hurdler's trail-leg hip ROM needed within a single stride cycle
is a flexibility-speed demand, while the same joint's ROM held under load during an
isometric hip-flexor stretch-strengthening exercise is closer to a flexibility-strength
demand; per this framework, a program addressing only one would not necessarily transfer to
the other.

**Related** — [[claim--active-flexibility-correlates-more-with-sporting-proficiency-than-passive]],
[[heuristic--eccentric-quasi-isometrics-for-active-flexibility-and-starting-strength]].

# A Two-Branch, Load/State-Based Taxonomy of Stretching Techniques

**What it is** — The authors argue the traditional four categories of stretching (static,
ballistic, passive, PNF/contract-relax) are an incomplete and sometimes overlapping way to
describe technique, and propose instead a model (Fig 3.34) built from two variables: the
rate of stretching, and the type of load and state of the muscle. This yields two broad
types, each with sub-categories:
1. **Static Stretching**: Free Static Stretching (no external load, under (a) muscle
relaxation or (b) isometric contraction, sometimes called Active Static Stretching), and
Passive Static Stretching (external load applied to (a) relaxed or (b) isometrically
contracted muscle).
2. **Dynamic Stretching**: Ballistic Stretching (passive momentum exceeds static ROM, on
(a) relaxed or (b) contracted muscle, done slowly or rapidly); Active Stretching
(continuous muscle activity exceeds static ROM, as in normal full-range sporting
movement); PNF Stretching (intermittent or continuous phases of static or dynamic muscle
action plus relaxation or passive movement, in specific activation/relaxation patterns);
and Plyometric (Impulsive) Stretching (rapid termination of eccentric loading, a brief
isometric phase, then an explosive rebound using stored elastic energy and powerful reflex
contraction; not intended to increase ROM but to increase speed-strength of movement,
viewable as a form of ballistic stretching done impulsively). The authors state PNF is
misleadingly regarded as a specialized flexibility-only system: in professional practice it
conditions neuromuscular processes, isometric and dynamic strength, muscular endurance, and
functional flexibility more completely than many machine-based routines, using
three-dimensional spiral and diagonal movement patterns, so several "distinct" stretching
types may be seen as a subset of PNF's full discipline. (PDF pp. 194-195, printed pp.
183-184.)

**Why it works** — The authors' rationale for the taxonomy is that specificity of exercise
means each category can be used effectively and safely for specific subjects at a specific
training stage to achieve optimal stability and mobility; they state active and PNF
stretching involving progressive contraction against external load, through and beyond the
static ROM, appear to offer the most effective means of improving full-range functional
sporting performance, though no comparative data are given in this passage.

**When to apply** — Use this two-variable scheme (rate x load/muscle-state) to classify
any named stretching modality encountered elsewhere, and to select a category matched to
training goal and stage: static stretching for the average person mainly targeting static
flexibility; active/PNF stretching against external load when the target is full-range
functional performance.

**When NOT to apply** — This is the authors' own reorganization of stretching
terminology, not an experimentally validated hierarchy of effectiveness; the claim that
active/PNF stretching is "the most effective" is stated without a comparative citation in
this passage. Confidence is capped at `supported` because the taxonomy is a classification
tool, not itself an empirical finding.

**Example** — The book's own example: gently bouncing ballistic stretching performed over
a gradually increasing ROM is, per this taxonomy, a special case of contract-relax/hold-relax
PNF activity, not a separate, inherently more dangerous category (printed 186; see
[[heuristic--ballistic-stretching-safe-with-gradual-progressive-protocol]]).

**Related** — [[heuristic--ballistic-stretching-safe-with-gradual-progressive-protocol]],
[[framework--flexibility-speed-strength-endurance-qualities]].

14	# Ballistic Stretching Can Be Applied Safely if Rate and Progression Are Controlled
15	
16	**What it is** — Against the "well-meaning, but very misleading" blanket statement that
17	ballistic stretching is generally harmful and should be avoided, the authors argue this
18	makes no distinction between the rates and techniques used to apply it. They state most
19	forms of ballistic stretching could safely be included within the scope of PNF: gentle
20	bouncing ballistic stretching over a gradually increasing ROM is a special type of
21	contract-relax/hold-relax PNF activity and can be applied safely and effectively; static
22	stretches can also be alternated with periodic gentle ballistic stretches, or carried out
23	against the resistance of stretched elastic bands, as further variants. A "principle of
24	progressive gradual stretching increase" (increasing speed and range safely and
25	effectively up to the level of plyometric activity) is proposed to extend this. Citing
26	Russian research (Matveyev, 1981), the authors give a specific protocol: ballistic
27	stretching can be most effectively and safely used in 3-5 sets of 8-12 repetitions, with
28	amplitude of movement gradually increasing with each repetition; no further repetitions
29	should be performed once ROM becomes impaired by fatigue, a rule the authors suggest may
30	apply with equal validity to other forms of stretching. (PDF pp. 197-198, printed pp.
31	186-187.)
32	
33	**Why it works** — The authors' argument is that ballistic stretching's risk comes from
34	rate and technique (uncontrolled, high-amplitude, unprogressed bouncing), not from the
35	ballistic action itself; gradually increasing amplitude keeps each repetition within the
36	tissue's current adapted range rather than exceeding it, and stopping once fatigue impairs
37	ROM avoids stretching an already-compromised, less-controlled muscle.
38	
39	**When to apply** — Where ballistic or dynamic stretching is wanted (e.g. as
40	sport-specific preparation, since ballistic actions are a frequent component of most
41	sports and conventional static/dynamic stretching does not always address that specific
42	joint-action demand), apply it as 3-5 sets of 8-12 reps with amplitude increasing gradually
43	each rep, and stop the set once fatigue starts to reduce ROM.
44	
45	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence capped at `supported`: single Soviet-era citation
46	(Matveyev, 1981), no independent replication located in this library.** Do not apply
47	ballistic stretching abruptly at full amplitude from the first repetition; that is the
48	specific pattern the authors' own argument depends on avoiding. Do not continue a ballistic
49	stretching set once ROM is visibly reduced by fatigue; the text states this explicitly as
50	the stopping rule.
51	
52	**Example** — The book's own contrast: the "well-meaning, but very misleading" advice to
53	avoid ballistic stretching "at all costs" is the position this heuristic is written
54	against; the authors instead prescribe the specific graduated protocol above rather than a
55	blanket avoidance rule (printed 186).
56	
57	**Related** — [[heuristic--no-unsafe-stretch-only-unsafe-execution-for-individual]],
58	[[framework--stretching-techniques-taxonomy-static-vs-dynamic]].

SUPERTRAINING
stretches against the resistance offered by stretched elastic bands to provide yet another variant. One may even 
apply a principle o f progressive gradual stretching increase to increase safely and effectively the speed and range 
of ballistic stretching right up to the level of plyomctric activity. This approach offers some benefits over static 
and conventional dynamic stretching becausc ballistic actions are a frequent component of most sports and other 
forms of stretching usually do not address this specificity of joint action.
Interestingly, Russian research has shown that ballistic stretching, can be most effectively and safely used if it 
is performed in 3-5 sets of 8-12 repetitions, with the amplitude of movement gradually increasing with each 
repetition (Matveyev, 1981). No further repetitions should be performed if the range o f movement becomes 
impaired by fatigue, an approach which may be applied with equal validity to all other forms of stretching.
3.5.9 Low Flexibility versus Non-functional M uscle Tension
Limitations in functional ROM should not automatically be attributed to joint stiffness alone, because this can 
lead to an unnecessary emphasis on stretching. Limitations to full ROM can also be caused by various forms of 
spurious tension or excessive muscle tension such as coordination tension, which may accompany the appropriate 
muscle tension required by the given movement. This non-functional tension can occur in both phasic and tonic 
muscles before, during and after the movement.
The level of proficiency of the athlete has a marked influence on the reflex ability o f the muscles to contract 
and relax (Fig 3.35). Rapidity of both contraction and relaxation increases with level of mastery, with a decrease 
in relaxation time becoming especially evident. The importance of teaching athletes to relax the muscles rapidly 
and efficiently to enhance the functional range of sporting movement then becomes obvious. 
It is of little 
consequence to have highly flexible joints with well conditioned, supple connective tissues and a large range of 
movement, if action is limited by any spurious muscle tension. Flexibility training, therefore, should always be 
combined with neuromuscular training to produce efficient, functional ROM.
LEVEL OF QUALIFICATION
Figure 3.35 Muscle contraction and relaxation times of athletes of increasing levels of qualification, as measured by electromyography 
(based on data of Matveyev, 1981). Contraction time is the time from a given signal to the onset of electrical activity in the muscle, 
while relaxation time is the time taken from the signal to disappearance of electrical activity. Level I refers to the novice; Level 2 is a 
Class 3 athlete; Level 3 is a Class 2 athlete; Level 4 is a Classl alhlete; Level 5 is a Master of Sport.
Some of the ways of improving the ability to relax the muscles are:
• Contract-relax, hold-relax and other PNF methods which use the different stretch reflexes to promote muscle 
relaxation (sec 7.2).
• Sudden unloading, the sudden removal of external resistance imposed under strong isometric or dynamic 
conditions (e.g. the end of the jerk, completion o f a heavy squat or bench press, throwing of a shot or 
medicine ball, short bursts of strong electromuscular contraction). 
It has been shown that this means 
produces the greatest relaxation response of all the means currently used. They become even more effective if 
the powerful and rapid contraction-relaxation process is related as closely as possible to the given sporting 
actions.
• The change of muscle groups from a state of tension to relaxation in a controlled, gradual manner or in a series 
of stages (e.g. Jacobsen's progressive relaxation method).
187

===== PDF idx 199 (printed 188) =====
SUPERTRAINING
• Control of spurious tension in the muscles of the face and hands, which tends to reflect general tension fairly 
well.
• The use of controlled visualisation of the muscles progressing from contraction to relaxation and back.
• The use of autogenic training, progressive relaxation, meditation or massage.
• The use of breathing patterns on the basis that tension is associated with breath inhalation and holding, with 
breath holding (the Valsalva manoeuvre) being used where maximal force and spinal stabilisation must be 
produced. Conversely, relaxation is associated with gentle, controlled exhalation. Appropriate techniques of 
breathing should always be combined with all phases of movement to enhance mobility, stability and 
relaxation.
• The execution of exercises against a background of exhaustion of selected musclc groups (the so-called pre- 
exhaustion principle commonly used in bodybuilding for increasing stress on chosen muscle groups), provided 
that movement technique does not suffer.
• The use of distracting or focusing activities which cause the athlete to concentrate on stimuli other than those 
associated with the given sporting action (e.g. music, talking to a training partner while running, thinking of 
something pleasant). These methods may involve internalisation or extemalisation of focus, the suitability of 
any method being determined on an individual basis.
• The gentle use of rhythmic cyclical, swinging, shaking or circling movements of the body and limbs to relax

15	
16	**What it is** — Following the claim that spurious muscle tension, not just tissue
17	stiffness, can limit functional ROM (see
18	[[claim--spurious-muscle-tension-limits-rom-independent-of-tissue-flexibility]]), the
19	authors list methods for improving the ability to relax muscles: (1) contract-relax,
20	hold-relax, and other PNF methods using stretch reflexes to promote relaxation; (2) sudden
21	unloading, the abrupt removal of external resistance under strong isometric or dynamic
22	conditions (e.g. the end of a jerk, completion of a heavy squat/bench press, releasing a
23	thrown shot or medicine ball, short bursts of strong electromuscular contraction), reported
24	as producing the greatest relaxation response of all listed means, and becoming more
25	effective the more closely the contraction-relaxation process is tied to the actual
26	sporting action; (3) changing muscle groups from tension to relaxation in a controlled,
27	gradual manner or through a series of stages (e.g. Jacobsen's progressive relaxation
28	method); (4) controlling spurious tension in the face and hands specifically, since these
29	tend to reflect general body tension well; (5) controlled visualization of muscles
30	progressing from contraction to relaxation and back; (6) autogenic training, progressive
31	relaxation, meditation, or massage; (7) breathing pattern control, on the basis that
32	tension is associated with inhalation and breath-holding (the Valsalva manoeuvre, used
33	where maximal force and spinal stabilization are needed) while relaxation is associated
34	with gentle, controlled exhalation; appropriate breathing should be combined with all
35	phases of movement to enhance mobility, stability, and relaxation; (8) the "pre-exhaustion
36	principle," exercising against a background of exhaustion of selected muscle groups
37	(common in bodybuilding) to increase stress on chosen groups, provided movement technique
38	does not suffer; (9) distracting or focusing activities that direct attention away from
39	stimuli tied to the sporting action (music, conversation with a training partner, pleasant
40	thoughts), which may work through internal or external focus depending on the individual;
41	(10) gentle rhythmic, cyclical, swinging, shaking, or circling movements of the body and
42	limbs to relax muscles just strongly contracted (as in some dance, swimming, or Tai Chi
43	movements). (PDF pp. 200-201, printed pp. 187-188.)

46	relaxation response "of all the means currently used," without giving the underlying

52	drills tied closely to the actual sport action are named as the single most effective
53	listed method, so pairing method 2 with the specific sporting movement (rather than a
54	generic drill) is the book's own emphasis.

# Ten Ways Coaches Can Train an Athlete's Ability to Relax Muscles on Demand

**What it is** — Following the claim that spurious muscle tension, not just tissue
stiffness, can limit functional ROM (see
[[claim--spurious-muscle-tension-limits-rom-independent-of-tissue-flexibility]]), the
authors list methods for improving the ability to relax muscles: (1) contract-relax,
hold-relax, and other PNF methods using stretch reflexes to promote relaxation; (2) sudden
unloading, the abrupt removal of external resistance under strong isometric or dynamic
conditions (e.g. the end of a jerk, completion of a heavy squat/bench press, releasing a
thrown shot or medicine ball, short bursts of strong electromuscular contraction), reported
as producing the greatest relaxation response of all listed means, and becoming more
effective the more closely the contraction-relaxation process is tied to the actual
sporting action; (3) changing muscle groups from tension to relaxation in a controlled,
gradual manner or through a series of stages (e.g. Jacobsen's progressive relaxation
method); (4) controlling spurious tension in the face and hands specifically, since these
tend to reflect general body tension well; (5) controlled visualization of muscles
progressing from contraction to relaxation and back; (6) autogenic training, progressive
relaxation, meditation, or massage; (7) breathing pattern control, on the basis that
tension is associated with inhalation and breath-holding (the Valsalva manoeuvre, used
where maximal force and spinal stabilization are needed) while relaxation is associated
with gentle, controlled exhalation; appropriate breathing should be combined with all
phases of movement to enhance mobility, stability, and relaxation; (8) the "pre-exhaustion
principle," exercising against a background of exhaustion of selected muscle groups
(common in bodybuilding) to increase stress on chosen groups, provided movement technique
does not suffer; (9) distracting or focusing activities that direct attention away from
stimuli tied to the sporting action (music, conversation with a training partner, pleasant
thoughts), which may work through internal or external focus depending on the individual;
(10) gentle rhythmic, cyclical, swinging, shaking, or circling movements of the body and
limbs to relax muscles just strongly contracted (as in some dance, swimming, or Tai Chi
movements). (PDF pp. 200-201, printed pp. 187-188.)

**Why it works** — The authors state method 2 (sudden unloading) produces the greatest
relaxation response "of all the means currently used," without giving the underlying
mechanism in this passage; the other methods are listed without comparative effectiveness
data or a stated mechanism beyond their general description.

**When to apply** — Use this list as a menu when an athlete needs targeted work on
reflexive muscle relaxation rather than (or alongside) tissue stretching: sudden-unloading
drills tied closely to the actual sport action are named as the single most effective
listed method, so pairing method 2 with the specific sporting movement (rather than a
generic drill) is the book's own emphasis.

**When NOT to apply** — No dosage, frequency, or measured outcome data are given for any
of the ten methods in this passage; treat this as a menu of techniques the authors report
as used in practice, not a validated, ranked protocol (apart from the single stated
observation that method 2 is most effective). Confidence is capped at `supported`.

**Example** — The book's own example: the abrupt release of tension at the top of a jerk,
or immediately after a heavy squat or bench press rep, is offered as a sudden-unloading
relaxation drill that is more effective the more closely it mirrors the athlete's actual
competitive movement (printed 187).

**Related** — [[claim--spurious-muscle-tension-limits-rom-independent-of-tissue-flexibility]],
[[heuristic--reflex-based-techniques-for-flexibility-training]].

# A Flexible, Well-Conditioned Joint Can Still Have Limited Functional ROM From Spurious Muscle Tension

**What it is** — The authors state that limitations in functional ROM should not
automatically be attributed to joint stiffness alone, since this can lead to an
unnecessary emphasis on stretching. Limitations to full ROM can also be caused by "spurious
tension" or excessive, non-functional muscle tension such as coordination tension, which
may accompany the appropriate tension a given movement requires; this non-functional
tension can occur in both phasic and tonic muscles, before, during, or after the movement.
Athlete proficiency level has a marked influence on the reflex ability of muscles to
contract and relax: rapidity of both contraction and relaxation increases with mastery,
with a decrease in relaxation time being especially evident (Fig 3.35, data from Matveyev,
1981, measured by EMG across five qualification levels from novice to Master of Sport,
showing relaxation time dropping from about 0.4s at Level 1 to about 0.22s at Level 5,
converging with contraction time). The authors conclude it is of little consequence to have
highly flexible joints with well-conditioned, supple connective tissue if action is limited
by spurious muscle tension instead; flexibility training should therefore always be
combined with neuromuscular training aimed at efficient, functional ROM, not tissue
stretching alone. (PDF pp. 199-200, printed pp. 187-188, Fig 3.35.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no separate mechanism for why proficiency specifically
speeds relaxation more than contraction; the Matveyev (1981) EMG data are reported as the
empirical basis for the mastery-relaxation relationship, without further explanation.

**When to apply** — When an athlete presents with apparently limited functional ROM in a
sport movement despite passing a passive flexibility screen, consider spurious/coordination
tension and relaxation ability as an alternative or additional target, rather than
defaulting to more stretching.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence capped at `supported`: the Fig 3.35 data are a single
cited source (Matveyev, 1981) with an unspecified sample, and the five qualification
levels (novice through Master of Sport) are specific to that source's population, not
necessarily transferable as normative relaxation-time targets for a Baylor roster.** Do not
use this claim to dismiss a genuine tissue-flexibility deficit; the authors frame this as an
additional cause of limited ROM, not a replacement for checking tissue-level flexibility.

**Example** — The book's own example, via Fig 3.35: a novice athlete's slower reflex
relaxation (about 0.4s) compared to a Master of Sport's faster relaxation (about 0.22s) at
the same level of tissue flexibility illustrates that training age/mastery, not just
tissue conditioning, changes how quickly non-functional tension clears during a movement.

**Related** — [[framework--methods-for-improving-voluntary-muscle-relaxation]],
[[heuristic--reflex-based-techniques-for-flexibility-training]].

method); (4) controlling spurious tension in the face and hands specifically, since these
tend to reflect general body tension well; (5) controlled visualization of muscles
progressing from contraction to relaxation and back; (6) autogenic training, progressive
relaxation, meditation, or massage; (7) breathing pattern control, on the basis that
tension is associated with inhalation and breath-holding (the Valsalva manoeuvre, used

with gentle, controlled exhalation; appropriate breathing should be combined with all
phases of movement to enhance mobility, stability, and relaxation; (8) the "pre-exhaustion
principle," exercising against a background of exhaustion of selected muscle groups
(common in bodybuilding) to increase stress on chosen groups, provided movement technique
does not suffer; (9) distracting or focusing activities that direct attention away from
stimuli tied to the sporting action (music, conversation with a training partner, pleasant
thoughts), which may work through internal or external focus depending on the individual;

limbs to relax muscles just strongly contracted (as in some dance, swimming, or Tai Chi

relaxation response "of all the means currently used," without giving the underlying
mechanism in this passage; the other methods are listed without comparative effectiveness

reflexive muscle relaxation rather than (or alongside) tissue stretching: sudden-unloading
drills tied closely to the actual sport action are named as the single most effective

generic drill) is the book's own emphasis.

**When NOT to apply** — No dosage, frequency, or measured outcome data are given for any

as used in practice, not a validated, ranked protocol (apart from the single stated
observation that method 2 is most effective). Confidence is capped at `supported`.

or immediately after a heavy squat or bench press rep, is offered as a sudden-unloading
relaxation drill that is more effective the more closely it mirrors the athlete's actual
competitive movement (printed 187).

14	# The Stretching Matrix: Any Stretch Is the Reverse of the Action That Contracts the Same Muscle Group
15	
16	**What it is** — The authors present a generalized system, built from standard muscle
17	action charts, for devising a stretch for any major muscle group: "the reverse of any
18	action to contract a given muscle group becomes a stretch for that same muscle group." A
19	series of matrices (Figs 3.36-3.40, in this excerpt covering trunk/neck, upper arm,
20	forearm, lower extremity, and foot) list each muscle against the joint actions that stretch
21	it. The system requires identifying which joints a given muscle crosses before deciding how
22	to stretch it, since a muscle's action, and therefore its stretch, can differ depending on
23	which joint's chart is consulted; using only one matrix for a biarticular or multiarticular
24	muscle can produce a less-than-maximal stretch. The authors' worked example: psoas (as part
25	of iliopsoas) is stretched by hip extension and medial rotation per the lower-extremity
26	matrix, but as a trunk muscle it is also stretched by combined trunk extension and lateral
27	extension per the trunk/neck matrix; a fencer's front lunge maximally stretches iliacus
28	(hip extension alone) but will not maximally stretch psoas unless the trunk is also
29	extended and laterally flexed toward the leading leg. A second worked example: the oblique
30	muscles and quadratus lumborum both perform lateral trunk flexion, but only the obliques
31	also rotate the trunk and only quadratus lumborum extends it, so only concurrent trunk
32	flexion plus lateral extension maximally stretches quadratus lumborum, while flexion plus
33	lateral extension plus rotation is needed to maximally stretch the obliques. (PDF pp.
34	199-202, printed pp. 188-191, Figs 3.36-3.39.)
35	
36	**Why it works** — The mechanism is definitional, not empirical: if muscle contraction
37	produces a given joint action, moving the joint through the opposite action necessarily
38	lengthens (stretches) that muscle, following directly from standard functional anatomy
39	rather than a cited study.
40	
41	**When to apply** — Use the matrices to design a novel stretch for any muscle by first
42	identifying every joint and degree of freedom the muscle crosses (via multiple figures if
43	needed), then combining the reverse actions simultaneously rather than one at a time, to
44	achieve a maximal stretch. Useful for building or auditing a stretching routine's actual
45	target versus its intended target.
46	
47	**When NOT to apply** — This is an anatomical design method, not an outcome-tested
48	training system; the book does not report ROM-gain or performance data from using this
49	matrix approach specifically. Confidence is capped at `supported` because it is a
50	logically-derived tool, not itself an empirical claim. Do not assume a single-joint stretch
51	fully stretches a muscle that crosses multiple joints; the authors are explicit this is the
52	main pitfall the matrices are meant to prevent.
53	
54	**Example** — The book's own example: to stretch biceps brachii (which crosses both
55	elbow and shoulder), the elbow must be extended and the shoulder extended and abducted with
56	the forearm pronated simultaneously (per Figs 3.37-3.38); consulting only the forearm
57	matrix (elbow extension alone) would under-stretch the muscle (printed 189).
58	
59	**Related** — [[framework--movement-matrix-system-for-multiarticular-exercise-selection]].

12	---
13	
14	# A Sport's Own Movements, Progressively Loaded, Can Replace a Dedicated Stretching Session
15	
16	**What it is** — The authors call it "possibly the most heretical remark to make about
17	stretching" that dedicated stretching sessions may not even be necessary, noting many
18	athletes dispense entirely with special stretching or even warm-up sessions without
19	suffering injury in training or competition; the prescription of stretching and warm-up
20	or cool-down has become "a well-accepted ritual," which the authors state does not by
21	itself make it essential. They propose a "principle of gradual progressive stretching and
22	activity increase": the athlete begins each movement gently and non-ballistically under
23	limited static and dynamic conditions, then progressively increases range, speed,
24	complexity, intensity and other aspects of movement until the actual sporting movements
25	themselves are performed under light and eventually near-competitive conditions. In weight
26	training, the same principle is applied by beginning every exercise with a few preparatory
27	repetitions at a light load, progressively increasing the load over a few sets, and using a
28	narrower-than-normal grip or stance early in the progression (e.g. bench press, squat) to
29	reduce range/speed of movement and tissue/joint stress at the start. The authors' concluding
30	position: it is unnecessary to devise many highly specific individual flexibility drills
31	for the whole body, since this would be time-consuming and inefficient; functional
32	movements already used in the sport, combined with the stretching techniques discussed
33	earlier, can replace a prolonged session of dozens of single-joint stretches, provided the
34	routine still increases both passive/static ROM and functional flexibility-strength for all
35	static, dynamic, and necessary ballistic joint actions. (PDF pp. 203-204, printed pp.
36	192-193.)
37	
38	**Why it works** — The authors give no controlled comparison (stretching vs. no
39	stretching, or dedicated-stretch vs. movement-based warm-up) for injury or performance
40	outcomes in this passage; the claim rests on informal observation ("many athletes dispense
41	entirely...without suffering injury") rather than a cited study.
42	
43	**When to apply** — Where session time is limited, consider replacing a block of isolated,
44	single-joint stretches with a progressively loaded, sport-specific movement warm-up
45	(narrow-grip/stance light sets building toward working load and range), on the premise
46	that this can achieve the same flexibility-preparation goal more efficiently, provided full
47	ROM and the necessary joint actions for that sport are actually included.
48	
49	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence `untested`: no controlled outcome data given in this
50	passage.** Do not use this as a blanket argument against ever including dedicated
51	flexibility work; the authors' own surrounding sections (see
52	[[framework--four-methods-of-enhancing-rom-ranked-by-effectiveness]]) state that durable,
53	long-term ROM change requires a specific, regularly repeated conditioning component, which
54	a purely movement-based warm-up may not supply for an athlete with a genuine long-term ROM
55	deficit in a specific joint.
56	
57	**Example** — The book's own example: beginning a bench press session with a narrower
58	grip and lighter load, then progressively widening/loading toward the working set, applies
59	this principle by using the exercise itself (rather than a separate stretch) to prepare the
60	shoulder joint's ROM and tissue tolerance (printed 192).
61	
62	**Related** — [[framework--four-methods-of-enhancing-rom-ranked-by-effectiveness]],
63	[[framework--stretching-matrix-system-reverse-of-contraction-action]].
64

===== PDF idx 200 (printed 189) =====
SUPERTRAINING
In all the figures given, matrices arc given which provide the appropriate end position to be reachcd in movements 
for stretching the major muscle groups of the body. In applying them, one should always ascertain from one or 
more of these matrices which joints are crossed by a given muscle and only then decide on the optimal way of 
sretching all the muscles involved.
As stated before, muscles often cross more than one joint and use of a single matrix may result in a less than 
maximum stretch. For example, if one consults Figure 3.38 as a guide for stretching the various flexors of the 
elbow, then one neglects the fact that two of them (biceps brachii and triceps) also cross the shoulder joint. Thus, 
to stretch the biccps, it is necessary to extend both the shoulder and the elbow joints, while the forearm is 
simultaneously pronated.
In the case of the triceps, the elbow has to be flexed, while the shoulder joint must be extended both 
backwards (in the sagittal plane) and abducted (in the frontal plane). It is often helpful to consult the Movement 
Matrices to ascertain which muscles are responsible for producing a given joint action (see 3.7). In fact, if one 
employs movement patterns that are similar to those used in one’s sport, one can achieve simultaneous 
strengthening and flexibility. For example in executing a squat or bench press, you can increase your strength- 
flexibility (see Chi) by progressively starting from a somewhat deeper position and quasi-isomctrically 
prcstretching the relevant muscles before the upward concentric movement begins.
189
Stretching those muscles are included simultaneously. Thus, concurrent trunk flexion and lateral extension will 
m aximally stretch quadrants lumborum.
Figure 3 J 6  Actions for stretching the muscles of the trunk and back

===== PDF idx 201 (printed 190) =====
SUPERTRAINING
190

===== PDF idx 202 (printed 191) =====
SUPERTRAJN/NC
191

===== PDF idx 203 (printed 192) =====
SUPERTRAINING
Figure 3.40 Actions for stretching the muscles acting on the foot
The versatility of this stretching matrix system may be appreciated if one realises that many o f the actions of the 
joints concerned may be performed in different basic postures such as standing, lying or sitting. You may use 
them to analyse the numerous stretches of dance and gymnastics, as well as yoga postures (asanas) and thereby 
acquire the skills for using the matrices easily and creatively.
These matrices are not intended to exhaustively cover stretches for all the muscle groups; they were 
presented to introduce the concept of the Stretching Matrix system and to offer basic examples of how to apply it 
by means of specific exercises. The inventive coach should be able to use the existing series of matrices to devise 
new stretching manoeuvres and to enhance the effectiveness of stretches which he may already be using.
Since dynamic stretching in functional movement patterns provides the most valuable form of sport specific 
stretching, the Stretching Matrix concept may be extended to produce a method of full range of movement from a 
position of full elongation of a muscle to full contraction of the same muscle group and vice versa
Is Stretching Always Necessary?
Possibly the most heretical remark to make about stretching is to suggest that the dedicated use of stretching 
sessions may not even be necessary, especially since many athletes dispense entirely with special stretching or 
even warm-up sessions before of after training without suffering injury in training or competition. The prescription 
of stretching and warm-up or cooling down sessions has become a well-accepted ritual, but that does not imply that 
this is essential.
While some forms of stretching may be necessary to deform connective tissues to increase range of movement 
or to re-educate neural facilitatory and inhibitory processes to permit greater “functional” use of a joint, pre-event 
stretching sessions do not always have to take the form of a discrete component of training. One can use the actual 
movements from a sport to serve as a highly adequate and effective way of preparing the body for subsequent
192

===== PDF idx 204 (printed 193) =====
SUPERTRAINING
work. In this case, the athlete simply begins each movement gently and non-ballistically under limited static and 
dynamic conditions and follows a principle ofgradual progressive stretching and activity increase by progressively 
increasing range, speed, complexity, intensity and other aspects of movement until the actual sporting movements 
themselves are executed under light and ultimately near-competitive conditions.
In weight training situations, you simply begin every exercise with a few preparatory repetitions using a light 
load and progressively increase the load over a very few sets to reach one’s serious training loads until the 
movement feels unrestricted and fluent. In doing so, you commence with a limited range and speed of movement 
and place less stress on the tissues and joints, for instance, by taking a narrower than normal grip in the bench 
press (or other forms of pressing) or a narrower foot spacing during the squat (if one normally uses a medium to 
wide grip or stance in these exercises).
Concluding Remark
It is unnecessary to devise a host of highly specific individual flexibility manoeuvres to enhance flexibility of the 
entire body, as this would be time-consuming and inefficient. Instead you may use functional movements that are 
commonly encountered in the your sport and apply the different stretching techniques discussed earlier. In most 
cases, a few appropriate dynamic stretches of gradually increasing range, tension and duration using multi-jointed 
actions encountered in your sport will replace a prolonged session with dozens of single-jointed stretches.
You should always remember that the fundamental purpose of stretching is to enhance performance and 
reduce the likelihood of injury. Therefore, all stretching routines should increase not only your passive or static 
range of movement, but also your functional flcxibility-strength for all static and dynamic joint actions likely to be 
needed in your sport, including any necessary ballistic manoeuvres that seem to strike such fear into the hearts of 
the average fitness instructor.
3.7 The Movement Matrix System
The relationship between joint and muscle actions may be described conveniently by means of a series of 
Movement Matrices. There are two ways of using these matrices:
• reading off the muscles corresponding to a given joint action
• reading off the actions produced by a given muscle group
These matrices will be of special value if the reader needs to analyse or devise exercises according to the scheme of 
Chapter 8. Examples of these Movement Matrices are given in the next few pages, the only major omission being 
the matrix corresponding to actions of the wrist and fingers.
It is important to emphasize that it sometimes may be necessary to apply more than one Movement Matrix 
simultaneously, because some muscles cross more than one joint (even then, it is vital to take consider the 
complications associated with multiarticular action, as discussed in the closing section o f this chapter). 
For 
example, if we wish to devise a dynamic stretching pattern for gastrocnemius, which crosses both the knee and the 
ankle joints, we should consult Figures 3.41 and 3.42 to ascertain which matrix is more appropriate for a given 
situation (e.g. a single joint exercise) or if both matrices should be used for a multi-joint exercise.
If we wish to devise a suitable exercise for maximally training the biceps brachii, which crosses the elbow and 
shoulder joints, then we have to consult Figures 3.43 and 3.44. The matrices concerned show that the biceps flex 
both the shoulder and the elbow, so that both of these joints should be extended if the biceps are to operate from 
a starting position of full pre-stretch to an end position of full flexion.

any method being determined on an individual basis.

3.6 The Stretching Matrix System
Numerous texts have been written giving prolific illustrations of specific stretches, but it is rare to find one that 
provides a generalised system for describing all types of stretches and enabling one to create an unlimited 
repertoire of novel stretches. Such a system may readily be derived from muscle action charts if one remembers 
that the reverse o f any action to contract a given muscle group becomes a stretch fo r that same muscle group. 
The following series of tables have been constructed on this basis to enable the user to stretch any particular 
major muscle group which appears at the left of each matrix.
For example, if we refer to Figure 3.36 we can devise stretches for many of the muscles involved with motion 
of the trunk and neck.
If you wish to stretch multijidus, you must flex the trunk forwards and laterally, as well as rotate the trunk, 
then repeat the same actions to the other side of the trunk. The same actions will stretch the erector spinae and 
quadratus lumborum (which is stretched without any trunk rotation). Rectus abdominis is stretched by backward 
extension of the trunk, while psoas is stretched by extension of the trunk combined with lateral extension. Even 
though the hip flexors are sometimes referred to as the iliopsoas musclcs, iliacus does not attach to the spine or 
ribs, so it cannot move the trunk and therefore, cannot be stretched by trunk extension.
It should be pointed out that the same muscle is involved in the actions of several joints and is described by 
more than one of the matrices in this section. For instance, psoas (as part of iliopsoas) also appears in Figure 
3.39 as a flexor of the hip and consequently may be stretched by extending the hip joint and rotating it medially. 
In other words, iliacus can be stretched only by hip extension and medial rotation, whereas psoas is stretched by 
means of these same actions combined with trunk extension and lateral extension.
To examine an actual stretching manoeuvre, we may refer to the front lunge as done by a fencer. If you lean 
forward with the trunk inclined forward and almost parallel to the ground, iliacus could be maximally stretched, 
while psoas would not be fully stretched unless you extended your trunk as far back as possible, while 
simultaneously extending it laterally to the side of your leading leg. This example of stretching the iliopsoas group

similar or overlap to a certain extent.

# The Stretching Matrix: Any Stretch Is the Reverse of the Action That Contracts the Same Muscle Group

**What it is** — The authors present a generalized system, built from standard muscle
action charts, for devising a stretch for any major muscle group: "the reverse of any
action to contract a given muscle group becomes a stretch for that same muscle group." A
series of matrices (Figs 3.36-3.40, in this excerpt covering trunk/neck, upper arm,
forearm, lower extremity, and foot) list each muscle against the joint actions that stretch
it. The system requires identifying which joints a given muscle crosses before deciding how
to stretch it, since a muscle's action, and therefore its stretch, can differ depending on
which joint's chart is consulted; using only one matrix for a biarticular or multiarticular
muscle can produce a less-than-maximal stretch. The authors' worked example: psoas (as part
of iliopsoas) is stretched by hip extension and medial rotation per the lower-extremity
matrix, but as a trunk muscle it is also stretched by combined trunk extension and lateral
extension per the trunk/neck matrix; a fencer's front lunge maximally stretches iliacus
(hip extension alone) but will not maximally stretch psoas unless the trunk is also
extended and laterally flexed toward the leading leg. A second worked example: the oblique
muscles and quadratus lumborum both perform lateral trunk flexion, but only the obliques
also rotate the trunk and only quadratus lumborum extends it, so only concurrent trunk
flexion plus lateral extension maximally stretches quadratus lumborum, while flexion plus
lateral extension plus rotation is needed to maximally stretch the obliques. (PDF pp.
199-202, printed pp. 188-191, Figs 3.36-3.39.)

**Why it works** — The mechanism is definitional, not empirical: if muscle contraction
produces a given joint action, moving the joint through the opposite action necessarily
lengthens (stretches) that muscle, following directly from standard functional anatomy
rather than a cited study.

**When to apply** — Use the matrices to design a novel stretch for any muscle by first
identifying every joint and degree of freedom the muscle crosses (via multiple figures if
needed), then combining the reverse actions simultaneously rather than one at a time, to
achieve a maximal stretch. Useful for building or auditing a stretching routine's actual
target versus its intended target.

**When NOT to apply** — This is an anatomical design method, not an outcome-tested
training system; the book does not report ROM-gain or performance data from using this
matrix approach specifically. Confidence is capped at `supported` because it is a
logically-derived tool, not itself an empirical claim. Do not assume a single-joint stretch
fully stretches a muscle that crosses multiple joints; the authors are explicit this is the
main pitfall the matrices are meant to prevent.

**Example** — The book's own example: to stretch biceps brachii (which crosses both
elbow and shoulder), the elbow must be extended and the shoulder extended and abducted with
the forearm pronated simultaneously (per Figs 3.37-3.38); consulting only the forearm
matrix (elbow extension alone) would under-stretch the muscle (printed 189).

**Related** — [[framework--movement-matrix-system-for-multiarticular-exercise-selection]].

# The Stretching Matrix: Any Stretch Is the Reverse of the Action That Contracts the Same Muscle Group

**What it is** — The authors present a generalized system, built from standard muscle
action charts, for devising a stretch for any major muscle group: "the reverse of any
action to contract a given muscle group becomes a stretch for that same muscle group." A
series of matrices (Figs 3.36-3.40, in this excerpt covering trunk/neck, upper arm,
forearm, lower extremity, and foot) list each muscle against the joint actions that stretch
it. The system requires identifying which joints a given muscle crosses before deciding how
to stretch it, since a muscle's action, and therefore its stretch, can differ depending on
which joint's chart is consulted; using only one matrix for a biarticular or multiarticular
muscle can produce a less-than-maximal stretch. The authors' worked example: psoas (as part
of iliopsoas) is stretched by hip extension and medial rotation per the lower-extremity
matrix, but as a trunk muscle it is also stretched by combined trunk extension and lateral
extension per the trunk/neck matrix; a fencer's front lunge maximally stretches iliacus
(hip extension alone) but will not maximally stretch psoas unless the trunk is also
extended, "while simultaneously extending it laterally to the side of your leading leg."
The book's own lateral terms are themselves inconsistent across this passage: multifidus
and quadratus lumborum are said to be stretched by flexing the trunk "forwards and
laterally" (i.e. lateral flexion), while the oblique-vs-quadratus-lumborum discussion two
paragraphs later uses "lateral extension" of the trunk for both. This entry flags rather
than resolves that inconsistency. A second worked example: the oblique muscles and
quadratus lumborum both perform lateral flexion of the trunk, but "the obliques, unlike
quadratus lumborum, do not extend the trunk and, therefore, are not stretched by flexion of
the trunk," and quadratus lumborum does not rotate the trunk (the obliques do), so it is not
stretched by trunk rotation. Only lateral extension of the trunk stretches both, but not
maximally for either unless their other specific actions are added: quadratus lumborum
needs concurrent trunk flexion plus lateral extension; the obliques need lateral extension
plus rotation, not flexion (flexion does not stretch the obliques at all, per the quote
above). Separately, a strength-flexibility tip from the same passage: progressively
starting a squat or bench press from a somewhat deeper position and quasi-isometrically
pre-stretching the relevant muscles before the concentric phase begins can build strength
and flexibility together (printed 189). (PDF pp. 199-202, printed pp. 188-191, Figs
3.36-3.39.)

**Why it works** — The mechanism is definitional, not empirical: if muscle contraction
produces a given joint action, moving the joint through the opposite action necessarily
lengthens (stretches) that muscle, following directly from standard functional anatomy
rather than a cited study.

**When to apply** — Use the matrices to design a novel stretch for any muscle by first
identifying every joint and degree of freedom the muscle crosses (via multiple figures if
needed), then combining the reverse actions simultaneously rather than one at a time, to
achieve a maximal stretch. Useful for building or auditing a stretching routine's actual
target versus its intended target.

**When NOT to apply** — This is an anatomical design method, not an outcome-tested
training system; the book does not report ROM-gain or performance data from using this
matrix approach specifically. Confidence is capped at `supported` because it is a
logically-derived tool, not itself an empirical claim. Do not assume a single-joint stretch
fully stretches a muscle that crosses multiple joints; the authors are explicit this is the
main pitfall the matrices are meant to prevent.

**Example** — The book's own example: to stretch biceps brachii (which crosses both
elbow and shoulder), the elbow must be extended and the shoulder extended and abducted with
the forearm pronated simultaneously (per Figs 3.37-3.38); consulting only the forearm
matrix (elbow extension alone) would under-stretch the muscle (printed 189).

the warm-up is determined both by central nervous and muscular system changes. In fact, use of the term 
“warming up” is often highly misleading, because this type of pre-exercise or pre-competition activity may play 
an even more important role in preparing the nervous system for the major sporting activity which is about to 
follow. In many cases, little or no general physical “warming up” may be necessary, as is often the case in 
Olympic lifting or gymnastics, where the athletes rely primarily on the competitive exercises or variations of them 
to “warm up”. Similarly, most or all warming up is unnecessary for endurance athletes, like marathoners, simply 
because the event offers more than adequate specific warming up. Consequently, the term “warm up” should be 
replaced by a term such as “pre-activity preparation”, which may involve neural ‘priming’, actual warming up of 
physical tissues, and psychological readying.
Naturally, the special part of the warm-up preceding all types of strength work is of particular interest (see 
review by Thompson, 1958; Swegan & Jankosky, 1958; Grose, 1958; Sedgwick & Whalen, 1964).
It is known that a muscle contracts more rapidly and more intensely the higher its temperature within its safe 
physiological range (Beritov, 1947). The electrical activity of a muscle also increases with rising body temperature 
(Golenhofen & Goptert, 1958; Book & Golenhofen, 1959), and after stimulation, the period of the active state 
decreases (Hill, 1951; MacPherson & Wilkie, 1954). Increasing the temperature locally increases strength, as 
measured on a dynamometer (Robbins, 1942) and by the amount of time over which a muscle is able to maintain a 
given tension or execute a measured volume of work (Nukada, 1955). A hot shower increases isometric endurance 
(Nukada, 1955), as well as the speed of muscular contraction and endurance in cyclic work, by 7.5-9.0% 
(Assmusen & Boje, 1945; Miudo, 1946; Carlisle, 1956; DeVries, 1959).
On the other hand, cooling can decrease strength and lengthen contraction time. Muscles cooled to 18C have a 
woric capacity period that is 2-3 times shorter than normal (Tikhomirova, 1961; Fray & Smith, 1941). It is known 
that massage has no influence on endurance in cyclic exercises (Karpovich & Hale, 1956; DeVries, 1959), but 
increases the power of explosive work (Skubic & Hodgkins, 1957; Merlino, 1959).
However, maximal work capacity can be achieved only after a series of muscle contractions, the number and 
character of which are determined by the functional state of the body and the intensity of the subsequent work. 
Repetitive work as a form of warm-up increases speed of movement (Swegan & Janosky, 1958), although if this 
work is of moderate intensity, then it is not beneficial for strength production. An active warm-up which includes 
intense exercises is an effective means of successfully preparing for speed-strength exercises and explosive 
exercises, in particular (Hippie, 1956; Michacl et al, 1957; Pacheco, 1957).
Thus, it was found that women basketball players increased their jumps by 1.0-4.5 cm (Panaiotov, 1962) and 
long jumpers by up to 10 cm (Diachkov, 1961). The punching strength of boxers increased an average of 400-700 
Newtons, while their striking time decreased by 0.02-0.04 seconds. It is interesting that the rest period between 
strong, rapid punches shows no significant relationship to punching force (R = 0.40), whereas after a warm-up,

Using similar statistical methods to investigate the cause for the different rate of growth for the press, Siff and 
Medvedev have both suggested that the discrepancy possibly lies in the widespread use of anabolic substances 
since the late 1950s, in particular. It is reasonable to expect performance in the press to improve more rapidly 
than in the more technically demanding other two lifts, because the press is slower and is more dependent on 
muscle hypertrophy and relative strength. Since anabolic substances have a powerful effect on muscle growth and 
none on neuromuscular skill, they would be expected to offer greater benefits to slower or more closely quasi­
isometric lifts such as the press and the powerlifting squat, bench press and deadlift.

human strength over an extended period of time, not only to determine the trends of world performance, but also 
to plan the desired improvements for the individual.

# A Sport's Own Movements, Progressively Loaded, Can Replace a Dedicated Stretching Session

**What it is** — The authors call it "possibly the most heretical remark to make about
stretching" that dedicated stretching sessions may not even be necessary, noting many
athletes dispense entirely with special stretching or even warm-up sessions without
suffering injury in training or competition; the prescription of stretching and warm-up
or cool-down has become "a well-accepted ritual," which the authors state does not by
itself make it essential. They propose a "principle of gradual progressive stretching and
activity increase": the athlete begins each movement gently and non-ballistically under
limited static and dynamic conditions, then progressively increases range, speed,
complexity, intensity and other aspects of movement until the actual sporting movements
themselves are performed under light and eventually near-competitive conditions. In weight
training, the same principle is applied by beginning every exercise with a few preparatory
repetitions at a light load, progressively increasing the load over a few sets, and using a
narrower-than-normal grip or stance early in the progression (e.g. bench press, squat) to
reduce range/speed of movement and tissue/joint stress at the start. The authors' concluding
position: it is unnecessary to devise many highly specific individual flexibility drills
for the whole body, since this would be time-consuming and inefficient; functional
movements already used in the sport, combined with the stretching techniques discussed
earlier, can replace a prolonged session of dozens of single-joint stretches, provided the
routine still increases both passive/static ROM and functional flexibility-strength for all
static, dynamic, and necessary ballistic joint actions. (PDF pp. 203-204, printed pp.
192-193.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no controlled comparison (stretching vs. no
stretching, or dedicated-stretch vs. movement-based warm-up) for injury or performance
outcomes in this passage; the claim rests on informal observation ("many athletes dispense
entirely...without suffering injury") rather than a cited study.

**When to apply** — Where session time is limited, consider replacing a block of isolated,
single-joint stretches with a progressively loaded, sport-specific movement warm-up
(narrow-grip/stance light sets building toward working load and range), on the premise
that this can achieve the same flexibility-preparation goal more efficiently, provided full
ROM and the necessary joint actions for that sport are actually included.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence `untested`: no controlled outcome data given in this
passage.** Do not use this as a blanket argument against ever including dedicated
flexibility work; the authors' own surrounding sections (see
[[framework--four-methods-of-enhancing-rom-ranked-by-effectiveness]]) state that durable,
long-term ROM change requires a specific, regularly repeated conditioning component, which
a purely movement-based warm-up may not supply for an athlete with a genuine long-term ROM
deficit in a specific joint.

**Example** — The book's own example: beginning a bench press session with a narrower
grip and lighter load, then progressively widening/loading toward the working set, applies
this principle by using the exercise itself (rather than a separate stretch) to prepare the
shoulder joint's ROM and tissue tolerance (printed 192).

**Related** — [[framework--four-methods-of-enhancing-rom-ranked-by-effectiveness]],
[[framework--stretching-matrix-system-reverse-of-contraction-action]].

14	# A Muscle's Anatomical "Flexor/Extensor" Label Does Not Reliably Predict What It Actually Accelerates
15	
16	**What it is** — The authors report that classical functional anatomy, which labels a
17	muscle as a flexor or extensor of a joint it crosses based on the torque it produces about
18	that single joint, has been challenged by biomechanical analysis of multi-articular joint
19	actions (Zajac & Gordon, 1989). Because the body is a linked system of joints, muscles that
20	do not even span a given joint can still produce acceleration about it, and the actions of
21	individual joints do not simply superimpose linearly in a multi-joint movement (no simple
22	relationship holds between velocity, angle, and torque about a single joint in a complex
23	movement). Zajac and Gordon argue it is more accurate to say "muscle X accelerates joint A
24	into flexion" than "muscle X flexes joint A." Their worked example: soleus, an ankle-only
25	muscle usually labelled an ankle extensor, accelerates the knee (which it does not span)
26	into extension up to about twice as much as it accelerates the ankle (which it does span)
27	into extension, near upright standing posture (Fig 3.47). Separately, work derived from
28	Lombard's Paradox ("antagonist muscles can act in the same contraction mode as their
29	agonists") found the rectus femoris and hamstrings act in three different ways during
30	cycling (Andrews, 1985, 1987), since in actions like cycling and squatting the quadriceps
31	and hamstrings can both contract concentrically at the same time despite being classically
32	regarded as opposing muscles. A muscle capable of several different joint actions does not
33	necessarily perform all of them in every movement: gluteus maximus, which can extend and
34	abduct the hip, does not necessarily accelerate the hip into both simultaneously, and its
35	extensor torque may even accelerate the hip into adduction instead (Andrews, 1982, 1985;
36	Mansour & Pereira, 1987). Gastrocnemius, usually described simply as a knee flexor and
37	ankle extensor, can in fact perform three different combined actions depending on knee
38	angle (Fig 3.48): flex the knee and extend the ankle, flex the knee and flex the ankle, or
39	extend the knee and extend the ankle. (PDF pp. 210-211, printed pp. 199-200, Figs 3.47-3.48.)
40	
41	**Why it works** — The mechanism is the linked, non-linear dynamics of a multi-joint
42	skeletal system (induced-acceleration analysis, per Zajac & Gordon, 1989): because segments
43	are connected, a force applied by a muscle at one joint propagates through the chain and can
44	accelerate a joint that muscle does not cross, and the net effect at any joint depends on
45	the whole system's configuration (joint angles) at that instant, not on the muscle's
46	anatomical classification alone.
47	
48	**When to apply** — Use this to caution against selecting or excluding an exercise based
49	solely on a muscle's textbook flexor/extensor label; the authors argue, following Zajac and
50	Gordon, that it is more useful to examine muscle action in terms of synergism (how muscles
51	work together across the whole kinetic chain) than in terms of isolated agonism/antagonism
52	(Basmajian, 1978, as cited by Zajac & Gordon), since a generalized approach that reduces
53	movement to single-joint actions fails to capture that muscle action is task-dependent.
54	
55	**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is `supported`: the cited induced-acceleration analysis
56	method (Zajac & Gordon, 1989) is a well-established biomechanical modeling approach, but
57	this entry reports the book's specific worked examples (soleus/knee, gluteus
58	maximus/adduction, gastrocnemius's three actions) as given, without independently
59	re-deriving them; treat the specific numeric ratios (e.g. "twice as much") as reported by
60	the cited source rather than independently verified here. Do not use this claim to argue
61	anatomical muscle-action charts are useless; the authors use those same charts elsewhere
62	(see [[framework--movement-matrix-system-for-multiarticular-exercise-selection]]) as a
63	starting point, with this entry as the stated caveat on their limits for complex,
64	multi-joint movement.

66	**Example** — The book's own example: during a standing overhead press that used to be
67	part Olympic Weightlifting, the trunk's back-bending action is caused not only by a
68	Newton's-third-law reaction to the overhead press but also by the triceps (which crosses
69	both elbow and shoulder) accelerating the trunk backward as it extends the elbow, an effect
70	counteracted by rectus abdominis (trunk flexion) and the hip flexors (hip extension)
71	(printed 200).

18	flexion during heavy lifts from the ground can damage intervertebral discs; a competent

20	during the lift. If this active tension is overdone, the spinal ligaments become slack and
21	most of the load is instead borne by the muscles; conversely, if the muscles are

# Spinal Ligaments Share Load With the Erector Spinae During Heavy Pulls From the Ground

**What it is** — The authors state spinal ligament involvement during deadlifting or
cleans is valuable for reducing the stress placed on the erector spinae, and that spinal
flexion during heavy lifts from the ground can damage intervertebral discs; a competent
lifter actively increases erector spinae tension to diminish flattening of the lumbar spine
during the lift. If this active tension is overdone, the spinal ligaments become slack and
most of the load is instead borne by the muscles; conversely, if the muscles are
inadequately contracted, excessive stress is placed on the ligaments. The authors describe
a skilled lifter as one able to optimize the balance between spinal muscles and ligaments,
enhancing lifting efficiency and reducing injury likelihood; they state similar rhythms and
patterns of muscular and other soft-tissue involvement are essential for strength-training
efficiency and safety generally. (PDF p. 209, printed pp. 198-199.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no cited source or measured data for this specific
muscle-ligament load-sharing claim in this passage; it follows logically from the joint
stabilization sequence described elsewhere in the chapter (muscle/SEC as primary
stabilizer, ligament/PEC engaging as muscular contribution changes; see
[[framework--joint-stabilization-sequence-across-range-of-motion]]), applied here
specifically to the lumbar spine during a pull, but is not derived from a named study.

**When to apply** — Useful as a coaching frame for cueing lumbar position during heavy
deadlifts and cleans: the goal is neither maximal erector spinae tension (which the text
says can make ligaments too slack to share load appropriately) nor minimal tension
(overloading the ligaments and discs), but an actively maintained, non-flexed lumbar
position that keeps both tissues sharing the load as intended.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence `untested`: no citation or measured data given for
this specific claim in this passage.** Do not present this as an established biomechanical
finding to Athletic Medicine or in athlete-facing injury-risk communication without
independent verification; it is the authors' own technique-coaching synthesis. This entry
is about muscle-ligament load *sharing*, distinct from the moment-arm/torque-reduction
principle already in this library (see
[[principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique]]), which addresses keeping the bar
path close to the body rather than the muscle-versus-ligament balance at the lumbar spine
itself.

**Example** — Inference: a lifter who rounds the lower back on a heavy deadlift (excess
lumbar flexion, per this claim, meaning inadequately contracted erector spinae) shifts more
stress onto the spinal ligaments and discs than a lifter who maintains a neutral,
actively-braced lumbar spine throughout the pull.

**Related** — [[framework--joint-stabilization-sequence-across-range-of-motion]],
[[principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique]].
