===== PDF idx 209 (printed 198) =====
SUPERTRAINING
F ig u re  3.46 Actions of Muscles of the Trunk and Back
To identify which muscles are active during any movement, one need not necessarily use an EMG 
(electromyograph), unless the objective is accurate research. 
Instead, firm palpation with the fingers over 
appropriate surface areas of the body will provide a good working knowledge of which muscles or other tissues are 
involved. These may be checked by referring to any anatomical chart. Though skilled palpation can identify 
regions of maximum and minimum muscle tension, the more accurate degree to which each muscle group is involved 
at any given stage of a movement has to be determined by means of an EMG or a myotensiometer, which we used 
to examine the relationship between joint torque and corresponding changes in muscle tension (Siff, 1986).
This type of testing confirms that it is misleading and inaccurate to refer to muscle isolation exercises, because 
the degree of isolation (or dominant involvement) of a single muscle group depends on how large the resistance b 
(Ch 4.2.9). In general, the greater the load, the greater the overflow and the greater the involvement of other muscle 
groups. A large degree of isolation can be produced by means of electrical stimulation, by concentrated exercise 
with little or no added load, or by means of loadless training (Ch 2.2.4), but this generally develops more muscle 
hypertrophy than functional strength, since this is the main aim of'isolation' training.
Some final remarks are warranted. Lest one be tempted to consider that the muscles alone are responsible for 
all stabilisation and mobilisation, we must remember that ligaments, fascia and joint capsules play an important rok 
in passively stabilising some joints to enable the body to actively use the muscles to execute other tasks. Although 
this stabilising role is well known in preventing joint damage when loading threatens to move a joint beyond its 
active structural limits, these soft tissues also play a vital role during non-emergency situations.
For example, spinal ligament involvement during dcadlifting or cleans is invaluable for decreasing the stress <m 
the erector spinae. Spinal flexion during heavy lifts from the ground can damage the intervertebral discs, so
198

===== PDF idx 210 (printed 199) =====
SUPERTRAINING
competent lifters strive to diminish the flattening of the lumbar spine by actively concentrating on increasing 
erector spinae tension. If this is overdone, the various spinal ligaments become slack and most of the load is borne 
by the muscles. Conversely, if the muscles are inadequately contracted, then excessive stress is placed on the 
ligaments. The skilled lifter is able to optimise the required balance between the spinal muscles and ligaments, 
thereby enhancing lifting efficiency and diminishing the likelihood of injury. Similar rhythms and patterns of 
muscular and other soft tissue involvement are essential for all strength training efficiency and safety.
Limitations of Anatom ical M ovem ent Analysis
Standard anatomical textbook approaches describing the action of certain muscle groups in controlling isolated joint 
actions, such as flexion, extension and rotation, frequently are used to identify which musclcs should be trained to 
enhance performance in sport. Virtually every bodybuilding and sports training publication invokes this approach 
in describing how a given exercise or machine ‘works* a given muscle group, as do most of the clinical texts on 
muscle testing and rehabilitation.
The appropriateness of this tradition, however, recently has been questioned on the basis o f biomechanical 
analysis of multi-articular joint actions (Zajac & Gordon, 1989). This classical method of functional anatomy 
defines a given muscic, for instance, as a flexor or extensor, on the basis of the torque that it produces around a 
single joint, but the nature of the body as a linked system of many joints means that muscles which do not span 
other joints can still produce acceleration about those joints.
The anatomical approach implies that complex multi-articular movement is simply the linear superimposition 
of the actions of the individual joints which are involved in that movement. However, the mechanical systems of the 
body are nonlinear and superposition docs not apply, since there is no simple relationship between velocity, angle 
and torque about a single joint in a complex sporting movement. Besides the fact that a single muscle group can 
simultaneously perform several different stabilising and moving actions about one joint, there is also a fundamental 
difference between the dynamics of single and multiple joint movements, namely that forces on one segment can be 
caused by motion of other segments. In the case of uniarticular musclcs or even biarticular muscles (like the biceps 
or triceps), where only one of the joints is constrained to move, the standard approach is acceptable, but not if 
several joints are free to move concurrently.
Because joint acceleration and individual joint torque are linearly related, Zajac and Gordon (1989) consider it 
more accurate to rephrase a statement such as “muscle X flexes joint A” as “muscle X acts to accelerate joint A into 
flexion” Superficially, this may seem a matter of trivial semantics, but the fact that muscles certainly do act to 
accelerate all joints has profound implications for the analysis of movement. For instance, muscles which cross the 
ankle joint can extend and flex the knee joint much more than they do the ankle.
Biomechanical analysis reveals that multi articular muscles may even accelerate a spanned joint in a direction 
opposite to that of the joint to which it is applying torque.
In the apparently simple action of standing, soleus, usually labelled as an extensor of the ankle, accelerates the 
knee (which it does not span) into extension (Fig 3.47) twice as much as it acts to accelerate the ankle (which it 
spans) into extension for positions near upright posture (Zajac & Gordon, 1989).
Ftjure 3.47 Effect of soleus on the angular acceleration o f the knee relative to the ankle (based on Zajac & Gordon, 1989).
199

===== PDF idx 211 (printed 200) =====
SUPERTRAINING
In work derived from Lombard’s Paradox (‘Antagonist muscles can act in the same contraction mode as their] 
agonists’), Andrews (1985, 1987) found that the rectus femoris of the quadriceps and all the hamstrings act in three] 
different ways during cycling, emphasizing that biarticular muscles are considered enigmatic. 
This paradosl 
originally became apparent when it was noticed that in actions such as cycling and squatting, extension of the knee 
and the hip occurs simultaneously, so that the quadriceps and hamstrings are both operating concentrically at the 
same time. Theoretically, according to the concept of concurrent musclc antagonism, the hamstrings should contract 
eccentrically while the quadriceps are contracting concentrically, and vice versa, since they are regarded as opposing 
muscles.
Others have shown that a muscle which is capable o f carrying out several different joint actions, does no( 
necessarily do so in every movement (Andrews, 1982, 1985). For instance, gluteus maximus, which can extend and 
abduct the hip, will not necessarily accelerate the hip simultaneously into extension and abduction, but its extensor 
torque may even accelerate the hip into adduction (Mansour & Pereira, 1987).
Gastrocnemius, which is generally recognised as a flexor of the knee and an extensor of the ankle, actually can cany 
out the following complex tasks (see Fig 3.48):
(a) flex the knee and extend the ankle
(b) flex the knee and flex the ankle
(c) extend the knee and extend the ankle
Figure 3.48 The three possible actions of gastrocnemius revealed by the relative moment-arm ratios of the knee and ankle joints (based 
on Zajac & Gordon, 1989).
During the standing press, which used to be part of Olympic Weightlifting, the back bending action of the trunk is 
due not only to a Newton 111 reaction to the overhead pressing action, but also due to acceleration caused by the 
thrusting backwards of the triceps muscle which crosses the shoulder joint, as well as the elbow joint. This same 
action of the triceps also occurs during several gymnastic moves on the parallel, horizontal and uneven bars. This 
back extending action of the triceps is counteracted by the expected trunk flexing action of rectus abdominis and the 
hip extension action of the hip flexors, accompanied by acceleration of the trunk by the hip flexors.
Appreciation of this frequently ignored type of action by many niultiarticular muscles enables us to select and 
use resistance training exercises far more effectively to meet an athlete's specific sporting needs and to offer 
superior rehabilitation of the injured athlete.
Because of this multiplicity of actions associated with multiarticular complex movement, Zajac and Gordon 
stress a point made by Basmajian (1978), namely that it may be more useful to examine muscle action in terms of 
synergism rather than agonism and antagonism. This is especially important, since a generalised approach to 
understanding human movement on the basis of breaking down all movement into a series of single joint actions fails 
to take into account that muscle action is task dependent.
200

===== PDF idx 212 (printed 201) =====
SUPERTRAINING
THE MEANS OF SPECIAL 
STRENGTH TRAINING
Opinion concerning the means and methods of strength training often repeats itself, with the beginning of the 
modem era identifying more clearly the motor mechanisms of sports technique. This has helped to determine the 
means of strength training more precisely. However, with the improvement in sporting achievements, the effect 
of these means became less marked. The volume of the same exercises was increased, but it was found that this 
approach also has its limitations (Verkhoshansky, 1977). Once again, researchers turned to analysis o f sports 
movements, now equipped with better measuring technology.
This new cycle of research initiated further progress in training methodology. This was the case, for example, 
when information regarding the significance of strength in sport emerged from the laboratory and coaches looked 
optimistically to weight training. The next trend was towards specificity, since studies indicated that the strength 
necessary for the successful execution of one movement has little effect on another movement. Naturally, this

# A Muscle's Anatomical "Flexor/Extensor" Label Does Not Reliably Predict What It Actually Accelerates

**What it is** — The authors report that classical functional anatomy, which labels a
muscle as a flexor or extensor of a joint it crosses based on the torque it produces about
that single joint, has been challenged by biomechanical analysis of multi-articular joint
actions (Zajac & Gordon, 1989). Because the body is a linked system of joints, muscles that
do not even span a given joint can still produce acceleration about it, and the actions of
individual joints do not simply superimpose linearly in a multi-joint movement (no simple
relationship holds between velocity, angle, and torque about a single joint in a complex
movement). Zajac and Gordon argue it is more accurate to say "muscle X accelerates joint A
into flexion" than "muscle X flexes joint A." Their worked example: soleus, an ankle-only
muscle usually labelled an ankle extensor, accelerates the knee (which it does not span)
into extension up to about twice as much as it accelerates the ankle (which it does span)
into extension, near upright standing posture (Fig 3.47). Separately, work derived from
Lombard's Paradox ("antagonist muscles can act in the same contraction mode as their
agonists") found the rectus femoris and hamstrings act in three different ways during
cycling (Andrews, 1985, 1987), since in actions like cycling and squatting the quadriceps
and hamstrings can both contract concentrically at the same time despite being classically
regarded as opposing muscles. A muscle capable of several different joint actions does not
necessarily perform all of them in every movement: gluteus maximus, which can extend and
abduct the hip, does not necessarily accelerate the hip into both simultaneously, and its
extensor torque may even accelerate the hip into adduction instead (Andrews, 1982, 1985;
Mansour & Pereira, 1987). Gastrocnemius, usually described simply as a knee flexor and
ankle extensor, can in fact perform three different combined actions depending on knee
angle (Fig 3.48): flex the knee and extend the ankle, flex the knee and flex the ankle, or
extend the knee and extend the ankle. (PDF pp. 210-211, printed pp. 199-200, Figs 3.47-3.48.)

**Why it works** — The mechanism is the linked, non-linear dynamics of a multi-joint
skeletal system (induced-acceleration analysis, per Zajac & Gordon, 1989): because segments
are connected, a force applied by a muscle at one joint propagates through the chain and can
accelerate a joint that muscle does not cross, and the net effect at any joint depends on
the whole system's configuration (joint angles) at that instant, not on the muscle's
anatomical classification alone.

**When to apply** — Use this to caution against selecting or excluding an exercise based
solely on a muscle's textbook flexor/extensor label; the authors argue, following Zajac and
Gordon, that it is more useful to examine muscle action in terms of synergism (how muscles
work together across the whole kinetic chain) than in terms of isolated agonism/antagonism
(Basmajian, 1978, as cited by Zajac & Gordon), since a generalized approach that reduces
movement to single-joint actions fails to capture that muscle action is task-dependent.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is `supported`: the cited induced-acceleration analysis
method (Zajac & Gordon, 1989) is a well-established biomechanical modeling approach, but
this entry reports the book's specific worked examples (soleus/knee, gluteus
maximus/adduction, gastrocnemius's three actions) as given, without independently
re-deriving them; treat the specific numeric ratios (e.g. "twice as much") as reported by
the cited source rather than independently verified here. Do not use this claim to argue
anatomical muscle-action charts are useless; the authors use those same charts elsewhere
(see [[framework--movement-matrix-system-for-multiarticular-exercise-selection]]) as a
starting point, with this entry as the stated caveat on their limits for complex,
multi-joint movement.

**Example** — The book's own example: during a standing overhead press that used to be
part Olympic Weightlifting, the trunk's back-bending action is caused not only by a
Newton's-third-law reaction to the overhead press but also by the triceps (which crosses
both elbow and shoulder) accelerating the trunk backward as it extends the elbow, an effect
counteracted by rectus abdominis (trunk flexion) and the hip flexors (hip extension)
(printed 200).

**Related** — [[framework--movement-matrix-system-for-multiarticular-exercise-selection]],
[[heuristic--identify-moved-stabilized-and-both-joints-before-selecting-exercises]].

# A Muscle's Anatomical "Flexor/Extensor" Label Does Not Reliably Predict What It Actually Accelerates

**What it is** — The authors report that classical functional anatomy, which labels a
muscle as a flexor or extensor of a joint it crosses based on the torque it produces about
that single joint, has been challenged by biomechanical analysis of multi-articular joint
actions (Zajac & Gordon, 1989). Because the body is a linked system of joints, muscles that
do not even span a given joint can still produce acceleration about it, and the actions of
individual joints do not simply superimpose linearly in a multi-joint movement (no simple
relationship holds between velocity, angle, and torque about a single joint in a complex
movement). Zajac and Gordon argue it is more accurate to say "muscle X accelerates joint A
into flexion" than "muscle X flexes joint A." Their worked example: soleus, an ankle-only
muscle usually labelled an ankle extensor, accelerates the knee (which it does not span)
into extension up to about twice as much as it accelerates the ankle (which it does span)
into extension, near upright standing posture (Fig 3.47). Separately, work derived from
Lombard's Paradox ("antagonist muscles can act in the same contraction mode as their
agonists") found the rectus femoris and hamstrings act in three different ways during
cycling (Andrews, 1985, 1987), since in actions like cycling and squatting the quadriceps
and hamstrings can both contract concentrically at the same time despite being classically
regarded as opposing muscles. A muscle capable of several different joint actions does not
necessarily perform all of them in every movement: gluteus maximus, which can extend and
abduct the hip, does not necessarily accelerate the hip into both simultaneously, and its
extensor torque may even accelerate the hip into adduction instead (Andrews, 1982, 1985;
Mansour & Pereira, 1987). Gastrocnemius, usually described simply as a knee flexor and
ankle extensor, can in fact perform three different combined actions depending on knee
angle (Fig 3.48): flex the knee and extend the ankle, flex the knee and flex the ankle, or
extend the knee and extend the ankle. (PDF pp. 210-211, printed pp. 199-200, Figs 3.47-3.48.)

**Why it works** — The mechanism is the linked, non-linear dynamics of a multi-joint
skeletal system (induced-acceleration analysis, per Zajac & Gordon, 1989): because segments
are connected, a force applied by a muscle at one joint propagates through the chain and can
accelerate a joint that muscle does not cross, and the net effect at any joint depends on
the whole system's configuration (joint angles) at that instant, not on the muscle's
anatomical classification alone.

**When to apply** — Use this to caution against selecting or excluding an exercise based
solely on a muscle's textbook flexor/extensor label; the authors argue, following Zajac and
Gordon, that it is more useful to examine muscle action in terms of synergism (how muscles
work together across the whole kinetic chain) than in terms of isolated agonism/antagonism
(Basmajian, 1978, as cited by Zajac & Gordon), since a generalized approach that reduces
movement to single-joint actions fails to capture that muscle action is task-dependent.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is `supported`: the cited induced-acceleration analysis
method (Zajac & Gordon, 1989) is a well-established biomechanical modeling approach, but
this entry reports the book's specific worked examples (soleus/knee, gluteus
maximus/adduction, gastrocnemius's three actions) as given, without independently
re-deriving them; treat the specific numeric ratios (e.g. "twice as much") as reported by
the cited source rather than independently verified here. Do not use this claim to argue
anatomical muscle-action charts are useless; the authors use those same charts elsewhere
(see [[framework--movement-matrix-system-for-multiarticular-exercise-selection]]) as a
starting point, with this entry as the stated caveat on their limits for complex,
multi-joint movement.

**Example** — The book's own example: during a standing overhead press that used to be
part Olympic Weightlifting, the trunk's back-bending action is caused not only by a
Newton's-third-law reaction to the overhead press but also by the triceps (which crosses
both elbow and shoulder) accelerating the trunk backward as it extends the elbow, an effect
counteracted by rectus abdominis (trunk flexion) and the hip flexors (hip extension)
(printed 200).

**Related** — [[framework--movement-matrix-system-for-multiarticular-exercise-selection]],
[[heuristic--identify-moved-stabilized-and-both-joints-before-selecting-exercises]].

**What it is** — The authors state spinal ligament involvement during deadlifting or
cleans is valuable for reducing the stress placed on the erector spinae, and that spinal
flexion during heavy lifts from the ground can damage intervertebral discs; a competent
lifter actively increases erector spinae tension to diminish flattening of the lumbar spine
during the lift. If this active tension is overdone, the spinal ligaments become slack and
most of the load is instead borne by the muscles; conversely, if the muscles are
inadequately contracted, excessive stress is placed on the ligaments. The authors describe
a skilled lifter as one able to optimize the balance between spinal muscles and ligaments,
enhancing lifting efficiency and reducing injury likelihood; they state similar rhythms and
patterns of muscular and other soft-tissue involvement are essential for strength-training
efficiency and safety generally. (PDF p. 209, printed pp. 198-199.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no cited source or measured data for this specific
muscle-ligament load-sharing claim in this passage; it follows logically from the joint
stabilization sequence described elsewhere in the chapter (muscle/SEC as primary
stabilizer, ligament/PEC engaging as muscular contribution changes; see
[[framework--joint-stabilization-sequence-across-range-of-motion]]), applied here
specifically to the lumbar spine during a pull, but is not derived from a named study.

**When to apply** — Useful as a coaching frame for cueing lumbar position during heavy
deadlifts and cleans: the goal is neither maximal erector spinae tension (which the text
says can make ligaments too slack to share load appropriately) nor minimal tension
(overloading the ligaments and discs), but an actively maintained, non-flexed lumbar
position that keeps both tissues sharing the load as intended.

# The Movement Matrix System: Reading Off Muscles From a Joint Action, or Actions From a Muscle

**What it is** — The authors present a companion series of Movement Matrices (Figs 3.41-3.46
in this excerpt: lower extremity, foot, shoulder, arm/humerus, forearm, trunk and neck) that
can be read two ways: to find the muscles corresponding to a given joint action, or to find
the actions produced by a given muscle group. The authors state these are needed whenever a
reader wants to analyse or devise exercises, and that it is often necessary to apply more
than one Movement Matrix simultaneously, because some muscles cross more than one joint.
Their worked examples: gastrocnemius crosses both the knee and ankle, so Figs 3.41 and 3.42
(lower extremity, foot) must both be consulted to determine whether a single-joint or a
combined multi-joint exercise is more appropriate for a given goal; biceps brachii crosses
the elbow and shoulder, so maximal training of biceps requires extending both joints from a
position of full pre-stretch to full flexion at the end position (Figs 3.43-3.44). This
dual-joint action of gastrocnemius (knee flexion plus ankle plantarflexion together) occurs
naturally during the double-knee-bend (scoop) phase of the weightlifting clean, or in
"glute-ham-gastroc raises," a modified prone hyperextension over a pommel horse with the
feet pressed against a vertical plate (Yessis, 1992). (PDF pp. 204-208, printed pp. 193-197,
Figs 3.41-3.46.)

**Why it works** — As with the Stretching Matrix, this is a definitional reading of
standard functional-anatomy relationships (which muscles produce which joint actions), not
an empirical finding with its own separate mechanism.

**When to apply** — Use the paired-matrix approach when selecting or designing an exercise
for a multiarticular muscle: check every matrix the target muscle appears in before
concluding a single-joint exercise trains it fully, and consider whether a combined,
multi-joint version (like the clean's double-knee bend, for gastrocnemius) better matches
the muscle's natural dual action than an isolated single-joint exercise would.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a reference and design tool built from standard anatomical
muscle-action data, not a validated training-outcome comparison between single-joint and
multi-joint exercise selection; the book does not report performance or hypertrophy data
comparing the two approaches here. See also
[[claim--multiarticular-muscle-action-cannot-be-predicted-from-joints-spanned]] for the
authors' own caution that even this matrix approach is an incomplete model of real
multiarticular muscle function.

**Example** — The book's own example: because gastrocnemius flexes the knee and
plantarflexes the ankle, the glute-ham-gastroc raise (a modified prone hyperextension with
feet braced) trains both actions together, unlike a standing calf raise (ankle only) or a
leg curl (knee only) performed in isolation (printed 193).

**Related** — [[framework--stretching-matrix-system-reverse-of-contraction-action]],
[[heuristic--identify-moved-stabilized-and-both-joints-before-selecting-exercises]].

# The Movement Matrix System: Reading Off Muscles From a Joint Action, or Actions From a Muscle

**What it is** — The authors present a companion series of Movement Matrices (Figs 3.41-3.46
in this excerpt: lower extremity, foot, shoulder, arm/humerus, forearm, trunk and neck) that
can be read two ways: to find the muscles corresponding to a given joint action, or to find
the actions produced by a given muscle group. The authors state these are needed whenever a
reader wants to analyse or devise exercises, and that it is often necessary to apply more
than one Movement Matrix simultaneously, because some muscles cross more than one joint.
Their worked examples: gastrocnemius crosses both the knee and ankle, so Figs 3.41 and 3.42
(lower extremity, foot) must both be consulted to determine whether a single-joint or a
combined multi-joint exercise is more appropriate for a given goal; biceps brachii crosses
the elbow and shoulder, so maximal training of biceps requires extending both joints from a
position of full pre-stretch to full flexion at the end position (Figs 3.43-3.44). This
dual-joint action of gastrocnemius (knee flexion plus ankle plantarflexion together) occurs
naturally during the double-knee-bend (scoop) phase of the weightlifting clean, or in
"glute-ham-gastroc raises," a modified prone hyperextension over a pommel horse with the
feet pressed against a vertical plate (Yessis, 1992). (PDF pp. 204-208, printed pp. 193-197,
Figs 3.41-3.46.)

**Why it works** — As with the Stretching Matrix, this is a definitional reading of
standard functional-anatomy relationships (which muscles produce which joint actions), not
an empirical finding with its own separate mechanism.

**When to apply** — Use the paired-matrix approach when selecting or designing an exercise
for a multiarticular muscle: check every matrix the target muscle appears in before
concluding a single-joint exercise trains it fully, and consider whether a combined,
multi-joint version (like the clean's double-knee bend, for gastrocnemius) better matches
the muscle's natural dual action than an isolated single-joint exercise would.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a reference and design tool built from standard anatomical
muscle-action data, not a validated training-outcome comparison between single-joint and
multi-joint exercise selection; the book does not report performance or hypertrophy data
comparing the two approaches here. See also
[[claim--multiarticular-muscle-action-cannot-be-predicted-from-joints-spanned]] for the
authors' own caution that even this matrix approach is an incomplete model of real
multiarticular muscle function.

**Example** — The book's own example: because gastrocnemius flexes the knee and
plantarflexes the ankle, the glute-ham-gastroc raise (a modified prone hyperextension with
feet braced) trains both actions together, unlike a standing calf raise (ankle only) or a
leg curl (knee only) performed in isolation (printed 193).

**Related** — [[framework--stretching-matrix-system-reverse-of-contraction-action]],
[[heuristic--identify-moved-stabilized-and-both-joints-before-selecting-exercises]].

silence may persist in muscles being passively stretched "irrespective of whether this is
done slowly or rapidly" (Basmajian, 1978, printed 177-178), and the book itself defends
graded, progressive ballistic (fast) stretching elsewhere as safe and effective (printed
186). Slow entry is a preference the book states elsewhere, not a physiological requirement
this reflex framework itself proves.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry covers the basic reflex arcs only; it does not by
itself justify any specific stretching protocol, duration, or frequency. **`proven` applies
to:** spindles sensing muscle length and rate of length change via Ia and II afferents; the
stretch reflex having phasic (dynamic) and tonic (static) components; GTOs sensing tendon
tension; gamma motor neurons setting spindle sensitivity. **Not proven:** the Guyton
bag/chain assignment given above (bag fibres = dynamic response, chain fibres = static
response, secondaries "almost entirely" on chain fibres); modern physiology instead splits
bag1 (dynamic) and bag2 (static) fibres, with secondaries also supplying bag2 (Inference,
verify, e.g. Proske 1997 or Macefield & Knellwolf 2018). Also not proven: the static reflex

input.old_string:
bag/chain assignment given above (bag fibres = dynamic response, chain fibres = static
response, secondaries "almost entirely" on chain fibres); modern physiology instead splits
bag1 (dynamic) and bag2 (static) fibres, with secondaries also supplying bag2 (Inference,
verify, e.g. Proske 1997 or Macefield & Knellwolf 2018). Also not proven: the static reflex
operating "for periods up to several hours" (Guyton's textbook claim, no data given in this
source); and the GTO's "inverse stretch reflex" as a relaxing, protective reflex, since Ib
inhibition is reported to weaken or reverse during active contraction and does not explain
PNF gains (Inference, verify, e.g. Chalmers 2004, Sports Biomech 3:159; Sharman, Cresswell &
Riek 2006, Sports Med 36:929).
input.new_string:
bag/chain assignment given above (bag fibres = dynamic response, chain fibres = static
response, secondaries "almost entirely" on chain fibres). Inference: modern physiology is
reported to use a different bag1/bag2/chain scheme instead, not independently confirmed
against a specific source in this ingest. Also not proven: the static reflex operating "for

# The Muscle Spindle, Golgi Tendon Organ, and the Stretch Reflex Family

**What it is** — Joint flexibility is shaped not only by tissue structure and mechanical
properties but by the degree of motor unit activity in the relevant muscles: muscle
contraction raises muscle tension, which counteracts stretching. Two receptor types govern
this: muscle spindles (Fig 3.32), which detect changes in muscle fibre length and rate of
length change, and Golgi tendon organs (GTOs), which monitor tension in the muscle tendon
during contraction or stretching. The spindle produces the "stretch reflex" (contraction in
response to lengthening); the GTO produces the "inverse stretch reflex" (relaxing a
contracting muscle if its tension becomes excessive). Spindles contain 3-10 intrafusal
fibres of two types (nuclear bag and nuclear chain), innervated by primary (large type Ia)
and secondary (smaller type II) sensory receptors; primary receptors innervate both fibre
types and are held responsible for the strong dynamic response, while nuclear chain fibres
(innervated by both receptor types) are held responsible for the static response. Gamma
efferent fibres split similarly into gamma-dynamic (exciting bag fibres, powerful dynamic
response) and gamma-static (exciting chain fibres, persistent static response) (Guyton,
1984). The full stretch reflex (myotatic reflex, Fig 3.33) comprises a dynamic (phasic)
reflex (strong but brief contraction on sudden length change), a static (tonic) reflex
(weaker but sustained for up to several hours while tension persists), and a negative
stretch reflex (inhibitory relaxation when a muscle is suddenly shortened, opposing
shortening the way the myotatic reflex opposes lengthening). GTO firing shows the same
dynamic/static split: an intense initial (dynamic) response to sudden tension change,
settling to a lower steady-state (static) response proportional to tension; the book
reports Matthews (1973) as having moved the GTO from a purely protective role to a
continuous tension monitor, described in the book as the "inverse stretch reflex," a
relaxing, protective reflex. Repeated reflex production, like voluntary effort, fatigues:
reflex tension diminishes with repeated stimulation, and "rebound" (a second reflex of the
same type becoming progressively harder to elicit for a time after the first) is named as a
likely contributor to cyclic activities such as locomotion, swimming and cycling (Guyton,
1984). (PDF pp. 187-190, printed pp. 176-179, Figs 3.32-3.33.)

**Why it works** — This is established, independent-of-text mammalian neurophysiology for
the core mechanisms only (see the `proven` scope in When NOT); the book's own extensions
(the Guyton bag/chain scheme, the several-hours static reflex, the GTO framed as a
protective relaxation reflex, rebound's role in specific cyclic sports) are less
established.

**When to apply** — Inference: a fast, sudden stretch evokes a stronger dynamic stretch
reflex response than a slow one, so pacing a stretch's entry speed changes how much
reflex resistance is provoked at the moment of the stretch. This is weaker than a flat rule
that slow entry lets the muscle relax: the source also reports that electromyographic
silence may persist in muscles being passively stretched "irrespective of whether this is
done slowly or rapidly" (Basmajian, 1978, printed 177-178), and the book itself defends
graded, progressive ballistic (fast) stretching elsewhere as safe and effective (printed
186). Slow entry is a preference the book states elsewhere, not a physiological requirement
this reflex framework itself proves.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry covers the basic reflex arcs only; it does not by
itself justify any specific stretching protocol, duration, or frequency. **`proven` applies
to:** spindles sensing muscle length and rate of length change via Ia and II afferents; the
stretch reflex having phasic (dynamic) and tonic (static) components; GTOs sensing tendon
tension; gamma motor neurons setting spindle sensitivity. **Not proven:** the Guyton
bag/chain assignment given above (bag fibres = dynamic response, chain fibres = static
response, secondaries "almost entirely" on chain fibres); modern physiology instead splits
bag1 (dynamic) and bag2 (static) fibres, with secondaries also supplying bag2 (Inference,
verify, e.g. Proske 1997 or Macefield & Knellwolf 2018). Also not proven: the static reflex
operating "for periods up to several hours" (Guyton's textbook claim, no data given in this
source); and the GTO's "inverse stretch reflex" as a relaxing, protective reflex, since Ib
inhibition is reported to weaken or reverse during active contraction and does not explain
PNF gains (Inference, verify, e.g. Chalmers 2004, Sports Biomech 3:159; Sharman, Cresswell &
Riek 2006, Sports Med 36:929).

**Example** — The book's own example: many "plyometric drills" are performed too slowly to
elicit the powerful dynamic spindle response essential for speed-strength development,
because the dynamic response requires a rapid rate of length change, not just any
stretch-shorten action (printed 177).

**Related** — [[heuristic--reflex-based-techniques-for-flexibility-training]],
[[framework--joint-stabilization-sequence-across-range-of-motion]].

# Breath-Holding (Valsalva) Stabilises the Spine Under Heavy Load; Exhaling Through Effort Is the Authors' Named Risk, Except for Cardiac or Hypertensive Athletes

**What it is** — The authors state that breathing pattern, duration, and rate have a
profound effect on strength production. The Valsalva manoeuvre, breath-holding, plays a
vital role in raising intra-abdominal pressure to support and stabilise the lumbar spine
during heavy lifting, with the abdominal and oblique muscles acting as an anatomical
corset. Spinal stress is diminished during high-resistance-loaded movement against
resistance when breath is held, and exhalation during lifting increases the risk of lumbar
injury; the authors call it unwise to follow the popular medical advice to exhale during
effort during strenuous lifting, squatting, or overhead pressing, though they name that
advice as appropriate specifically for patients with cardiac disease or hypertension.
Common sporting actions, jumping, throwing, pushing against an opponent, striking a ball,
standing up from a squat, kicking, elicit involuntary breath-holding because it enhances
performance and control accuracy in short-duration movements; archery and pistol shooting
stability and accuracy are tied to brief breath-holding phases; other cited research found
speed-strength actions are optimally enhanced when lung air volume is held at about 75% of
maximum capacity (Vorobyev, 1978). The spinal-stress and exhalation-injury-risk claim above
is presented as fact: "it has been corroborated on many occasions," with no citation given
in the book (printed 172). A study of 34 qualified weightlifters (Blokhin &
Monastirskii, 1985) recorded bar movement and breathing (spirometry) during the clean and
jerk at 60-90% of 1RM and identified three breathing-phase variants (A, B, C) across the
pull, rack, and jerk. All lifters held their breath during the pull and during the jerk in
every variant; when breathing did occur at other phases, the text states exhalation volume
always exceeded inhalation volume by at least 125 ml. The study's own reported means
contradict this at the rack (bar-on-chest) phase: inhalation 1620±280 ml vs exhalation
1454±301 ml, inhalation larger. The overhead-fixation pair fits the stated rule (exhalation
1263±192 ml vs inhalation 1138±239 ml, a 125 ml difference). Both as printed; not resolved
by the authors (printed 172). Variant B was judged optimal for maximal effort;
variant A occurs when the athlete makes technical corrections mid-lift; variant C is
characteristic of submaximal lifts. Recommendation: breath-holding should precede and
accompany maximal efforts, followed by brief exhalation-inhalation unless a technical
correction is needed, in which case breath-holding should persist; submaximal loads can use
longer normal-breathing phases and shorter breath-holding phases; neither rapid short
hyperventilation nor a forced maximal inhalation is desirable during maximal-effort lifting.
(PDF pp. 183-184, printed pp. 172-173, "3.4.9 Breathing and Strength Production," Fig 3.31.)

**Why it works** — The authors give the mechanism directly: breath-holding raises
intra-abdominal pressure, and the abdominal and oblique muscles use that pressure as an
anatomical corset to support and stabilise the lumbar spine, reducing spinal stress under
high-resistance loading. Inference: this is broadly consistent with the modern
strength-training convention of Valsalva or bracing during heavy compound lifts, though
this entry does not independently verify that separate literature.

**When to apply** — Inference: cue breath-holding through the concentric drive of a heavy
compound lift (squat, deadlift, overhead press), with a brief exhale-inhale at or near
lockout rather than exhaling through the sticking point, for healthy athletes lifting near
maximal loads. For submaximal work, normal breathing between reps is acceptable, with
breath-holding reserved for the effort phase itself; the book gives no specific cue
language, only the breathing-phase recommendation quoted above.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors themselves name the exception: athletes with cardiac
disease or hypertension should follow the standard medical advice to exhale during effort,
not hold their breath. Inference: this is presumably because Valsalva raises intrathoracic
and blood pressure (e.g. MacDougall et al. 1985, J Appl Physiol 58:785, verify), but the
source does not state this mechanism itself, or give any guidance on how long a breath hold
is safe; it addresses spinal stability and performance, not cardiovascular risk management.
The 34-lifter breathing-phase study is specific to the snatch/clean-and-jerk pull-rack-jerk
sequence at 60-90% of 1RM; it is not validated for sustained isometric holds, high-rep
sets, or other lift patterns.

**Example** — Inference: cue a lifter to inhale to roughly the described optimal range,
hold through the pull off the floor and the drive through the sticking point of a heavy
deadlift or squat, then exhale briefly at lockout before the next rep, rather than exhaling
on the way up.

**Related** — None found in the staging library or vault on breathing pattern and lifting
technique specifically; flagged for a reciprocal link if a future entry addresses
intra-abdominal pressure or bracing directly.

# The Bone-Tendon Junction Has a Graded Stiffness Transition That Anabolic Steroids Can Disrupt

**What it is** — The authors state the stress concentration at the insertion of a ligament
or tendon into more rigid bone is decreased by the existence of three progressively
stiffer transitional composite materials, a system which "can be disrupted by ingestion of
anabolic steroids." They add, separately, that elastic fibres occur in small concentrations
in the intercellular matrix of tendons and most ligaments, and may help restore the crimped
collagen fibre configuration after stretching or muscle contraction. (PDF p. 192, printed
p. 181.)

A different, cited steroid-collagen statement appears nearby: "alteration in hormonal
balance during pregnancy, menstruation and administration of exogenous hormones (such as
anabolic steroids and cortisone) can affect the mechanical characteristics of collagenous
tissue, so that stretching techniques should be adjusted accordingly" (Viidik, 1973, printed
183). This is the book's only cited steroid-collagen line; it is a separate claim (general
mechanical-property change, not specifically the bone-tendon transitional-stiffness
gradient) from the uncited claim above.

**Why it works** — The authors give no citation or further mechanism for either statement
in this passage (no source is named for the transitional-material system or the steroid
disruption claim); it is presented as an assertion, not a derived or referenced finding
here.

**When to apply** — Inference: useful only as background when discussing anabolic steroid

# Ordinary Stretching Increases ROM by Raising Stretch Tolerance, Not by Changing Muscle Viscoelastic Properties

**What it is** — The authors state: "Static and cyclic stretching, as commonly performed
by athletes (up to 90 seconds duration each), increases joint range of motion by
increasing stretch tolerance while the viscoelastic characteristics of the muscle remain
unaltered" (printed as "Magnussen et al, 1998"; likely Magnusson SP, 1998, a review in
Scand J Med Sci Sports 8:65-77, verify). (PDF p. 192, printed p. 181.)

G5, internal tension not recorded elsewhere, spanning four pages the authors do not
reconcile: printed 179 (PDF 190) frames pre-event stretching as producing "short-term
(elastic)" tissue change; printed 180 (PDF 191) says warmth improves "plastic deformation"
of collagenous tissue and that cooling with ice "seems to stabilise connective tissues at
their new length" (Sapega et al., 1981); printed 181 (this section) says static stretching
"has a more pronounced effect on the PEC" than ballistic, and that "prolonged slow
stretching can cause permanent viscous deformation of connective tissue"; printed 176 says
tendons and ligaments "can be permanently deformed or damaged by over-zealous or prolonged
stretching." All four describe some form of tissue-level change from stretching, which sits
against this section's own claim that viscoelastic properties "remain unaltered." Ch1
[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]] (printed 41-42) says static
stretching mainly loads the PEC, consistent with this section's PEC/SEC distinction but not
with "unaltered."

**Why it works** — The authors give no further mechanism for why stretch tolerance itself
increases; the citation (Magnusson et al., 1998) is offered as the source of the finding,
not explained here. Inference: "stretch tolerance" implies the limiting factor in a typical
short-duration static/cyclic stretch is the point at which the nervous system perceives the
stretch as uncomfortable, a perceptual/sensory account, not the muscle-tendon unit's actual
length-tension (stiffness) properties, which this citation reports as unchanged. A separate,
weaker inference sometimes offered in the literature is a reflex-protective threshold
account (verify, e.g. Weppler & Magnusson 2010, Phys Ther 90:438); the book does not raise
this, and it is a distinct claim from sensory tolerance, not interchangeable with it.

**When to apply** — Inference: use this to set an accurate expectation for a single
stretching session or short block: an acute or short-term ROM gain from static/cyclic
stretching in this duration range should be read as increased tolerance to the sensation of
stretch, not as evidence the muscle-tendon unit itself has become mechanically more
compliant. The book's own separate claim that brief pre-training stretching mainly produces
short-term flexibility change (see
[[framework--four-methods-of-enhancing-rom-ranked-by-effectiveness]]) describes that
short-term change as elastic tissue change, not as a sensory-tolerance effect; the two
accounts are not the same mechanism, and the book does not connect them.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not extend this specific claim (static/cyclic stretching, up to
90 seconds per stretch) to other stretching modes (ballistic, PNF, long-duration static
holds well beyond 90 seconds) without separate evidence; the book does not state this
mechanism applies to those. Do not use "stretch tolerance increased, tissue unchanged" to
argue stretching has no tissue-level benefit at all: this entry describes the mechanism of
short-duration ROM gain specifically, not the long-term soft-tissue adaptations covered
elsewhere (see [[claim--ligament-tendon-adaptation-and-detraining-response]]).

**Example** — Inference: an athlete who gains 5 degrees of hip flexion after a single
90-second hamstring stretch has very likely become more tolerant of that stretch sensation
in that session, not changed the mechanical stiffness of the hamstring muscle-tendon unit;
retesting the next day without further stretching would be expected to show the gain has
mostly reverted.

**Related** — [[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]],
[[claim--stretching-benefits-list-from-older-literature-review]].

# What Each Soft Tissue Contributes to Joint Stiffness, and Short- vs Long-Term Stretch Change

**What it is** — With stretch reflex mechanisms minimally involved and muscles relaxed
(rarely the case during dynamic functional movement), the relative contribution of soft
tissues to joint stiffness is given as (Johns & Wright, 1962): muscles and their fascial
sheaths 41%, structures of the joint capsule including ligaments 35%, skin 11%, tendons and
their sheaths 10%. As printed these sum to 97%, not 100%. The figure often cited for Johns &
Wright (1962, J Appl Physiol 17:824) elsewhere is different (capsule 47%, muscle 41%, tendon
10%, skin 2%, verify); this book's 35% and 11% values may be misprints of that source, or a
different breakdown; not resolved here. Inference: the original study is usually described
as cat wrist-joint data (verify); the book gives no species. Since nothing can be done to
alter joint structure itself, appropriate stretching must target these soft tissues to
increase flexibility, and stretching can produce short-term (elastic), long-term (plastic),
or combined short/long-term changes in tissue characteristics. The authors state the
average pre-event or pre-training warm-up stretching session mainly targets short-term
flexibility, and that this distinction is often insufficiently emphasized: changing
long-term flexibility requires a specific, regularly repeated conditioning component built
into the overall training programme, not just brief preparatory sessions. (PDF p. 190,
printed p. 179.)

G5, internal tension not recorded elsewhere: this section frames pre-event stretching as
producing "short-term (elastic)" tissue change, while a later section (3.5.6, Magnusson,
citation printed "Magnussen et al, 1998") attributes static/cyclic-stretching ROM gains to
increased stretch tolerance with viscoelastic tissue properties reported "unaltered"
(printed 181; see
[[claim--static-cyclic-stretching-increases-rom-via-stretch-tolerance-not-tissue-change]]).
The book does not reconcile "short-term elastic tissue change" here with "unaltered tissue
properties" there.

**Why it works** — The percentage breakdown is the authors' cited figure (Johns & Wright,
1962) with no further mechanism given. Inference: the elastic-vs-plastic distinction
follows directly from standard viscoelastic tissue behavior (elastic deformation recovers,
plastic deformation persists); the book treats this as background rather than deriving it
here.

**When to apply** — Use the percentage breakdown to set expectations: muscle/fascia is the

against the parallel text extraction, which matched. Vault grep confirmed: no Chalmers,
Sharman, Lauersen, Herbert & Gabriel, Proske, Macefield, MacDougall, Weppler, Saraceni,
Benjamin, or Johns & Wright material exists in `SecondBrain/Knowledge/library`; every one of
those citations was therefore left uninserted (bare "Inference:" language, no citation

de Noronha & Kamper 2011 (Cochrane CD004577.pub3) was independently re-verified (identifiers
and wording match the review) and kept with full citation, per instruction.

- `claim--irradiation-effect-raises-prime-mover-force-and-endurance.md` | Heavy rewrite. Split the Mukhammedova (1958, qualitative, no percentages) and Popov (1938, the 39-42%/8-22% figures and the post-fatigue extensor/flexor result) findings, which the entry had merged and misattributed; fixed "flexors" to "extensors" in the post-fatigue sentence; removed the false "without prior right-arm fatigue" qualifier from the 8-22% figure; added the 25% vertical-jump amortisation figure; added a **When to apply** section (was missing, G3); extended the locator to PDF 177-178/printed 166-167.

1. **"Isolation" is load-dependent** (printed 198/PDF 209). "The greater the load, the greater the overflow and the greater the involvement of other muscle groups"; isolation by electrical stimulation, low load, or loadless training develops more hypertrophy than functional strength; palpation vs. EMG/myotensiometer (Siff 1986). Ties the irradiation entry (3.4.3) to exercise selection (3.7).
2. **Overtraining is not an energy sum** (printed 170/PDF 181). Overload vs. overuse types; a few-maximal-attempts workout may cause overload-type overtraining more readily than a longer, moderate-weight workout; overload may come more from stress-raising technique than from load itself; actual work is 5-12 min of a 1.5-2.5 h session. 3. **The other reflexes** (printed 178-179/PDF 189-190). Crossed extensor reflex (0.2-0.5s delay, relevant to unilateral dumbbell work); reciprocal inhibition; rebound (repeated maximal acyclic efforts harder, cyclic easier); local muscle spasm as a "physiological splint."

- Johns & Wright "usually cited" values (capsule 47%/muscle 41%/tendon 10%/skin 2%) and the "cat wrist joint" species claim: not inserted. Unconfirmed in vault; recorded only that the book's own printed figures (41/35/11/10) sum to 97%.
- Chalmers 2004, Sharman 2006 (GTO/Ib-inhibition counter-evidence in the stretch-reflex entry), Proske 1997/Macefield & Knellwolf (bag1/bag2 scheme), MacDougall et al. 1985 (Valsalva blood-pressure mechanism), Weppler & Magnusson 2010 (reflex-protective-threshold account), Benjamin et al. 2006 (fibrocartilaginous entheses anatomy), Saraceni et al. 2020 (flexion-injury premise, spinal-ligaments entry): none inserted as named citations. All unconfirmed in vault; each point is stated as a bare, uncited Inference instead.
- `eccentric-quasi-isometrics` and `identify-moved-stabilized` (both GO): the review's optional additions (a supporting quote and a Moyer Related link; the "isolation is load-dependent" point) were not applied, since these entries were GO-verdict and the review marked the additions optional.
- Missing ideas 1-5 from the review (see below): not added as new entries, per instruction to list rather than atomize them.

## Missing ideas (not added as entries, per instruction)

1. **"Isolation" is load-dependent** (printed 198/PDF 209). "The greater the load, the greater the overflow and the greater the involvement of other muscle groups"; isolation by electrical stimulation, low load, or loadless training develops more hypertrophy than functional strength; palpation vs. EMG/myotensiometer (Siff 1986). Ties the irradiation entry (3.4.3) to exercise selection (3.7).
2. **Overtraining is not an energy sum** (printed 170/PDF 181). Overload vs. overuse types; a few-maximal-attempts workout may cause overload-type overtraining more readily than a longer, moderate-weight workout; overload may come more from stress-raising technique than from load itself; actual work is 5-12 min of a 1.5-2.5 h session. (Partially folded into the exercise-economy entry's When NOT; not made its own entry.)
3. **The other reflexes** (printed 178-179/PDF 189-190). Crossed extensor reflex (0.2-0.5s delay, relevant to unilateral dumbbell work); reciprocal inhibition; rebound (repeated maximal acyclic efforts harder, cyclic easier); local muscle spasm as a "physiological splint."
4. **Multi-directional and rotational stretching** (printed 181, 186/PDF 192, 197). Collagen fibre orientation differs by tissue; "very few rotational stretches about the longitudinal axes of the limbs are ever used"; PNF spiral-diagonal patterns give superior 3D functional ROM. Plus printed 175 (PDF 186): ROM in one direction depends on concurrent movement in another, so single-plane lab ROM measures may be equivocal.
5. **Hormonal state and stretching** (printed 183/PDF 194). Pregnancy, menstruation, exogenous hormones (steroids, cortisone) change collagen mechanics, "so that stretching techniques should be adjusted accordingly" (Viidik, 1973). Partially folded into the steroid entry and the ligament-adaptation entry (both now cite this Viidik line), but not made its own entry.

- Dupuy 2018, Carvalho 2012, Chatzopoulos 2014, Collings 2026 (vault research-papers) could each add a reciprocal link back to the relevant Supertraining entry above.

- G5 lists eight internal contradictions in the global findings section; the task text asked for "each of the six internal contradictions." All eight were recorded (Table 3.10 vs printed 168 narrative; breathing volumes vs "exhalation always exceeded" statement; Iashvili vs Tumanyan on static/passive stretching and active flexibility; stretch tolerance "unaltered" vs elastic/plastic tissue change (four-page spread); stretching benefits/warm-up-injury claims vs the printed-192 "many athletes dispense entirely... without injury" line; Fig 3.34 separating ballistic from PNF vs the text's PNF-subset claim; triceps text vs its own Figs 3.37 and 3.44; "prior stretching decreases isometric force" vs the force-enhancement finding in the cited paper). # The Muscle Spindle, Golgi Tendon Organ, and the Stretch Reflex Family

**What it is** — Joint flexibility is shaped not only by tissue structure and mechanical
properties but by the degree of motor unit activity in the relevant muscles: muscle
contraction raises muscle tension, which counteracts stretching. Two receptor types govern
this: muscle spindles (Fig 3.32), which detect changes in muscle fibre length and rate of
length change, and Golgi tendon organs (GTOs), which monitor tension in the muscle tendon
during contraction or stretching. The spindle produces the "stretch reflex" (contraction in
response to lengthening); the GTO produces the "inverse stretch reflex" (relaxing a
contracting muscle if its tension becomes excessive). Spindles contain 3-10 intrafusal
fibres of two types (nuclear bag and nuclear chain), innervated by primary (large type Ia)
and secondary (smaller type II) sensory receptors; primary receptors innervate both fibre
types and are held responsible for the strong dynamic response, while nuclear chain fibres
(innervated by both receptor types) are held responsible for the static response. Gamma
efferent fibres split similarly into gamma-dynamic (exciting bag fibres, powerful dynamic
response) and gamma-static (exciting chain fibres, persistent static response) (Guyton,
1984). The full stretch reflex (myotatic reflex, Fig 3.33) comprises a dynamic (phasic)
reflex (strong but brief contraction on sudden length change), a static (tonic) reflex
(weaker but sustained for up to several hours while tension persists), and a negative
stretch reflex (inhibitory relaxation when a muscle is suddenly shortened, opposing
shortening the way the myotatic reflex opposes lengthening). GTO firing shows the same
dynamic/static split: an intense initial (dynamic) response to sudden tension change,
settling to a lower steady-state (static) response proportional to tension; the book
reports Matthews (1973) as having moved the GTO from a purely protective role to a
continuous tension monitor, described in the book as the "inverse stretch reflex," a
relaxing, protective reflex. Repeated reflex production, like voluntary effort, fatigues:
reflex tension diminishes with repeated stimulation, and "rebound" (a second reflex of the
same type becoming progressively harder to elicit for a time after the first) is named as a
likely contributor to cyclic activities such as locomotion, swimming and cycling (Guyton,
1984). (PDF pp. 187-190, printed pp. 176-179, Figs 3.32-3.33.)

**Why it works** — This is established, independent-of-text mammalian neurophysiology for
the core mechanisms only (see the `proven` scope in When NOT); the book's own extensions
(the Guyton bag/chain scheme, the several-hours static reflex, the GTO framed as a
protective relaxation reflex, rebound's role in specific cyclic sports) are less
established.

**When to apply** — Inference: a fast, sudden stretch evokes a stronger dynamic stretch
reflex response than a slow one, so pacing a stretch's entry speed changes how much
reflex resistance is provoked at the moment of the stretch. This is weaker than a flat rule
that slow entry lets the muscle relax: the source also reports that electromyographic
silence may persist in muscles being passively stretched "irrespective of whether this is
done slowly or rapidly" (Basmajian, 1978, printed 177-178), and the book itself defends
graded, progressive ballistic (fast) stretching elsewhere as safe and effective (printed
186). Slow entry is a preference the book states elsewhere, not a physiological requirement
this reflex framework itself proves.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry covers the basic reflex arcs only; it does not by
itself justify any specific stretching protocol, duration, or frequency. **`proven` applies
to:** spindles sensing muscle length and rate of length change via Ia and II afferents; the
stretch reflex having phasic (dynamic) and tonic (static) components; GTOs sensing tendon
tension; gamma motor neurons setting spindle sensitivity. **Not proven:** the Guyton
bag/chain assignment given above (bag fibres = dynamic response, chain fibres = static
response, secondaries "almost entirely" on chain fibres). Inference: modern physiology is
reported to use a different bag1/bag2/chain scheme instead, not independently confirmed
against a specific source in this ingest. Also not proven: the static reflex operating "for
periods up to several hours" (Guyton's textbook claim, no data given in this source); and
the GTO's "inverse stretch reflex" as a relaxing, protective reflex. Inference: Ib
inhibition is reported elsewhere in the literature to weaken or reverse during active
contraction, which would mean it does not explain PNF gains as the book implies; not
independently confirmed against a specific source in this ingest.

**Example** — The book's own example: many "plyometric drills" are performed too slowly to
elicit the powerful dynamic spindle response essential for speed-strength development,
because the dynamic response requires a rapid rate of length change, not just any
stretch-shorten action (printed 177).

**Related** — [[heuristic--reflex-based-techniques-for-flexibility-training]],
[[framework--joint-stabilization-sequence-across-range-of-motion]].

1984). (PDF pp. 187-190, printed pp. 176-179, Figs 3.32-3.33.)

**Why it works** — This is established, independent-of-text mammalian neurophysiology for
the core mechanisms only (see the `proven` scope in When NOT); the book's own extensions
(the Guyton bag/chain scheme, the several-hours static reflex, the GTO framed as a
protective relaxation reflex, rebound's role in specific cyclic sports) are less
established.

**When to apply** — Inference: a fast, sudden stretch evokes a stronger dynamic stretch
reflex response than a slow one, so pacing a stretch's entry speed changes how much
reflex resistance is provoked at the moment of the stretch. This is weaker than a flat rule
that slow entry lets the muscle relax: the source also reports that electromyographic
silence may persist in muscles being passively stretched "irrespective of whether this is
done slowly or rapidly" (Basmajian, 1978, printed 177-178), and the book itself defends
graded, progressive ballistic (fast) stretching elsewhere as safe and effective (printed
186). Slow entry is a preference the book states elsewhere, not a physiological requirement
this reflex framework itself proves.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry covers the basic reflex arcs only; it does not by
itself justify any specific stretching protocol, duration, or frequency. **`proven` applies
to:** spindles sensing muscle length and rate of length change via Ia and II afferents; the
stretch reflex having phasic (dynamic) and tonic (static) components; GTOs sensing tendon
tension; gamma motor neurons setting spindle sensitivity. **Not proven:** the Guyton
bag/chain assignment given above (bag fibres = dynamic response, chain fibres = static
response, secondaries "almost entirely" on chain fibres). Inference: modern physiology is
reported to use a different bag1/bag2/chain scheme instead, not independently confirmed
against a specific source in this ingest. Also not proven: the static reflex operating "for
periods up to several hours" (Guyton's textbook claim, no data given in this source); and
the GTO's "inverse stretch reflex" as a relaxing, protective reflex. Inference: Ib
inhibition is reported elsewhere in the literature to weaken or reverse during active
contraction, which would mean it does not explain PNF gains as the book implies; not
independently confirmed against a specific source in this ingest.

**Example** — The book's own example: many "plyometric drills" are performed too slowly to
elicit the powerful dynamic spindle response essential for speed-strength development,
because the dynamic response requires a rapid rate of length change, not just any
stretch-shorten action (printed 177).

**Related** — [[heuristic--reflex-based-techniques-for-flexibility-training]],
[[framework--joint-stabilization-sequence-across-range-of-motion]].
